    Canto 10 (Part 1)

    B – Birth (1-5) Canto Ten details the name, fame, form, qualities and beautiful pastimes of Sri Krishna. His birth, and the events surrounding it, were completely transcendental, as was His entire life on earth. The Lord is unborn, but appears in our vision and later disappears – just like the sun which rises and sets at certain junctures, but remains ever present, always illuminating some place within the cosmos. Note: The pastimes of Canto Ten are not in chronological order. Based on the statements of various scriptures, acaryas have presented different opinions on the sequence of these transcendental events.

    Baby Krishna’s Appearance

    Canto 10 (Part 1)

    B – Birth (1-5) Baby Krishna’s Appearance Chapter 3 At the most auspicious moment, in an atmosphere surcharged with goodness, peace and beauty, Sri Krishna, in His four-handed form, appeared in the prison house, causing great wonder to Vasudeva and Devaki. They offered choice prayers and beseeched the Lord to conceal His four-handed form and appear as an ordinary child. Though overjoyed, they were simultaneously anxious about Kamsa’s next move. The Lord glorified Vasudeva and Devaki, explaining that He had been their son in two previous lives. Krishna then transformed into His original human form. By divine arrangement, Vasudeva mystically escaped the prison and travelled to Gokula, where he exchanged Krishna with the daughter born of Yasoda (Yogamaya). He then returned to the prison house with his ‘newborn daughter.’

    Previous Balarama Transferred and Garbha-Stuti Next Kamsa’s Frustration Last updated 1 year ago

    Balarama Transferred and Garbha-Stuti

    Canto 10 (Part 1)

    B – Birth (1-5) Balarama Transferred and Garbha-Stuti Chapter 2 After the tragic death of the first six children, the seventh child was mystically transported from the womb of Devaki to the womb of Rohini, who was blessed with a beautiful son named Balarama. Yogamaya (Krishna’s internal energy), who arranged this, was ordered to take birth from Mother Yasoda, the wife of Nanda Maharaja who was living in Gokula (Vrindavana). Now the Supreme Lord was ready to appear. He entered the womb of Devaki through the heart of Vasudeva, at which point she became extremely effulgent. Sensing a divine descent, all the demigods spontaneously gathered to offer prayers of gratitude to the Lord in the womb ( garbha-stuti ). Kamsa, suspecting a providential conspiracy, became increasingly fearful, so much so that he couldn’t stop thinking about Krishna.

    Kamsa’s Frustration

    Canto 10 (Part 1)

    B – Birth (1-5) Kamsa’s Frustration Chapter 4 When Kamsa heard about the birth he rushed in and picked up the baby girl to kill her. Just then, she slipped out of his hands, appeared as the eight-armed goddess Durga, and informed him that Krishna had already taken birth elsewhere. His plans thwarted, Kamsa apologised to Vasudeva and Devaki, and set them free. Ironically, he even spoke eloquent philosophy to comfort them amidst such tragic events. Vasudeva and Devaki patiently listened, and were so saintly that they held no grudge whatsoever, ready and willing to forgive the evil King despite his atrocities. Unfortunately, Kamsa’s heart hadn’t changed. After being incited by his devious ministers, he enlisted the help of various demons to kill all the children born in the recent past, and thus began a fresh campaign of cruelty. While on their rampage, nobody was spared, and even the demigods, saintly persons, cows and brahmanas were violently persecuted.

    Krishna’s Birth

    Canto 10 (Part 1)

    B – Birth (1-5) Krishna’s Birth “The Supreme Personality of Godhead chooses a mother and father from whom to take birth again and again. The Lord took birth originally from Sutapa and Prisni, then from Kasyapa and Aditi, and again from the same father and mother, Vasudeva and Devaki. “In other appearances also,” the Lord said, “I took the form of an ordinary child just to become your son so that we could reciprocate eternal love.” Jiva Goswami has explained this verse in his Krishna- sandarbha, Ninety-sixth Chapter, where he notes that in text 37 the Lord says, amuna vapusa , meaning “by this same form.” In other words, the Lord told Devaki, “This time I have appeared in My original form as Sri Krishna.”” (SB 10.3.43) Over a 24-hour period, the sun passes over all the continents of the earth. When it passes over a particular geographical location we perceive the great orb rising and setting - it seems to come and go. The sun, however, is constantly shining and ever-present. Only from our perspective does it appear to rise and set. Similarly, from the human perspective, Krishna seems to take birth and then die. His pastimes, however, are being eternally enacted ( nitya-lila ) – in the spiritual world, somewhere in the material world, and ultimately in the hearts of His devotees who constantly remember Him. Over the expanse of universal time, Krishna passes over a multitude of material universes. Though beginningless, causeless and the source of everything, Krishna seemingly takes birth in this world and performs beautiful pastimes. The details of when Krishna was born, therefore, are not as important as the details of why He appears. He Himself explains the reason for His descent in the Bhagavad-gita: “Whenever and wherever there is a decline in religious practice, O descendant of Bharata, and a predominant rise of irreligion – at that time I descend Myself.” ( BG 4.7 ). Krishna further explains the benefits of hearing about, discussing and deeply understanding His birth in this world: “One who knows the transcendental nature of My appearance and activities does not, upon leaving the body, take his birth again in this material world, but attains My eternal abode, O Arjuna.” ( BG 4.9 ) When Lord Sri Krishna desired to appear in this world, He first entered the heart of Vasudeva, and from there He passed to the pure heart of Devaki. Nursed by her intense maternal affection, Sri Krishna purified the womb of Devaki. Then, on the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhadra, on Wednesday, while the moon was in the constellation of Rohini, in the depth of night, the Lord appeared in His four-armed form, holding the conch, disc, club and lotus, adorned with crest, pendant and other ornaments, wearing a great profusion of curls and clad in yellow robes. The Lord’s advent was truly unique. Although the events surrounding Krishna’s birth seem tragic and unfortunate, such occurrences are not the consequences of material karma. These are the special arrangements of the Lord to add a touch of transcendental drama to the delicious sweetness of His pastimes. Indeed, our teachers explain that just as diamonds are set upon a dark background to enhance their shine, the Lord’s pastimes are often set upon the dark background of the material world to further highlight their beauty and excellence.

    An Interesting Detail

    Canto 10 (Part 1)

    B – Birth (1-5) Krishna’s Birth An Interesting Detail Our general understanding, as the Srimad-Bhagavatam narrates, is that Krishna was born as the son of Vasudeva and Devaki in the prison house of Kamsa, after which He was secretly transported to Gokula where He was swapped with the daughter of Nanda and Yasoda. Krishna then remained in Gokula and performed many wonderful pastimes with His ‘foster’ parents. Our acaryas , however, offer an esoteric nuance and ‘inside story’ to Krishna’s birth. They explain that though there are many forms of Krishna, the original and most complete is that of Krishna in Vrindavana. This form of Krishna is known as Nandanandana, Krishna who is the son of Nanda Maharaja, and He never, at any time, leaves Vrindavana. Even though it would superficially seem so, Krishna, the son of Nanda Maharaja, never takes one step out of of that enchanting land ( vrindavanam parityajya sa kvacin naiva gacchati ). Even when He seems to leave, He remains in Vrindavana in an unmanifested state. Thus, according to acaryas like Visvanatha Chakravarti Thakura, Yasoda had actually given birth to twins; a boy and a girl. The boy was Krishna in His original form, and when Vasudeva arrived with his baby, an expansion of Krishna (Vasudeva), the expansion merged into Krishna’s original form, the son of Yasoda. Later, Vasudeva returned to Kamsa’s cell in Mathura with the baby girl, as the traditional story reveals.

    Krishna Appearing in Our Life

    Canto 10 (Part 1)

    B – Birth (1-5) Krishna’s Birth Krishna Appearing in Our Life As Krishna appeared in the land of Vrindavana, we pray that Krishna will appear in our lives. A closer study of these first five chapters reveals the devotional spirit which preceded Krishna’s appearance. It is this spirit we must seek to imbibe. 1. Desperation When Mother Bhumi saw no other means to mitigate the world’s problems, she became desperate. In that mood of desperation, she, along with the demigods, pleaded for help. Offering prayers at the milk ocean, they beseeched the Lord to descend to the world. Similarly, until we actually feel an acute desperation for Krishna’s presence in our life, He will not appear. Krishna remains remote but responsive, never forcing Himself into anyone’s life, but fully available when the soul is willing and desirous. A person once asked Socrates how to deepen their spirituality. In response, he took them to a nearby lake and dunked them in the water. After a few minutes he lifted them out as they gasped for air. He asked the person: “What were you thinking of whilst underwater?” The man replied that all he could think about was getting a gasp of air. Socrates then answered him: “When your desperation for God becomes as acute, He will immediately appear before you.” Do we have that desperation? 2. Dedication When Krishna appears in this world, He contemplates who His parents will be. Prisni and Sutapa had performed 12,000 years of extreme austerities, ardently praying that the Lord become their son. To fulfil their desire, Sutapa appeared as Vasudeva, Prisni appeared as Devaki, and the Lord happily agreed to become their son. Desperation for the Lord is exhibited in one’s dedication and commitment to spiritual practices. In this age, the recommended austerity is to engage in the sankirtana-yajna , and any intelligent person who dedicates themselves to this process can quickly attract the Lord’s attention. Do we have the dedication? 3. Purification Having chosen to appear within Devaki’s womb, the Lord proceeded to make the appropriate transcendental arrangements. Before He appeared, six of Devaki’s children were mercilessly slaughtered by the evil Kamsa. The acaryas explain that Devaki’s womb represents bhakti . The six children were actually the six sons of Marici, who represent lust, anger, greed, illusion, madness and envy. Kamsa represents material fear. Thus, when a devotee becomes fearful of material life, that fear kills the six unhelpful enemies and one’s bhakti becomes pure. At that time, Krishna takes birth. Thus, when our spiritual practices are purified, devoid of any material motivation, they quickly invoke Krishna’s presence and reciprocation. Do we have that purity? 4. Meditation When Krishna entered Devaki’s womb, all the demigods, Vasudeva, Devaki, and even Kamsa, were naturally drawn to Him. They couldn’t think about anything else. Krishna became their sole meditation. In the same way, the devotee’s mind, purified by devotional service, will become naturally drawn towards Krishna. Rupa Goswami, in a famous prayer, says: “Just as the minds of young girls are attracted to young boys, and just as the minds of young boys are attracted to young girls, allow my mind to be as naturally drawn towards you.” Queen Kunti also prays: “O Lord of Madhu, as the Ganges forever flows to the sea without hindrance, let my attraction be constantly drawn unto You without being diverted to anyone else.” 5. Revelation When Krishna appeared in the world at midnight, He exhibited His four-armed form with full regalia. At the request of His parents, He then transformed to His original two-armed form. Seeing the desperation, dedication, purification and meditation that His dear devotees embodied, by His own sweet will He finally gave them the revelation. That is the true way to contact God. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakura famously commented: “Don’t try and see God, but act in such a way that God will want to see you.”

    Nanda and Vasudeva Meet

    Canto 10 (Part 1)

    B – Birth (1-5) Nanda and Vasudeva Meet Chapter 5 In Vrindavana, there was a grand festival for baby Krishna’s birth. The town was beautifully decorated, the inhabitants brought wonderful gifts and Nanda Maharaja generously offered charity to the entire community. As per custom, Nanda Maharaja dutifully went to Mathura to pay his taxes to Kamsa. There he met Vasudeva, who enquired about the well-being of the two transcendental boys. Nanda described the jubilation and happiness in Vrindavana, but expressed his sincere sympathy for the tragic events that Vasudeva and Devaki had to go through. Foreseeing more disturbances from Kamsa, Vasudeva advised Nanda to return home immediately and remain vigilant.

    Preparation

    Canto 10 (Part 1)

    B – Birth (1-5) Preparation Chapter 1 Maharaja Pariksit requested Sukadeva Goswami to elaborate on the pastimes of Lord Krishna from beginning to end. Such descriptions, the King said, are the right medicine to overcome the disease of materialistic life. Sukadeva Goswami began by narrating the events leading up to the Lord’s appearance. The overburdened earth was being abused and exploited by demoniac kings. Bhumi (Mother Earth) took the form of a cow, and, along with Brahma, Siva and other demigods, went to the milk ocean and petitioned the Lord to descend. In trance, Brahma heard the reply of Ksirodakasayi Vishnu, who was well aware of their plight. To prepare the ground, He requested all the demigods to first appear in the Yadu dynasty. Thereafter, the Lord would also appear, along with His internal potency.

    The Omen

    Canto 10 (Part 1)

    B – Birth (1-5) The Omen Chapter 1 Sukadeva Goswami began the narration at the point where Vasudeva and Devaki were being driven home after their wedding ceremony. While happily steering the chariot, Kamsa, Devaki’s brother, suddenly heard an unembodied voice proclaiming that his sister’s eighth son would kill him! Shocked and bewildered, Kamsa instinctively caught hold of his sister and set about to kill her. Through philosophical reasoning and diplomatic manoeuvering, Vasudeva managed to pacify Kamsa. He convinced the ruthless demon to spare Devaki and instead take each newborn child and kill it. True to his word, Vasudeva dutifully delivered the first six children of Devaki, all of whom Kamsa mercilessly killed. Interestingly, Kamsa was actually prepared to spare those children, but Narada Muni encouraged him to kill them – the sage was expertly accelerating the appearance of the Lord.

    Important Words
    • kathitaḥ — has already been described
      Past passive participle of kath, 'to tell.' Parīkṣit acknowledges receipt before asking for more — the disciplic posture: I have heard, and because I have heard, I am qualified to ask the next question. Śravaṇam earns the right to praśna.
    • vaṁśa-vistāraḥ — broad description of the dynasties
      Vaṁśa = lineage, succession; vistāra = elaboration, spread. The Bhāgavatam does not abridge — it spreads out the family tree of dharma because Kṛṣṇa enters human history through a specific vaṁśa, not as an abstract principle.
    • soma-sūryayoḥ — of the moon-god and the sun-god
      Genitive dual. The two great royal lines (Candra-vaṁśa, Sūrya-vaṁśa) into which Bhagavān's avatāras appear — Rāma in the Sūrya line, Kṛṣṇa in the Candra (Yadu) line. The verse situates Kṛṣṇa's appearance in real, transmissible history, not myth.
    • caritam — the character, conduct
      From car, 'to move, act.' Carita is what someone did — biography rather than philosophy. The Bhāgavatam's evidence for Kṛṣṇa is not argument but caritam: His own and His devotees' deeds, witnessed and transmitted.
    • parama-adbhutam — supremely wonderful
      Parama (highest) + adbhuta (astonishing) — beyond the ordinarily astonishing. Parīkṣit applies this to the kings already heard, signaling that what is coming (Kṛṣṇa-līlā) must be more wonderful still. Adbhuta-rasa here functions as a doorway to the higher rasas the Tenth Canto will open.
    King Parīkṣit said: My dear lord, you have elaborately described the dynasties of both the moon-god and the sun-god, with the exalted and wonderful character of their kings.
    Purport

    At the end of the Ninth Canto, Twenty-fourth Chapter, Śukadeva Gosvāmī summarized the activities of Kṛṣṇa. He spoke of how Kṛṣṇa had personally appeared to reduce the burden on the earth, how He had manifested His pastimes as a householder, and how, soon after His birth, He had transferred Himself to His Vrajabhūmi-līlā. Parīkṣit Mahārāja, being naturally a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, wanted to hear more about Lord Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, to encourage Śukadeva Gosvāmī to continue speaking about Kṛṣṇa and give further details, he thanked Śukadeva Gosvāmī for having described the activities of Kṛṣṇa in brief. Śukadeva Gosvāmī had said: jāto gataḥ pitṛ-gṛhād vrajam edhitārtho hatvā ripūn suta-śatāni kṛtorudāraḥ utpādya teṣu puruṣaḥ kratubhiḥ samīje ātmānam ātma-nigamaṁ prathayañ janeṣu “The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, known as līlā-puruṣottama, appeared as the son of Vasudeva but immediately left His father’s home and went to Vṛndāvana to expand His loving relationships with His confidential devotees. In Vṛndāvana the Lord killed many demons, and afterward He returned to Dvārakā, where according to Vedic principles He married many wives who were the best of women, begot through them hundreds of sons, and performed sacrifices for His own worship to establish the principles of householder life.” ( Bhāg. 9.24.66 ) The Yadu dynasty belonged to the family descending from Soma, the moon-god. Although the planetary systems are so arranged that the sun comes first, before the moon, Parīkṣit Mahārāja gave more respect to the dynasty of the moon-god, the soma-vaṁśa, because in the Yādava dynasty, descending from the moon, Kṛṣṇa had appeared. There are two different kṣatriya families of the royal order, one descending from the king of the moon planet and the other descending from the king of the sun. When the Supreme Personality of Godhead appears, He generally appears in a kṣatriya family because He comes to establish religious principles and the life of righteousness. According to the Vedic system, the kṣatriya family is the protector of the human race. When the Supreme Personality of Godhead appeared as Lord Rāmacandra, He appeared in the sūrya-vaṁśa, the family descending from the sun-god, and when He appeared as Lord Kṛṣṇa, He did so in the Yadu dynasty, or yadu-vaṁśa, whose descent was from the moon-god. In the Ninth Canto, Twenty-fourth Chapter, of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, there is a long list of the kings of the yadu-vaṁśa. All the kings in both the soma-vaṁśa and sūrya-vaṁśa were great and powerful, and Mahārāja Parīkṣit praised them very highly ( rājñāṁ cobhaya-vaṁśyānāṁ caritaṁ paramādbhutam ). Nonetheless, he wanted to hear more about the soma-vaṁśa because that was the dynasty in which Kṛṣṇa had appeared. The supreme abode of the Personality of Godhead, Kṛṣṇa, is described in Brahma-saṁhitā as the abode of cintāmaṇi: cintāmaṇi-prakara-sadmasu kalpa-vṛkṣa-lakṣāvṛteṣu surabhīr abhipālayantam. The Vṛndāvana-dhāma on this earth is a replica of that same abode. As stated in Bhagavad-gītā (8.20) , in the spiritual sky there is another, eternal nature, transcendental to manifested and unmanifested matter. The manifested world can be seen in the form of many stars and planets such as the sun and moon, but beyond this is the unmanifested, which is imperceptible to those who are embodied. And beyond this unmanifested matter is the spiritual kingdom, which is described in Bhagavad-gītā as supreme and eternal. That kingdom is never annihilated. Although material nature is subject to repeated creation and annihilation, that spiritual nature remains as it is eternally. In the Tenth Canto of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, that spiritual nature, the spiritual world, is described as Vṛndāvana, Goloka Vṛndāvana or Vraja-dhāma. The elaborate description of the above-mentioned śloka from the Ninth Canto — jāto gataḥ pitṛ-gṛhād ( Bhāg. 9.24.66 ) — will be found here, in the Tenth Canto.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    King Parīkṣit said: My dear lord, you have elaborately described the dynasties of both the moon-god and the sun-god, with the exalted and wonderful character of their kings.
    Commentary

    In order to increase the speaker’s enthusiasm to speak about the most crucial topics, Pariksit praises the previous descriptions in the Bhagavatam. Because candra is the grandson of Brahma, because candra is his amsa, because he is the deity of the mind, and because Krsna appeared in that dynasty, candra is mentioned before surya, though the usual order would place surya first. Though the wonderful activities of Svayambhuva and his dynasty were related in the fourth canto, they did not culminate in sweetness. With Krsna of the moon dynasty and Rama of the sun dynasty, sweetness was finally attained. Thus, discussions of these dynasties became very prominent.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    I surrender to Madana-gopāla, Govinda, king of Vṛndāvana, who is anxious to give mercy to the wretched. I offer respects to the Supreme Lord, Kṛṣṇa-caitanya, the ocean of mercy, who appeared in Bengal to spread prema-bhakti. I offer respects to Mādhava-purī along with his disciples. By him the desire tree of Kṛṣṇa bhakti was sown among the people. I offer respects to Śrīdhara Svāmī, the sole protector of bhakti, who gave a systematic commentary for the purpose of perfecting bhakti. I offer respects to Sārvabhauma Vidyāvacaspati Bhaṭṭācārya, ornamented with all knowledge and who was the ornament of Bengal. The word śrī is added to rāja to indicate the great prema of Parīkṣit at the beginning of recitation of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes. It is conjugated as śrī-rājaḥ rather than śrī-rājā (as above) optionally. The King makes this request to inspire Śukadeva and give him joy by showing eagerness to hear in detail the stories about Kṛṣṇa, the root of all stories. You have related the dynasties, in detail, listing the sons and grandsons, not with the sole intention of telling about the births and lives of those individuals. He uses bhavatā (by you) to show respect. He places the word “moon” before “sun” to indicate the importance of Kṛṣṇa’s dynasty. You have also related the heroic deeds of the members of both dynasties. There were most astonishing deeds: for instance the marriage of Purūravā to Urvaśī and Puraṣjaya with his Indravāha pastimes. Though you related the exploits of the dynasty of Svāyambhūva Manu and others starting in the Third Canto, the exploits of the sun and moon dynasties are most astonishing, for in those dynasties have appeared Rāmacandra and Kṛṣṇa.

    Personal Guidance
    Hearing about Kṛṣṇa's appearance and activities is not optional storytelling — it is the doorway out of repeated birth and death.
    Practical Applications
    • Open the Tenth Canto today and read even one paragraph, treating the act of hearing as direct service to Kṛṣṇa.
    • When tempted to scroll news or entertainment, substitute fifteen minutes of Bhāgavatam hearing in its place.
    • Ask one specific question about Kṛṣṇa's appearance to a senior devotee or sādhu this week, modeling Parīkṣit's eager inquiry.
    Reflection Questions
    • When I hear about Kṛṣṇa's appearance in the Yadu dynasty, do I treat it as ancient history or as a confidential subject I am personally meant to penetrate — and what specifically have I done this week to penetrate it?
    • Parīkṣit calls the kings' character paramādbhutam — supremely wonderful — and then asks for more about Kṛṣṇa Himself. Where in my own hearing am I content to stop at 'wonderful stories' instead of pressing forward into the Personality whom those stories exist to reveal?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Parīkṣit was 60 and had seven days; you may have 60 years and an open calendar. That is not an advantage if those years go to scrolling, optimizing your résumé, and waiting for life to 'really start.' Pick one hour this week — same hour, same place — and read SB 10.1 aloud. Treat it as the meeting you would not cancel for an internship interview.
    • In your friend group, Kṛṣṇa's 'appearance in the Yadu dynasty' will sound either embarrassingly literal or quaintly cultural. You will be tempted to translate Him into a metaphor to make Him survive at the dining hall table. Don't. Learn to say 'I take this as historically real and I'm still working out what that means' — that sentence is more honest than either belief-signaling or apologetic hedging.
    • When choosing a partner, a major, a city — notice that Parīkṣit, facing death, asked about a vaṁśa, a lineage. You are also choosing a lineage: who you marry, where you train, whose authority you accept. Make those choices in front of someone who has actually heard Kṛṣṇa-kathā for forty years, not only in front of peers your own age.
    householder
    • The Yadu dynasty was a working royal family — politics, marriages, succession, wealth — and Kṛṣṇa entered exactly there. Your spreadsheet, your kids' school admissions, your aging parents' medical decisions are not obstacles to bhakti; they are the field where Kṛṣṇa's divyam character meets your sādhana. Stop waiting for a quieter season.
    • Parīkṣit asked Śukadeva about lineage because lineage transmits dharma. Audit, this month, what your children are actually receiving from you: which stories they hear at dinner, which adults you let shape them, what they see you do at 5 a.m. and at 10 p.m. A vaṁśa is built by repetition, not by occasional festivals.
    • Prabhupāda warns that without grasping Kṛṣṇa's appearance one stays in material bondage. For the householder, 'material bondage' is not abstract — it is the specific compulsion to take one more promotion, one more renovation, one more upgrade, postponing the question of what you are actually living for. Sit with your spouse this week and name one bondage you will both stop feeding.
    senior
    • You are now closer to Parīkṣit's situation than to the youth in the room — fewer years ahead than behind, and the question 'what do I want to hear before I go' is no longer theoretical. Choose your Śukadeva: which voice, which text, which association will you actually sit with daily? Stop sampling and commit.
    • The dynasties Parīkṣit asked about were the ones his ancestors and descendants belonged to. Your equivalent task is to leave a transmittable lineage — not your portfolio, not your professional reputation, but the specific bhakti-saṁskāras your grandchildren will remember. Write down three pastimes of Kṛṣṇa you want them to hear from your mouth, and start telling them.
    • Loosening attachment at this stage does not mean withdrawal; Parīkṣit became more eager, not less, in his final week. Look honestly at what you are still gripping — a house, a grievance, an adult child's choices, a designation at the temple — and offer one of them this month. The test of understanding janma karma ca me divyam is whether you can leave the body without that grip still tightening.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating the Tenth Canto as the 'fun part' to skip ahead to, bypassing the foundation of the first nine cantos that Parīkṣit deliberately heard first.
    • Hearing Kṛṣṇa's janma and karma as mythology or symbolism rather than as divya — transcendental events whose factual acceptance is the very condition Bhagavad-gītā 4.9 sets for liberation.
    • Approaching the descriptions of Kṛṣṇa with the same appetite one brings to the dynastic narratives — as entertainment or cultural heritage — instead of with Parīkṣit's mood of a man preparing to die in seven days.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Parīkṣit, hours from death, asks not for comfort but for more detail about Kṛṣṇa's family line. Share with your partner: when have you avoided going deeper into Kṛṣṇa-kathā because you felt you 'already knew enough'? Be honest — was it humility, or was it actually fatigue or distraction dressed up as understanding?
    • Prabhupāda says without grasping janma karma ca me divyam 'one cannot be liberated from material bondage.' That is a strong claim. Discuss: do you actually believe a sincere, ethical person who never hears about Kṛṣṇa's appearance is bound by karma? Where does this leave your non-devotee parents, friends, or colleagues — and how do you carry that without becoming sectarian or sentimentally universalist?
    • Śukadeva opens the Tenth Canto only after nine cantos of cosmology, dynasties, and devotee biographies. Many of us want to skip to Kṛṣṇa's pastimes immediately. Argue both sides with your partner: is the traditional sequence still necessary today, or is it acceptable for a modern seeker to begin with Daśama-skandha and work backward?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A is a long-time devotee visiting Student B, a college roommate who was raised culturally Hindu but is now agnostic. Student B asks, sincerely and without hostility: 'You keep saying Kṛṣṇa appeared in the Yadu dynasty. Why does it matter to you whether He literally took birth in a specific family 5,000 years ago? Isn't the teaching what counts?' Student A must respond using only what Parīkṣit's question and Prabhupāda's purport on SB 10.1.1 actually establish — without bluffing, without quoting verses they don't understand, and without dismissing the friend. After five minutes, switch roles. Then debrief: where did you reach for slogans? Where did you actually feel the divyam (transcendental nature) of Kṛṣṇa's janma and karma in your own conviction?

    Objections & Responses
    • Genealogies of solar and lunar dynasties read like ancient mythology. Why should a modern, scientifically literate person treat the Yadu-vaṁśa as historical and not as religious folklore that frames a moral teaching?
      The objection assumes 'history' means what archaeology can verify. Parīkṣit himself calls these dynasties paramādbhutam — supremely wonderful — precisely because they are not ordinary history. The Bhāgavata is a śabda-pramāṇa: knowledge received through a disciplic line, not reconstructed from artifacts. We don't ask the Bhāgavata to compete with carbon dating, and we don't ask geology to disclose Kṛṣṇa's birth. The relevant test Prabhupāda gives is the one from Bhagavad-gītā 4.9 — janma karma ca me divyam — does understanding Kṛṣṇa's appearance as transcendental actually free a person from repeated birth and death? That is verifiable in a practitioner's life, and that is the proof the tradition stakes itself on.
    • Saying 'without understanding Kṛṣṇa's appearance one cannot be liberated' sounds like every other religion claiming exclusive truth. How is this not just Hindu sectarianism with better Sanskrit?
      Fair challenge, and it deserves a careful answer rather than a defensive one. Prabhupāda is not saying 'only those who use the name Kṛṣṇa are saved.' He is pointing to a specific mechanism: liberation from the cycle of janma and mṛtyu requires knowing the Lord tattvataḥ — in truth, as a person, with His own divyam activities — not as an abstraction. Anyone, anywhere, who comes to that realization through whatever causeless mercy reaches them, attains the same destination — mām eti so 'rjuna. The exclusivity is not about a religion's brand; it is about the difference between knowing a person and theorizing about an idea. A Gauḍīya teacher should hold this firmly without weaponizing it — Caitanya Mahāprabhu Himself wept for the conditioned souls.
    Analogy

    Parīkṣit is like a man on the last day of a long voyage who, instead of asking what awaits the ship, turns to the captain and says, 'Tell me again, from the beginning, who the King is who sent us.' The Yadu and Soma-Sūrya dynasties are the route map; Kṛṣṇa is the King. The dying king hears the route to confirm whose service he was on the whole time.

    Stories
    Parīkṣit cursed at the river

    The young king, exhausted from hunting, had silently entered the meditation hut of the sage Śamīka and, in a flicker of dishonor, draped a dead snake on his neck. The sage's son Śṛṅgi cursed him — a serpent-bird would kill him in seven days.

    Parīkṣit could have raged or denied; instead he laid down his sword, retired to the bank of the Gaṅgā, and called the sages together. When Śukadeva arrived, he asked the question every dying person should ask: what should a man on the threshold of death hear, do, and remember? Out of that question the Bhāgavatam was spoken.

    This verse opens the Tenth Canto of that very conversation — Parīkṣit, having heard nine cantos, asks now for Kṛṣṇa's own appearance. The pious dynasties are recounted; he wants the King they were preparing for.

    Important Words
    • dharma-śīlasya — strictly attached to religious principles
      Compound: dharma + śīla (character, habit). The Yadus' qualification was not occasional piety but a settled habit of dharma. Kṛṣṇa enters a family already trained in dharma — sthāyī-bhāva of dharma prepares the ground for prema.
    • muni-sattama — O best of all munis
      Sat + tama = superlative, 'best.' Parīkṣit addresses Śukadeva by his qualification, not merely his name. Hearing kṛṣṇa-kathā is potent only when the speaker is qualified; the disciple's first task is to recognize and address that qualification.
    • aṁśena — with His plenary expansion Baladeva
      Instrumental of aṁśa, 'portion, plenary part.' Baladeva is non-different from Kṛṣṇa in tattva yet distinct in līlā as the original brother and servitor. The Gauḍīya line reads this as the simultaneous oneness-and-difference at the level of Bhagavān Himself — acintya-bhedābheda visible even in Vraja.
    • viṣṇoḥ — of Lord Viṣṇu
      Genitive. Read in Gauḍīya siddhānta as referring here to Kṛṣṇa Himself — the source — not to a separate Viṣṇu-tattva. The verse confirms Kṛṣṇa as Viṣṇu's source rather than His servant or expansion (cf. CC Ādi 2).
    • vīryāṇi — the glorious activities
      Plural of vīrya, 'potency, prowess.' Not principles, not symbols — concrete, narratable feats. Parīkṣit is specifically asking for līlā, the personal pastimes, because vīryāṇi reveal the Person in a way doctrine alone cannot.
    • śaṁsa — kindly describe
      Imperative of śaṁs, 'to praise, recite.' The same root that gives śāstra. Parīkṣit's request is not 'inform me' but 'praise Him aloud to me' — śravaṇam is intended to be sung, not surveyed.
    O best of munis, you have also described the descendants of Yadu, who were very pious and strictly adherent to religious principles. Now, if you will, kindly describe the wonderful, glorious activities of Lord Viṣṇu, or Kṛṣṇa, who appeared in that Yadu dynasty with Baladeva, His plenary expansion.
    Purport

    The Brahma-saṁhitā (5.1) explains that Kṛṣṇa is the origin of the viṣṇu-tattva. īśvaraḥ paramaḥ kṛṣṇaḥ sac-cid-ānanda-vigrahaḥ anādir ādir govindaḥ sarva-kāraṇa-kāraṇam “Kṛṣṇa, who is known as Govinda, is the supreme controller. He has an eternal, blissful, spiritual body. He is the origin of all. He has no other origin, for He is the prime cause of all causes.” yasyaika-niśvasita-kālam athāvalambya jīvanti loma-vilajā jagad-aṇḍa-nāthāḥ viṣṇur mahān sa iha yasya kalā-viśeṣo govindam ādi-puruṣaṁ tam ahaṁ bhajāmi “The Brahmās, the heads of the innumerable universes, live only for the duration of one breath of Mahā-Viṣṇu. I worship Govinda, the original Lord, of whom Mahā-Viṣṇu is but a portion of a plenary portion.” ( Brahma-saṁhitā 5.48 ) Govinda, Kṛṣṇa, is the original Personality of Godhead. Kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam . Even Lord Mahā-Viṣṇu, who by His breathing creates many millions upon millions of universes, is Lord Kṛṣṇa’s kalā-viśeṣa, or plenary portion of a plenary portion. Mahā-Viṣṇu is a plenary expansion of Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is a plenary expansion of Nārāyaṇa. Nārāyaṇa is a plenary expansion of the catur-vyūha, and the catur-vyūha are plenary expansions of Baladeva, the first manifestation of Kṛṣṇa. Therefore when Kṛṣṇa appeared with Baladeva, all the viṣṇu-tattvas appeared with Him. Mahārāja Parīkṣit requested Śukadeva Gosvāmī to describe Kṛṣṇa and His glorious activities. Another meaning may be derived from this verse as follows, Although Śukadeva Gosvāmī was the greatest muni, he could describe Kṛṣṇa only partially ( aṁśena ), for no one can describe Kṛṣṇa fully. It is said that Anantadeva has thousands of heads, but although He tries to describe Kṛṣṇa with thousands of tongues, His descriptions are still incomplete.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O best of munis, you have also described the descendants of Yadu, who were very pious and strictly adherent to religious principles. Now, if you will, kindly describe the wonderful, glorious activities of Lord Viṣṇu, or Kṛṣṇa, who appeared in that Yadu dynasty with Baladeva, His plenary expansion.
    Commentary

    You have also previously described the pious nature of Yadu. Though Yadu disobeyed his father’s order, because of his pure devotion, his exalted character is praised in the Ninth and Eleventh cantos. Pariksit addresses Sukadeva as the king of the munis—muni sattama, because as a muni he is completely knowledgeable, and as a devotee (sat), he is the chief since he established the supreme position of bhakti. "Please describe the exploits (viryani) of he who has appeared (avatirnasya), of that person whose amsa is Visnu in Vaikuntha." Another meaning is "Please describe the exploits partially (amsena), since it is impossible to describe the Lord’s pastimes completely."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    You have also described the details of Yadu’s dynasty and the astonishing activities of its kings to a great degree, since Yadu was filled with bhakti (dharma-śīlasya). Dharma means bhakti because it is said dharmo mad-bhakti-kṛt proktaḥ: dharma means bhakti to me. (SB 11.19.27) Yadu’s steady bhakti is described in the Eleventh Canto. Kuntī has also said yadoḥ priyasyānvavāye: you have taken birth to please King Yadu, one of your dearest devotees. (SB 1.8.32) Parīkṣit particularly mentions Yadu, because his dynasty became the best by the appearance of Kṛṣṇa, and he has in mind many questions concerning Kṛṣṇa. He addresses Śukadeva as the best of sages. He is a devotee of the Lord, and better than that he is absorbed in Kṛṣṇa. Best of all, he has intense prema at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. He thus indicates Śukadeva’s high qualification for what he spoke previously and for what he will speak in the upcoming chapters. The second line of the verse states Parīkṣit’s desire. Please describe to us the activities of Kṛṣṇa (viṣṇoḥ) who appeared in this world from his place known as Goloka in Yadu’s dynasty (tatra), since he was a great devotee. Śrīdhara Svāmī explains that the word aṁśena (Kṛṣṇa is an expansion of Viṣṇu) has been used for the common people in the assembly. The Gītā (9.25) says nāhaṁ prakāśaḥ sarvasya yogamāyā-samāvṛtaḥ: covered by my māyā I do not reveal myself to all people. The phrase can also mean “he appeared with a nature not easily understood by all.” Or it can mean “he appeared along with Balarāma, his aṁśa.” Such meanings must be given, because otherwise there is a contradiction to other statements in the Bhāgavatam: darśayām āsa lokaṁ svaṁ gopānāṁ tamasaḥ param Kṛṣṇa revealed to the cowherd men his abode, which is beyond material darkness. SB 10.28.14 kṛṣṇaṁ ca tatra cchandobhiḥ stūyamānaṁ su-vismitāḥ They were amazed to see Kṛṣṇa there, surrounded by the personified Vedas, who were offering him prayers. SB 10.28.17 Also of course there are the words kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam which will be explained in detail later. Brahmā also says: goloka-nāmni nija-dhāmni tale ca tasya devī-maheśa-hari-dhāmasu teṣu teṣu | te te prabhāva-nicayā vihitāś ca yena govindam ādi-puruṣaṁ tam ahaṁ bhajāmi || I worship the Supreme Lord Govinda by whom respective powers are given to the abodes of Durgā, Śiva and Viṣṇu, which are situated below his own planet of Goloka. Brahma-saṁhitā 5.43 rāmādi-mūrtiṣu kalā-niyamena tiṣṭhan nānāvatāram akarod bhuvaneṣu kintu | kṛṣṇaḥ svayaṁ samabhavat paramaḥ pumān yo govindam ādi-puruṣaṁ tam ahaṁ bhajāmi || I worship the Supreme Lord Govinda who, though appearing in the worlds in eternal forms such as Rāma and Nṛsiṁha with their characteristic powers, also appears personally in the supreme form of Kṛṣṇa with the most attractive pastimes. Brahma-saṁhitā 5.39 These verses defeat all doubts. There are other verses as well. The word viṣṇu is used to indicate Kṛṣṇa in this verse because it indicates that he as the highest position of pervasion (viṣṇu means the pervader). Please describe with excellence (śaṁsa) as if in verses of praise, the greatly powerful activites of Kṛṣṇa. This statement hints at the supremely astonishing nature of Krṣṇa’s activities among the activities of all forms of the Lord. The word naḥ (us) is used in the plural out of respect, with great desire to hear, or out of consideration of the other people listening. Or it can indicate humility, to receive mercy. The word naḥ can also modify viṣṇoḥ, indicating “Kṛṣṇa belonging to us Pāṇḍavas.” This would indicate his devotion to Kṛṣṇa and his great desire to hear about his activities.

    Personal Guidance
    Hearing Kṛṣṇa's pastimes is the highest activity — far surpassing even the noblest worldly histories of pious dynasties.
    Practical Applications
    • Replace fifteen minutes of news or social media today with a chapter from Kṛṣṇa Book or the Tenth Canto.
    • When you tell stories at dinner, include one pastime of Kṛṣṇa alongside the day's events — train your tongue toward what truly nourishes.
    • Before sleep, ask Kṛṣṇa specifically (not a vague 'higher power') to let you hear about Him tomorrow with deeper attention.
    Reflection Questions
    • When I sit to hear about Kṛṣṇa, am I actually hungry for His personal vīryāṇi, or am I settling for moral lessons and 'pious dynasty' content that leaves Him at a safe distance?
    • Whose 'glories' am I most eager to recount in my day — my family's lineage, my teachers', my own accomplishments — and how does that compete for the space Parīkṣit reserved for Kṛṣṇa-kathā?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Your feed is full of 'pious Yadus' — founder biographies, productivity gurus, athletes, even devotee influencers. Track for one week how many minutes you spend hearing about admirable humans versus hearing about Kṛṣṇa directly. Then ask: what shifted, and what didn't.
    • Parīkṣit, a king with seven days to live, asked for stories not strategy. When you face a real crunch — exam week, breakup, job rejection — what do you actually reach for? Discuss whether kṛṣṇa-kathā is on that list or only your backup-of-the-backup.
    • The verse honors the Yadus as dharma-śīla before moving to Kṛṣṇa. Don't skip dharma to leap into rasa — are you maintaining basic honesty, study discipline, regulation around screens and relationships? The leap to advanced hearing without that base tends to produce sentimentality, not bhakti.
    householder
    • You hear endless 'pious Yadu' content at work — leadership podcasts, parenting experts, financial sages. The verse asks: when do you and your spouse sit together and hear vīryāṇi of Kṛṣṇa? If the honest answer is 'rarely', plan one fixed weekly slot this week — not as program, as oxygen.
    • Children imitate what parents consume. If your kids see you absorbed in news and market updates but never in Bhāgavata-kathā, you are passing on the Yadu-dynasty stage and skipping the Kṛṣṇa stage. Discuss with your spouse what one piece of household media diet you will replace this month.
    • Money and career decisions often get framed as dharmic — supporting family, giving in charity, all true and to be honored like the Yadus here. But Parīkṣit's question reminds us — dharma is the floor, not the ceiling. Is there any decision in the next year where you would let kṛṣṇa-kathā and association weigh more than the optimal financial move?
    senior
    • Parīkṣit was your contemporary in spirit — told he had limited time and immediately asked for what matters. You may not have a curse on your head, but the body is giving its own notice. What are you still postponing in your hearing — what 'after I finish this project' is still in the way?
    • Legacy-thinking often defaults to the Yadu mode — what good lineage, values, wealth do I leave behind? Worthy, but the verse points further — what kṛṣṇa-kathā have you transmitted? Consider recording a few of your most beloved Bhāgavata passages or memories of hearing them, for grandchildren who may not ask now but will one day need it.
    • Loosening attachments at this stage is not done by force of will but by the heart finding something sweeter. Increase the dose of līlā-śravaṇa — Tenth Canto, Caitanya-caritāmṛta — and watch attachments thin out on their own. If they are not thinning, the dose is too low, not the principle wrong.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating Kṛṣṇa as merely one more avatāra of Viṣṇu rather than the source (kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam), which subtly demotes Him into an impersonal 'aspect' and dries up rasa in hearing.
    • Substituting study of cultural, ethical, or 'pious-Yadu' material for direct śravaṇam of Kṛṣṇa's personal activities, and calling that bhakti-cultivation.
    • Hearing Kṛṣṇa-līlā as mythology or symbol — extracting 'principles' while skipping the Person — so that even Daśama-skandha becomes a self-improvement text rather than meeting with Bhagavān.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Parīkṣit Mahārāja first hears about pious Yadus and then asks for Kṛṣṇa's vīryāṇi. In pairs, debate: is it spiritually mature to 'graduate' from stories of saintly devotees to hearing of Kṛṣṇa directly, or does that attitude itself betray a subtle pride? Bring evidence from your own hearing habits.
    • The verse implies a hierarchy: hearing of righteous men is good, but hearing of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa is supreme. Discuss as a group where the modern devotional community actually spends its hearing time — sociology, biography, philosophy, kīrtana, kathā of Kṛṣṇa. Where is the imbalance, and is anyone willing to name it honestly?
    • Jīva Gosvāmī establishes that Kṛṣṇa is the source and Viṣṇu the expansion, but many of us were first attracted through a Viṣṇu-tattva form (Nṛsiṁha, Rāma, Jagannātha, the deity in our home temple). Pair up and share: has the siddhānta of kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam actually changed your worship, or is it a doctrine you accept without it touching your heart?
    Role Play

    A long-time temple member (player A) approaches the class facilitator (player B) after a Sunday program and says, 'I've been hearing the Tenth Canto for thirty years. I'm tired of the stories. Can we please move to Vedānta-sūtra study or something more intellectual?' Player B must respond drawing on this verse — why did Parīkṣit, on the verge of death and already self-realized, still ask specifically for vīryāṇi, the līlā? Run the scene for four minutes, then swap roles.

    Objections & Responses
    • This verse just shows sectarian one-upmanship — the speaker wants to hear about his preferred deity Kṛṣṇa over the dynasty stories. Every tradition does this with its own iṣṭa. Why should I take it as universal truth rather than as devotional partisanship?
      A fair challenge, and Gauḍīya ācāryas faced it openly. The claim is not 'my deity is best because I love Him' but a tattva-siddhānta argued from śāstra — kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam (SB 1.3.28) — and demonstrated by Jīva Gosvāmī through the relations of aṁśa and aṁśī, expansion and source. Parīkṣit is not boosting a favorite; he is dying in seven days and asking for what alone can carry the soul across. The test is not theological argument but phala — what does sustained hearing of Kṛṣṇa-līlā actually do to a person's heart over years? Try it as an experiment, not a creed.
    • If Viṣṇu is non-different from Kṛṣṇa, as the purport says, then asking specifically for Kṛṣṇa's pastimes seems like splitting hairs. Worship any form, get the same result. Why this insistence on the original?
      Non-different in tattva, yes — one ghee — but with different rasa. A father is non-different from himself whether he is at the office or playing on the floor with his child, yet the child experiences something in the second form that the office form cannot give. Kṛṣṇa in Vraja reveals mādhurya — sweetness, accessibility, intimacy — that the awe-laden Vaikuṇṭha form, by His own choice, holds back. Worshiping any viṣṇu-tattva yields liberation, but Kṛṣṇa-līlā specifically yields prema, and prema is what the soul actually hungers for beneath its desire for liberation.
    Analogy

    Hearing the Yadu dynasty's pious deeds is like reading the architect's notes; hearing Kṛṣṇa's vīryāṇi is entering the house and meeting the owner. Parīkṣit has read the notes — he now asks for the Person who designed and dwells in them. The dynasty is the doorway; Kṛṣṇa is the room.

    Stories
    Jīva Gosvāmī on kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam

    When opponents argued that Kṛṣṇa was simply one more avatāra of Viṣṇu, Jīva Gosvāmī in his Krama-sandarbha turned to the very next verse Parīkṣit will hear later in the Bhāgavata — ete cāṁśa-kalāḥ puṁsaḥ kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam (SB 1.3.28) — and showed grammatically that 'tu' establishes Kṛṣṇa as the source, not the expansion.

    This verse's request for the vīryāṇi of Viṣṇu 'who appeared with Baladeva' is read by the Gauḍīya line in that light: the Viṣṇu spoken of here is Kṛṣṇa Himself, the original Person. Parīkṣit asks specifically for vīryāṇi — the personal exploits — not the cosmological functions Viṣṇu shares with other forms.

    Important Words
    • avatīrya — after descending
      Gerund of ava-tṝ, 'to cross down.' Avatāra is not 'incarnation' in the sense of being forced into matter — it is a voluntary descent. Kṛṣṇa is the descent (avatārī) Himself, not a deity who is incarnated into something foreign.
    • bhagavān — the Supreme Personality of Godhead
      From bhaga (opulence) + -vat (possessing) — defined in Viṣṇu Purāṇa (6.5.47) as one who possesses in full all six opulences. Gauḍīya siddhānta reserves bhagavān (as the highest realization) for the personal feature, above Brahman and Paramātmā realizations.
    • bhūta-bhāvanaḥ — the cause of the cosmic manifestation
      Bhūta (beings, manifested) + bhāvana (causing to be). Kṛṣṇa is not 'within' creation as one of its parts; He is the One by whose will all bhūtas come to be. Yet that same Person stands in Yadu-vaṁśa as a relative.
    • viśva-ātmā — the Supersoul of the entire universe
      Paramātmā feature — Kṛṣṇa as the inner controller. Gauḍīya distinction: viśva-ātmā does not mean 'I am the universe.' It means Bhagavān has a localized aspect in every heart, distinct from the jīva-ātmā, witnessing without becoming one with.
    • vada — kindly say
      Imperative of vad, 'to speak.' Knowledge of Kṛṣṇa is transmitted by speech, not by silent inference. Bhāgavata is śabda-pramāṇa — the Person must be spoken into the hearer's ear, not inferred from the world.
    • vistarāt — elaborately
      Ablative of vistara, 'expansion, detail.' Parīkṣit refuses summary. The flavor (rasa) of līlā lives in the particulars — what Yaśodā wore, what time of day, whose voice called from across the river. Highlight reels do not carry rasa.
    The Supersoul, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the cause of the cosmic manifestation, appeared in the dynasty of Yadu. Please tell me elaborately about His glorious activities and character, from the beginning to the end of His life.
    Purport

    In this verse the words kṛtavān yāni indicate that all the different activities Kṛṣṇa performed while present on earth are beneficial to human society. If religionists, philosophers and people in general simply hear the activities of Kṛṣṇa, they will be liberated. We have described several times that there are two kinds of kṛṣṇa-kathā, represented by Bhagavad-gītā, spoken personally by Kṛṣṇa about Himself, and Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, spoken by Śukadeva Gosvāmī about the glories of Kṛṣṇa. Anyone who becomes even slightly interested in kṛṣṇa-kathā is liberated. Kīrtanād eva kṛṣṇasya mukta-saṅgaḥ paraṁ vrajet ( Bhāg. 12.3.51 ). Simply by chanting or repeating kṛṣṇa-kathā, one is liberated from the contamination of Kali-yuga. Caitanya Mahāprabhu therefore advised, yāre dekha, tāre kaha ‘kṛṣṇa’-upadeśa (Cc. Madhya 7.128). This is the mission of Kṛṣṇa consciousness: to hear about Kṛṣṇa and thus be liberated from material bondage.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Supersoul, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the cause of the cosmic manifestation, appeared in the dynasty of Yadu. Please tell me elaborately about His glorious activities and character, from the beginning to the end of His life.
    Commentary

    "Previously you described very briefly how Krsna was taken from the prison to Vraja, but you could not describe everything in that description. O muni, you described it in only two verses. Now I pray that you describe this incident in many verses." Krsna is the one who descends to immerse the jivas (bhuta) in prema (bhuta bhavana -causing bhava for the living entities). Other verses in SB support this: nrlokam ramayam asa murtya sarvanga ramyaya He gave pleasure to mankind through his beautiful form. avitrptadrsam nrnam, (SB 9.24.64) Mankind was unsatisfied after tasting his sweetness. They developed a desire constantly taste. svamurtya lokalavanya...etc. (SB 11.1.6) The sweetness of Krsna’s beauty steals the functions of a l the senses. They no longer desire any other form. Drowning them in the ocean of his beauty, he gives them prema. He is called visvatma, soul of the universe, or paramatma because he is the object of love rather than the body or the jiva. This is explained in brahma’s prayers 10.14. "Please explain extensively (vistarat) since my intelligence is slow to grasp the subject."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “But all his activities are most astonishing.” Then describe all of those activities. This verse indicates the purpose of the Lord. Bhagavān, full of all powers, is the protector of all beings by his mercy (bhūta-bhāvanaḥ). He is a benefactor of all (viśvātmā) by his very nature, because he alone supports and inspires everyone with his śakti of consciousness and other factors. This also means that as the highest form, he is the ultimate form of prema. Therefore you should glorify all his activities whatever (yāni), in great detail, to bring out this purpose. Do not summarize them as previously. Though it is impossible to describe all the details, he requests this out of great eagerness.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa, cause of all causes and Supersoul in every heart, descended in the Yadu dynasty out of kindness — hear His activities in full.
    Practical Applications
    • Read one chapter of Kṛṣṇa Book or Tenth Canto today, hearing His pastimes from beginning with attention.
    • Pause before a decision and silently acknowledge Kṛṣṇa as the Supersoul in your heart guiding remembrance and forgetfulness.
    • Tell one family member or friend a specific Kṛṣṇa pastime you heard, keeping the vistarāt (elaborate) hearing alive in speech.
    Reflection Questions
    • When I retell or remember Kṛṣṇa's pastimes, where do I notice my mind reducing Him to symbol or principle rather than meeting Him as the supremely attractive person in Vraja?
    • What in my own heart resists letting bhūta-bhāvanaḥ — the maintainer seated within — actually maintain me, so that I keep trying to be my own cause?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Parīkṣit was 60 when he received this — but he had been groomed for kṛṣṇa-kathā since childhood. What are you absorbing daily that will form your reflexes when a real crisis hits at 30 or 40?
    • The Yadu dynasty was Kṛṣṇa's chosen family. You don't choose your birth family, but you DO choose your peer group, your influences, and eventually your spouse. Are you choosing in a way that makes Kṛṣṇa's appearance in your life more or less likely?
    • Don't dismiss the Tenth Canto pastimes as 'kid stuff' you'll get to later. Reading Kṛṣṇa's childhood līlās in your own youth — when you still have the capacity for wonder — forms a foundation that becomes very hard to lay down after thirty.
    householder
    • Kṛṣṇa appeared in a dynasty — within family, marriage, political alliances, and economic responsibilities. Householder life is not a detour from spiritual life; it is the very setting in which Kṛṣṇa Himself chose to perform His pastimes. Honor your varṇāśrama duties as the field of your bhakti.
    • Make daily kṛṣṇa-kathā non-negotiable in the home — even ten minutes of Bhāgavatam reading with your spouse and children. The Yadus heard about Kṛṣṇa because Kṛṣṇa was in their home; your home becomes 'Yadu-like' to the degree His pastimes are heard there.
    • Parīkṣit asked vistarāt — elaborately, not in summary. As a householder you will be tempted by 'highlight reels' and short-form content. Resist this in your spiritual diet. Sit with one verse and its purport for an extended period; do not optimize bhakti for efficiency.
    senior
    • You are now closer in years to Parīkṣit's situation than ever before — a definite remaining span, responsibilities winding down. The verse is a direct model: turn the remaining time toward systematic hearing of Kṛṣṇa's pastimes from beginning to end.
    • Use your authority in the family to ensure the next two generations actually hear kṛṣṇa-kathā, not merely inherit a vague 'Hindu' identity. The Yadu dynasty's glory was that Kṛṣṇa appeared there; your family's real wealth is whether His pastimes are spoken in it.
    • Resist the impersonalist drift that often seduces seniors — 'God is everywhere, all paths lead to the same place, no need for forms and stories.' Prabhupāda's purport insists Kṛṣṇa is the most beautiful person within the three worlds. At this stage, deepen your relationship with the personal Kṛṣṇa; do not dilute it.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Hearing 'Supersoul of all' and quietly sliding into impersonalism, as if Kṛṣṇa's personal form in Yadu-vaṁśa were a lower expression of a higher abstraction.
    • Skimming the līlā for moral lessons while skipping the vistarāt — the elaborate, particular details Parīkṣit specifically asked for.
    • Embellishing pastimes from imagination or sentiment rather than staying within what guru, sādhu, and śāstra (Bhāgavatam, ācāryas) actually transmit.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Parīkṣit asks to hear Kṛṣṇa's pastimes 'from beginning to end' (vistarāt) even while facing death in seven days. Discuss: when you have limited time left for something important (a deadline, an illness in the family, retirement), do you also reach for hearing about Kṛṣṇa, or for distraction? What does your honest answer reveal?
    • The verse calls Kṛṣṇa bhūta-bhāvanaḥ — the well-wisher and maintainer of all beings — yet He appeared specifically in the Yadu dynasty. Discuss whether Kṛṣṇa's partiality to His devotees and family contradicts His being the well-wisher of all, or whether it actually demonstrates it.
    • Kṛṣṇa is viśvātmā, seated in every heart, yet He also descends in a personal form in Vṛndāvana and Mathurā. Some in the group may feel 'God in the heart' is enough; others insist on the personal form. Surface the disagreement honestly — what is actually lost if we stop at the Supersoul and never approach the personal Kṛṣṇa?
    Role Play

    Two friends meet for chai. One has just started reading the Tenth Canto and is enthusiastic about Kṛṣṇa's childhood pastimes. The other says, 'I respect your bhakti, but stories of a blue cowherd boy stealing butter feel mythological to me. I prefer the Gītā's philosophy — that feels universal.' Role-play the conversation. The bhakti friend should not get defensive or preachy; he should explain why Parīkṣit, on the verge of death, asked for these very pastimes vistarāt rather than for more philosophy.

    Objections & Responses
    • If Kṛṣṇa is viśvātmā, the Supersoul in everyone's heart, then why do I need to hear external stories about Him appearing in some dynasty thousands of years ago? Isn't internal meditation enough?
      Prabhupāda's purport itself answers this: the same Kṛṣṇa who is in the heart as Supersoul is also the cause of all knowledge AND forgetfulness. Left to internal meditation alone, we project our own conditioning onto the 'inner voice' — that is why the same heart can rationalize lust, greed, and even violence as 'inner guidance.' Hearing the actual pastimes (śravaṇam) of the historical Kṛṣṇa in the Yadu dynasty gives the heart-Kṛṣṇa a definite form, name, and character to confirm or correct our perception. Parīkṣit, a self-realized soul who could meditate perfectly, still asked for the external narration vistarāt — that should settle the question.
    • Why should I, a modern person, take seriously a king asking a sage for stories? This is just devotional folklore, not something that addresses my actual problems at work, in my marriage, or with my health.
      Parīkṣit is not asking for entertainment — he has been cursed to die in seven days and is using his final hours with strategic precision. He is asking the question every honest person eventually asks: when everything I have built is about to be taken from me, what is worth attending to? The verse is the considered choice of a dying man with full clarity. Your problems are real but temporary; the Bhāgavatam begins from the standpoint that you, too, are running out of time. Hearing kṛṣṇa-kathā is what trains the consciousness to face that fact without panic.
    Analogy

    Kṛṣṇa is like the sun: at once present in every drop of dew as a tiny reflection (Paramātmā in every heart) and shining in one place in the sky as Himself (Bhagavān descending in the Yadu dynasty). To say 'the sun is everywhere in the dewdrops' is true; but you still raise your face when the sun itself rises. Parīkṣit, knowing both, raises his face.

    Stories
    Brahmā baffled in Vṛndāvana

    Later in this very Canto (SB 10.13), Lord Brahmā — knowing Kṛṣṇa to be the Supersoul of the cosmos — tested whether the cowherd boy in Vraja was really that same Person. He stole the calves and the boys.

    Kṛṣṇa expanded Himself into every missing calf and every missing boy, taking on their exact features for one year. When Brahmā returned and saw himself outdone, he fell at the feet of the cowherd child and prayed: 'I cannot understand You — You who are simultaneously the cause of the cosmic manifestation and a child rolling in the dust of Vraja.'

    Parīkṣit's request here — to hear Kṛṣṇa as bhūta-bhāvanaḥ and viśva-ātmā who appeared in a dynasty — receives its concrete answer there. The cause of all causes ate butter from His mother's hand.
