    Important Words
    • nivṛtta — released from
      Past participle of ni-vṛt, 'to turn away.' Not 'repressed' or 'denied' — turned around, the gaze pointed elsewhere. Material thirst doesn't die by suppression; it goes nivṛtta when kṛṣṇa-kathā becomes the more attractive object.
    • tarṣaiḥ — lust, material activities, thirst
      Instrumental plural of tarṣa, 'thirst.' Gauḍīya reading: not just sexual lust but the entire thirst-economy of the conditioned soul — for recognition, security, position. Nivṛtta-tarṣa names the qualified hearer; the rest of us hear while still being qualified, and the medicine works during the listening.
    • bhava-auṣadhāt — which is the right medicine for the material disease
      Bhava = repeated material existence; auṣadha = medicine. Compound is ablative, 'from this medicine.' Kṛṣṇa-kathā is here named diagnostically: not entertainment, not literature, but a specific remedy for a specific disease — saṁsāra-roga.
    • uttamaśloka — of the Supreme Personality of Godhead
      Uttama (highest) + śloka (verse, fame). One whose fame is celebrated in the highest verses — a name reserved in the Bhāgavatam for Bhagavān as the subject of paramparā praise. Not 'a divine being' but the particular Person whom the śāstras have always spoken.
    • guṇa-anuvādāt — from describing such activities
      Anuvāda = repeating after, recounting in the disciplic line. The medicine is potent precisely because it is anuvāda — relayed, not invented. The speaker repeats what was heard; that repetition is the channel.
    • paśu-ghnāt — either a butcher or one who is killing his own personal existence
      Paśu (animal) + ghna (slayer). Prabhupāda glosses doubly: a literal butcher (with no interest in the soul) or a self-butcher (the human form was given for hearing Bhagavān; refusing it kills the purpose of the body). The word is mercy compressed into one syllable.
    Glorification of the Supreme Personality of Godhead is performed in the paramparā system, that is, it is conveyed from the spiritual master to disciple. Such glorification is relished by those no longer interested in the false, temporary glorification of this cosmic manifestation. Descriptions of the Lord are the right medicine for the conditioned soul undergoing repeated birth and death. Therefore, who will cease hearing such glorification of the Lord except a butcher or one who is killing his own self?
    Purport

    In India it is the practice among the general populace to hear about Kṛṣṇa, either from Bhagavad-gītā or from Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, in order to gain relief from the disease of repeated birth and death. Although India is now fallen, when there is a message that someone will speak about Bhagavad-gītā or Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, thousands of people still gather to hear. This verse indicates, however, that such recitation of Bhagavad-gītā and Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam must be done by persons completely freed from material desires ( nivṛtta-tarṣaiḥ ). Everyone within this material world, beginning from Brahmā down to the insignificant ant, is full of material desires for sense enjoyment, and everyone is busy in sense gratification, but when thus engaged one cannot fully understand the value of kṛṣṇa-kathā, either in the form of Bhagavad-gītā or in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. If we hear the glories of the Supreme Personality of Godhead from liberated persons, this hearing will certainly free us from the bondage of material activities, but hearing Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam spoken by a professional reciter cannot actually help us achieve liberation. Kṛṣṇa-kathā is very simple. In Bhagavad-gītā it is said that Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Personality of Godhead. As He Himself explains, mattaḥ parataraṁ nānyat kiñcid asti dhanañjaya: “O Arjuna, there is no truth superior to Me.” ( Bg. 7.7 ) Simply by understanding this fact — that Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Personality of Godhead — one can become a liberated person. But, especially in this age, because people are interested in hearing Bhagavad-gītā from unscrupulous persons who depart from the simple presentation of Bhagavad-gītā and distort it for their personal satisfaction, they fail to derive the real benefit. There are big scholars, politicians, philosophers and scientists who speak on Bhagavad-gītā in their own polluted way, and people in general hear from them, being uninterested in hearing the glories of the Supreme Personality of Godhead from a devotee. A devotee is one who has no other motive for reciting Bhagavad-gītā and Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam than to serve the Lord. Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu has therefore advised us to hear the glories of the Lord from a realized person ( bhāgavata paro diya bhāgavata sthane ). Unless one is personally a realized soul in the science of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, a neophyte should not approach him to hear about the Lord, for this is strictly forbidden by Śrīla Sanātana Gosvāmī, who quotes from the Padma Purāṇa: avaiṣṇava-mukhodgīrṇaṁ pūtaṁ hari-kathāmṛtam śravaṇaṁ naiva kartavyaṁ sarpocchiṣṭaṁ yathā payaḥ One should avoid hearing from a person not situated in Vaiṣṇava behavior. A Vaiṣṇava is nivṛtta-tṛṣṇa; that is, he has no material purpose, for his only purpose is to preach Kṛṣṇa consciousness. So-called scholars, philosophers and politicians exploit the importance of Bhagavad-gītā by distorting its meaning for their own purposes. Therefore this verse warns that kṛṣṇa-kathā should be recited by a person who is nivṛtta-tṛṣṇa. Śukadeva Gosvāmī epitomizes the proper reciter for Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, and Parīkṣit Mahārāja, who purposefully left his kingdom and family prior to meeting death, epitomizes the person fit to hear it. A qualified reciter of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam gives the right medicine ( bhavauṣadhi ) for the conditioned souls. The Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement is therefore trying to train qualified preachers to recite Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam and Bhagavad-gītā throughout the entire world, so that people in general in all parts of the world may take advantage of this movement and thus be relieved of the threefold miseries of material existence. The instructions of Bhagavad-gītā and the descriptions of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam are so pleasing that almost anyone suffering from the threefold miseries of material existence will desire to hear the glories of the Lord from these books and thus benefit on the path of liberation. Two classes of men, however, will never be interested in hearing the message of Bhagavad-gītā and Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam — those who are determined to commit suicide and those determined to kill cows and other animals for the satisfaction of their own tongues. Although such persons may make a show of hearing Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam at a Bhāgavata-saptāha, this is but another creation of the karmīs, who cannot derive any benefit from such a performance. The word paśu-ghnāt is important in this connection. Paśu-ghna means “butcher.” Persons fond of performing ritualistic ceremonies for elevation to the higher planetary systems must offer sacrifices ( yajñas ) by killing animals. Lord Buddhadeva therefore rejected the authority of the Vedas because his mission was to stop animal sacrifices, which are recommended in Vedic ritualistic ceremonies nindasi yajña-vidher ahaha śruti-jātaṁ sa-daya-hṛdaya darśita-paśu-ghātaṁ keśava dhṛta-buddha-śarīra jaya jagadīśa hare ( Gīta-govinda ) Even though animal sacrifices are sanctioned in Vedic ceremonies, men who kill animals for such ceremonies are considered butchers. Butchers cannot be interested in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, for they are already materially allured. Their only interest lies in developing comforts for the temporary body. bhogaiśvarya-prasaktānāṁ tayāpahṛta-cetasām vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ samādhau na vidhīyate “In the minds of those who are too attached to sense enjoyment and material opulence, and who are bewildered by such things, the resolute determination of devotional service to the Supreme Lord does not take place.” ( Bg. 2.44 ) Śrīla Narottama dāsa Ṭhākura says: manuṣya-janama pāiyā, rādhā-kṛṣṇa nā bhajiyā, jāniyā śuniyā viṣa khāinu Anyone who is not Kṛṣṇa conscious and who therefore does not engage in the service of the Lord is also paśu-ghna, for he is willingly drinking poison. Such a person cannot be interested in kṛṣṇa-kathā because he still has a desire for material sense gratification; he is not nivṛtta-tṛṣṇa. As it is said, traivargikās te puruṣā vimukhā hari-medhasaḥ. Those interested in trivarga — that is, in dharma, artha and kāma — are religious for the sake of achieving a material position with which to gain better facilities for sense gratification. Such persons are killing themselves by willingly keeping themselves in the cycle of birth and death. They cannot be interested in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. For kṛṣṇa-kathā, topics about Kṛṣṇa consciousness, there must be a speaker and a hearer, both of whom can be interested in Kṛṣṇa consciousness if they are no longer interested in material topics. One can actually see how this attitude automatically develops in persons who are Kṛṣṇa conscious. Although the devotees of the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement are quite young men, they no longer read materialistic newspapers, magazines and so on, for they are no longer interested in such topics ( nivṛtta-tarṣaiḥ ). They completely give up the bodily understanding of life. For topics concerning Uttamaśloka, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the spiritual master speaks, and the disciple hears with attention. Unless both of them are free from material desires, they cannot be interested in topics of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. The spiritual master and disciple do not need to understand anything more than Kṛṣṇa because simply by understanding Kṛṣṇa and talking about Kṛṣṇa, one becomes a perfectly learned person ( yasmin vijñāte sarvam evaṁ vijñātaṁ bhavati, Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.3). The Lord sits within everyone’s heart, and by the grace of the Lord the devotee receives instructions directly from the Lord Himself, who says in Bhagavad-gītā (15.15) : sarvasya cāhaṁ hṛdi sanniviṣṭo mattaḥ smṛtir jñānam apohanaṁ ca vedaiś ca sarvair aham eva vedyo vedānta-kṛd veda-vid eva cāham “I am seated in everyone’s heart, and from Me come remembrance, knowledge and forgetfulness. By all the Vedas, I am to be known; indeed, I am the compiler of Vedānta, and I am the knower of the Vedas. ” Kṛṣṇa consciousness is so exalted that one who is perfectly situated in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, under the direction of the spiritual master, is fully satisfied by reading kṛṣṇa-kathā as found in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, Bhagavad-gītā and similar Vedic literatures. Since merely talking about Kṛṣṇa is so pleasing, we can simply imagine how pleasing it is to render service to Kṛṣṇa. When discourses on kṛṣṇa-kathā take place between a liberated spiritual master and his disciple, others also sometimes take advantage of hearing these topics and also benefit. These topics are the medicine to stop the repetition of birth and death. The cycle of repeated birth and death, by which one takes on different bodies again and again, is called bhava or bhava-roga. If anyone, willingly or unwillingly, hears kṛṣṇa-kathā, his bhava-roga, the disease of birth and death, will certainly stop. Therefore kṛṣṇa-kathā is called bhavauṣadha, the remedy to stop the repetition of birth and death. Karmīs, or persons attached to material sense enjoyment, generally cannot give up their material desires, but kṛṣṇa-kathā is such a potent medicine that if one is induced to hear kṛṣṇa-kīrtana, he will certainly be freed from this disease. A practical example is Dhruva Mahārāja, who at the end of his tapasya was fully satisfied. When the Lord wanted to give Dhruva a benediction, Dhruva refused it. Svāmin kṛtārtho ’smi varaṁ na yāce. “My dear Lord,” he said, “I am fully satisfied. I do not ask for any benediction for material sense gratification.” We actually see that even young boys and girls in the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement have given up their long practice of bad habits like illicit sex, meat-eating, intoxication and gambling. Because Kṛṣṇa consciousness is so potent that it gives them full satisfaction, they are no longer interested in material sense gratification.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Glorification of the Supreme Personality of Godhead is performed in the paramparā system; that is, it is conveyed from spiritual master to disciple. Such glorification is relished by those no longer interested in the false, temporary glorification of this cosmic manifestation. Descriptions of the Lord are the right medicine for the conditioned soul undergoing repeated birth and death. Therefore, who will cease hearing such glorification of the Lord except a butcher or one who is killing his own self?
    Commentary

    I am taking the remnants of whatever Sridhara Swami and Sanatana Goswami have left. King Pariksit says to Sukadeva, "I am a jiva bound up by the disease of material life. How can I cease drinking the great medicine of the pastimes of Krsna recited by you, the greatest of doctors endowed with the greatest fortune?" With that intention he speaks this verse. Who could stop drinking the sweet topics of Krsna which are like a medicine to cure the disease of material existence (bhavausadhat)? Trsna refers to thirst or attachment to material enjoyment. Nivrtta tarsaih refers to those who, taking the medicine of Krsna’s pastimes, have extinguished the trsna or thirst for material life. Liberated from bondage of maya, they therefore glorify this process more than jnana and other processes. "We glorify loudly this medicine, as it has cured us of our disease." Unlike other medicines, this medicine does not have bitter taste. Therefore he says srotra manobhiramat: It gives pleasure to the ear and mind. Therefore drink it with both ear and mind. Who will avoid these topics except the persons involved in killing animals in sacrifice with a longing to attain svarga loka enjoyment (pasughnah). Only these people will not listen. In verse 3.3.18 it is stated: Those involved in seeking dharma, artha, and kama have no taste for the name, qualities and pastimes of Lord Madhusudana resplendent with attractive pastimes. Another meaning: Who would give up drinking the topics of Krsna which are recited by guru, and then glorifying, for even those who are liberated loudly glorify . Upa in upagiyamanat indicates intense or continuous glorification. What more can be said about tasting it? You are the taster. Nivritta tarsaih indicates pure devotees, not jnanis, because of the use of present tense and the prefix upa in upagiyamanat. The jnanis meditate, but they do not chant the Lord’s glories intensely. Those who have opportunity to hear the pastimes of the Lord do not stop listening because it cures them of the material condition (bhavausadhat). Neither the speaker nor the listener tires of hearing about the Lord, because it is enjoyable (srotra manobhiramat). Only those desiring wealth and material enjoyment would stop hearing. Thus he says that only a killer of animals would cease hearing about the Lord, and no one else.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    One should not doubt my eagerness for such an elaborate description. That is expressed in this verse. Upagīyamānād: the Lord’s qualities are glorified by the liberated souls profusely or as the highest in nature (upa), for by constantly singing the Lord’s glories one attains the highest bliss as the supreme result. The liberated souls are both the jṣānīs and śuddha-bhaktas. They are the jīva-muktas living on earth and also person living in the spiritual realm with sālokya, sārṣṭi, sārūpya and sāmīpya. Bhavauṣadhāt: these talks are the medicine for the material world, destroying suffering for those desiring liberation. Śrotra-mano-’bhirāmāt: these talks give complete bliss to the ear by sound and to the mind by the meaning. However there is another type of person besides the desirer of liberation and material enjoyment: the person desiring bhakti. He is superior to the last two types mentioned. The first type, the liberated person, is naturally attracted and the fourth type of person, he who desires bhakti, is also qualified for hearing. Thus hearing the topics of the Lord is for the sādhakas and the siddhas. Who would not be satisfied with repeated topics of the famous (uttama-śloka) Lord’s qualities—such as his eternal and unlimited affection and generosity? The bliss of the Lord’s pastimes appearing in the minds of the first type, the liberated, with greater bliss than Brahman, out of intensity, transforms into song. This shows the predominance of singing the Lord’s glories in the perfected souls. These persons are pointed out first because of their perfected position. Those desiring liberation or material enjoyment are not considered perfected since the pastimes do not make their appearance spontaneously in their minds. They become absorbed in the pastimes because the topics give relief from misery (or give pleasure) through hearing. They have a predominance of hearing. These persons are less qualified than the first type. For those desiring liberation the topics appear in the mind as a sādhana for attaining their goal of liberation and give pleasure to the ear and mind because of the topics’ nature. But for those desiring material enjoyment the topics appear in the mind simply for pleasure of the ear and mind. The fourth type, those desiring bhakti, are inferior to the first type, but superior to the second and third type. There are three types of lists in the scriptures. In a list, the order may be from lesser to greater, greater to lesser, or randomly ordered. The first two types are employed to show the greatness or insignificance of an item compared to others. The random list is stated out of inattention or great prema. In the present verse the first three persons listed are in order of greater to lesser. The fourth type, the person desiring bhakti is randomly placed. Out of humility, such a devotee thinks that he is not detached in his attraction using his ear or mind, lacking liberation or desire for liberation. The word pumān (any man) is used in the verse. This means that others such as dependents, women, eunuchs or persons with disabilities would not be able to engage so freely in spiritual practice. Or men are mentioned because they predominant. Or pumān can refer to the jīva. Thus the topics of the Lord are for everyone. Vinā paśughnāt : only the animal killer is not attracted to the Lord’s topics, because of no interest in goals in this life or the next, since he is completely involved in giving suffering to others. It is said: rāja-putra ciraṁ jīva mā jīva muni putraka jīva vā mara vā sādho vyādha mā jivā mā mara The prince should live long. The son of the sage should not live. The devotee may live or not live. The hunter should not live nor die. The person who gives up the Lord’s topics is a hunter, throwing lances or punches at others, not caring that he ultimately gives himself suffering in this life and the next. This same topic is discussed in the glorification of topics of the Lord in the commentary named Bhagavad-bhakti-vilāsa. If topics about the Lord give such results, how much more will topics concerning Kṛṣṇa’s form and qualities will give results!

    Personal Guidance
    Hearing kṛṣṇa-kathā from realized souls in paramparā is the medicine for repeated birth and death — only the self-killer refuses it.
    Practical Applications
    • Hear or read Bhāgavatam daily from Prabhupāda's books or recordings — go to the paramparā source, not speculation.
    • When material desires for fame or pleasure arise, deliberately replace that hearing with one chapter of kṛṣṇa-kathā as medicine.
    • Identify one source of 'glorification of the cosmic manifestation' (news, gossip, entertainment) and replace it this week with hearing about Kṛṣṇa.
    Reflection Questions
    • When kṛṣṇa-kathā is being spoken, where does my mind drift first — and what does that drift reveal about the 'temporary glorification' I am still relishing?
    • Whose paramparā voice am I actually hearing Kṛṣṇa from daily, and where have I quietly substituted my own speculation or a non-paramparā source in its place?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice what you currently thirst for — career validation, romantic attention, recognition online. The verse doesn't shame these; it observes that as long as the thirst is loud, kṛṣṇa-kathā will sound quiet. Begin by hearing anyway; the thirst loosens through hearing, not before it.
    • You are not required to feel ecstasy in class to be 'doing it right.' The medicine works subcutaneously. Track instead whether over months your reactions to insult, failure, and desire are slowly changing — that is the bhavauṣadha acting.
    • Choose carefully who you let speak Kṛṣṇa into your ears. Algorithms will feed you charismatic speakers; paramparā asks you to feed yourself from sober ones. Audit your listening monthly — what voices are actually shaping your understanding of Kṛṣṇa?
    householder
    • Your household is a kṛṣṇa-kathā ecosystem whether you intend it or not. What gets glorified at your dinner table — promotions, property, neighbors' faults, or guṇānuvāda? The verse's medicine is administered in the daily speech of the home.
    • Honor your varṇāśrama duties as the field where hearing is metabolized. A householder who hears Bhāgavatam and then deals honestly with employees, clients, and in-laws is taking the medicine. One who hears and then resents these duties has heard with the ear only.
    • Protect a daily window — even fifteen minutes — of paramparā hearing that is not optimized for productivity, not multitasked. The verse calls this śrotra-mano-'bhirāmāt — pleasing to ear and mind. Give it conditions in which it can please you.
    senior
    • At your stage, nivṛtta-tarṣa is no longer aspirational language — much of the material thirst has naturally receded with the body. This is the verse's promised window. The hearing you do now lands differently than it did at forty; do not waste this clarity on television or grievance.
    • Consider becoming a transmitter, not only a receiver. Grandchildren, younger devotees, and seekers around you need someone who has heard Bhāgavatam for decades to relay it simply. You need not be a scholar — faithful relay is the paramparā's actual mechanism.
    • Examine honestly what you are still glorifying. Many seniors substitute glorification of their own past — career, family achievements, the 'old days' — for guṇānuvāda. The verse asks for a quiet final pivot: let Kṛṣṇa's qualities, not your biography, be what your speech returns to.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Hearing kṛṣṇa-kathā as literature or culture rather than as bhavauṣadhi, the actual medicine for repeated birth and death.
    • Bypassing the paramparā channel — preferring stimulating speakers, algorithmic clips, or one's own readings over śravaṇam from realized Vaiṣṇavas.
    • Mistaking emotional sentiment during hearing for genuine nivṛtta-tarṣa, while lusty desires remain unexamined and unsurrendered.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Prabhupāda equates one who refuses to hear kṛṣṇa-kathā with a paśughna — a butcher killing his own self. Is this rhetorical intensity, or a literal spiritual diagnosis? If literal, what do we make of sincere people across traditions who never encounter Bhāgavatam yet live ethical, contemplative lives?
    • The verse insists glorification must come through paramparā to be potent. But today many encounter Kṛṣṇa first through books, podcasts, or AI assistants — not a living guru. Does a verse heard outside an active disciplic relationship still carry bhavauṣadha potency?
    • Nivṛtta-tarṣa (one freed from material thirst) is named as the qualified hearer. Yet most of us begin hearing while still saturated with material desires. Is there a contradiction here, or does the verse describe the singer rather than gate the hearer?
    Role Play

    You are speaking with a 28-year-old software engineer in Bangalore who attends Bhāgavatam class weekly. He says: 'I love the philosophy and I chant 4 rounds, but honestly when I hear pastimes of Kṛṣṇa with the gopīs, my mind doesn't get medicine — it gets either bored or uncomfortable. The katha isn't working on me the way the verse promises. Am I the paśughna?' Respond as a personal guide — neither flattering nor crushing him. Address what nivṛtta-tarṣa actually requires, what hearing he should be doing at his stage, and whether his honesty is itself a qualification.

    Objections & Responses
    • This verse uses fear-language — calling non-hearers butchers and self-killers. Isn't that exactly the kind of religious coercion that has driven thoughtful people away from organized Vaiṣṇavism? A medicine shouldn't need to threaten the patient.
      The śāstra is not threatening — it is diagnosing. Śukadeva is speaking to Parīkṣit who has seven days to live; there is no time for soft language. The 'butcher' image is not aimed at outsiders to frighten them in; it is aimed at those who have already heard and turned away, naming what such turning-away costs them. Compare a physician telling a cardiac patient 'if you keep eating this way you will kill yourself' — that is not coercion, it is precision. Read in context, paśughnāt is mercy compressed into one word.
    • If kṛṣṇa-kathā only works when sung by the liberated, then most kīrtana and class I attend — given by conditioned souls like myself — must be spiritually inert. So why bother?
      The verse names the source of the current, not the only permitted conduit. When a conditioned speaker faithfully repeats what was heard from the paramparā — adding nothing, subtracting nothing, claiming nothing — the potency of the original liberated singer flows through. This is why Prabhupāda insisted on 'as it is.' The speaker is a pipe, not the well. Your local class is potent to the degree the speaker is transmitting rather than performing.
    Analogy

    Kṛṣṇa-kathā is the medicine for the disease of repeated birth — but only when poured from the right bottle. The pharmacy label is paramparā: spiritual master to disciple, vessel to vessel. A glass of the same nectar drawn from one's own imagination, however lovely it tastes, is not bhavauṣadha. The refuser of even the labeled medicine is, the verse says, a paśughna — slaughtering the very self he was given a body to save.

    Stories
    Mahārāja Khaṭvāṅga's forty-eight minutes

    King Khaṭvāṅga, after long service to the demigods, asked for one boon — to know how long he had left. He was told: a muhūrta, less than an hour.

    He returned at once to Earth, withdrew from his kingdom, fixed his mind on Bhagavān, and attained perfection in that single muhūrta. Prabhupāda cites him often as proof that kṛṣṇa-kathā taken seriously even at the last moment is bhavauṣadha — strong enough to cross the soul over.

    The verse calls the one who turns from such hearing paśughna; Khaṭvāṅga is the counter-image. Forty-eight minutes of attentive hearing did what eighty years of distraction could not.

    Ajāmila on his deathbed

    Ajāmila, a fallen brāhmaṇa who had spent decades in degradation, in his last moments called out the name of his youngest son — Nārāyaṇa. The Viṣṇudūtas arrived and overruled the Yamadūtas who had come for him; the holy name, even uttered without conscious devotion, had administered the bhavauṣadha (SB 6.1–3).

    The verse warns who would turn aside from such glorification. Ajāmila is its proof: even a half-attentive ear, brushed by paramparā-vibrated kṛṣṇa-kathā, is enough to override a lifetime of karma. The medicine is that potent — the only question is whether one keeps the lips closed.

    O learned speaker (Śukadeva Gosvāmī) .
    Important Words
    • pitāmahāḥ — my grandfathers, the five Pāṇḍavas
      Pitā + mahā — 'great fathers.' Parīkṣit is naming his own lineage as the proof of the verse he is asking Śukadeva to expand. The Pāṇḍavas are evidence; the Lord is the cause.
    • yat-plavāḥ — the shelter of the boat of Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet
      Yat (whose) + plava (boat, raft). The Pāṇḍavas had no other boat. Plava is a small vessel — not a battleship, not a strategy. Gauḍīya śaraṇāgati lives in this word: a boat is something you sit in, not something you operate.
    • vatsa-padam — as one steps over a small hoofprint of a calf
      Vatsa = calf; pada = footprint. The image is precise: a calf is small, and its hoof leaves a puddle a child can step over. Bhīṣma, the unconquerable, becomes a calf's puddle for one who has the right boat. Bhakti renormalizes scale.
    • śaraṇam — the shelter
      From śri, 'to resort to.' One of the great Vaiṣṇava terms — the act of taking refuge. Gauḍīya śaraṇāgati has six limbs (Hari-bhakti-vilāsa, citing Vaiṣṇava-tantra); Kuntī, by surrendering, qualified to be protected even inside her womb.
    • kāla-rūpaiḥ — in the forms of eternal time
      Kāla (time) + rūpa (form). Instrumental plural. Bhagavān as kāla is both deliverer of death and giver of life — He is not opposed to time, He is its very form. To understand Kṛṣṇa as kāla is to lose the fear of time.
    • māyā-manuṣyasya — of the Lord, who appeared as an ordinary human being by His own potency
      Māyā here = His yoga-māyā, His own internal potency — not the deluding material energy. Compound: 'of Him who, by His own [yoga-]māyā, [appears as] a man.' Acintya-bhedābheda in one word: He is fully Bhagavān and fully present in human form by His own choice.
    Taking the boat of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, my grandfather Arjuna and others crossed the ocean of the Battlefield of Kurukṣetra, in which such commanders as Bhīṣmadeva resembled great fish that could very easily have swallowed them. By the mercy of Lord Kṛṣṇa, my grandfathers crossed this ocean, which was very difficult to cross, as easily as one steps over the hoofprint of a calf. Because my mother surrendered unto Lord Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, the Lord, Sudarśana-cakra in hand, entered her womb and saved my body, the body of the last remaining descendant of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, which was almost destroyed by the fiery weapon of Aśvatthāmā. Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, appearing within and outside of all materially embodied living beings by His own potency in the forms of eternal time — that is, as Paramātmā and as virāṭ-rūpa — gave liberation to everyone, either as cruel death or as life. Kindly enlighten me by describing His transcendental characteristics.
    Purport

    As stated in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.14.58) : samāśritā ye pada-pallava-plavaṁ mahat-padaṁ puṇya-yaśo murāreḥ bhavāmbudhir vatsa-padaṁ paraṁ padaṁ padaṁ padaṁ yad vipadāṁ na teṣām “For one who has accepted the boat of the lotus feet of the Lord, who is the shelter of the cosmic manifestation and is famous as Murāri, or the enemy of the Mura demon, the ocean of the material world is like the water contained in a calf’s hoofprint. His goal is paraṁ padam, or Vaikuṇṭha, the place where there are no material miseries, not the place where there is danger at every step.” One who seeks shelter at the lotus feet of Lord Kṛṣṇa is immediately protected by the Lord. As the Lord promises in Bhagavad-gītā (18.66) , ahaṁ tvāṁ sarva-pāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ: “I shall deliver you from all sinful reactions. Do not fear.” By taking shelter of Lord Kṛṣṇa, one comes under the safest protection. Thus when the Pāṇḍavas took shelter at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, all of them were on the safe side of the Battlefield of Kurukṣetra. Parīkṣit Mahārāja, therefore, felt obliged to think of Kṛṣṇa in the last days of his life. This is the ideal result of Kṛṣṇa consciousness: ante nārāyaṇa-smṛtiḥ. If at the time of death one can remember Kṛṣṇa, one’s life is successful. Parīkṣit Mahārāja, therefore, because of his many obligations to Kṛṣṇa, intelligently decided to think of Kṛṣṇa constantly during the last days of his life. Kṛṣṇa had saved the Pāṇḍavas, Mahārāja Parīkṣit’s grandfathers, on the Battlefield of Kurukṣetra, and Kṛṣṇa had saved Mahārāja Parīkṣit himself when he was attacked by the brahmāstra of Aśvatthāmā. Kṛṣṇa acted as the friend and worshipable Deity of the Pāṇḍava family. Moreover, apart from Lord Kṛṣṇa’s personal contact with the Pāṇḍavas, Kṛṣṇa is the Supersoul of all living entities, and He gives everyone liberation, even if one is not a pure devotee. Kaṁsa, for example, was not at all a devotee, yet Kṛṣṇa, after killing him, gave him salvation. Kṛṣṇa consciousness is beneficial to everyone, whether one is a pure devotee or a nondevotee. This is the glory of Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Considering this, who will not take shelter at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa? Kṛṣṇa is described in this verse as māyā-manuṣya because He descends exactly like a human being. He is not obliged to come here, like karmīs, or ordinary living beings; rather, He appears by His own internal energy ( sambhavāmy ātma-māyayā ) just to show favor to the fallen conditioned souls. Kṛṣṇa is always situated in His original position as sac-cid-ānanda-vigraha, and anyone who renders service to Him is also situated in his original, spiritual identity ( svarūpeṇa vyavasthitiḥ ). This is the highest perfection of human life.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Taking the boat of Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet, my grandfather Arjuna and others crossed the ocean of the Battlefield of Kurukṣetra, in which such commanders as Bhīṣmadeva resembled great fish that could very easily have swallowed them. By the mercy of Lord Kṛṣṇa, my grandfathers crossed this ocean, which was very difficult to cross, as easily as one steps over the hoofprint of a calf. Because my mother surrendered unto Lord Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet, the Lord, Sudarśana-cakra in hand, entered her womb and saved my body, the body of the last remaining descendant of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, which was almost destroyed by the fiery weapon of Aśvatthāmā. Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, appearing within and outside of all materially embodied living beings by His own potency in the forms of eternal time—that is, as Paramātmā and as virāṭ-rūpa—gave liberation to everyone, either as cruel death or as life. Kindly enlighten me by describing His transcendental characteristics.
    Commentary

    "I should also hear the topics of Krsna because he is the protector of our dynasty." Thus he speaks this verse. My grandfather crossed the ocean of the kaurava army, though it was difficult to surmount because of Bhisma and others (devavratadi), who could defeat the devatas (amarnjayaih), who were like timingala fish, making it insignificant, like a calf’s hoof-print. The cause was surrender to the lotus feet of Krsna (yat plavah -the boat). Please speak about that person." Surrender to his lotus feet enables one to cross the ocean of material existence. "I must certainly hear about Krsna because he is my only protector." With this in mind he speaks this verse. The holder of the cakra (attacakrah), Krsna, just by his club (this is mentioned in the First Canto), entered into my mother who had surrendered to him, easily saved this body burned (viplustam) from the heat of Asvathama’s weapon (drauni astra) . ca indicates that he also protected the limbs of his mother. Krsna’s topics should be heard because He alone bestows the final goal on all. With this intention the present verse is spoken. Among all those with material bodies (akhila deha bhajam). Speak about he who awards death to those envious of devotees (bahih) and eternal life to those who are his dear devotees (antar). To devotees like Vasudeva he bestows bliss in the form of his human form-two handed or four handed and to people like Kamsa he appears as time or death. According to the statements of Bhagavatam, like the prescription of rock candy to a person afflicted with jaundice, though the Lord first appears as time to award death, he later awards them liberation. Prayacchatah (giving) is used in present tense to indicate that it is being seen before his eyes, or to convey the eternal nature of the Lord’s pastimes. Maya manushya means the Supreme Lord equipped with an eternal energy called maya, rather than a human with material body. Madhya bhasya pramanita sruti says: "ato mayamayam visnum pravadanti manisinah" "Thus the sages call him mayamay Visnu, visnu who possesses the energy called mayam."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Three verses indicate that he should constantly hear about Kṛṣṇa since his whole family was dedicated to him. The foes were very courageous. Bhīṣma the chief warrior (devavratādi) was difficult to kill because he was fixed in his vows since he could die at will. The enemy was difficult to overcome since Bhīṣma protected them. ekādaśa-sahasrāṇi yodhayed yas tu dhanvinām astra-śastra-pravīṇaś ca mahā-ratha iti smṛtaḥ amitān yodhayed yas tu samprokto ’tirathas tu saḥ A mahā-ratha is one who can fight alone with ten thousand archers, who is an expert in both weapons and scripture. An atiratha is one who fights with unlimited troops. The troops of Duryodhana and others were like an ocean because of their immense numbers. The word sma indicates that it was well known. Kṛṣṇa’s feet were like a boat, enabling Arjuna to defeat the enemy. But this boat did not carry Arjuna like a normal boat. Kṛṣṇa’s feet as a boat had special power to make the ocean small. Kṛṣṇa particularly gave me life. My limbs were burned up completely (vipluṣṭam) since the brahmāstra could not be countered and was extremely hot. The word idam (this body) indicates that the events happened in this very life not some other life and were plainly visible. There is no doubt about this. Because he was the last remaining Kuru, Kṛṣṇa was merciful to him and showed affection for his body. By preventing destruction of their family Kṛṣṇa preserved their fame and dharma. Though the Pāṇḍavas were also Kurus, the Pāṇḍavas are mentioned separately to show their special position. The Kurus were the others, who were without descendants, like a brāhmaṇa-sannyāsī. The Lord was most compassionate the other Kurus because he uprooted the demons completely and, by protecting the seed, gave them benefit in their future lives (since there were descendants to perform rites for them). The cakra is mentioned because of its prominent nature, but the Lord protected Parīkṣit using his club. astra-tejaḥ sva-gadayā nīhāram iva gopatiḥ The Lord was thus engaged in vanquishing the radiation of the brahmāstra using his club, just as the sun evaporates a drop of dew. SB 1.12.10 Or he held also his cakra to protect Parīkṣit out of great affection. The word ca indicates that Kṛṣṇa also protected his mother. She was saved because of the child in her womb. Otherwise she wished to die with her husband. This and the previous verse indicate that Parīkṣit would be ungrateful if he were to remain disinterested in the topics of the Lord. “My topics are recommended for those who are liberated. My topics, confidential, are for persons like you. These topics should be hidden from materialistic people.” Fearing such a rebuttal, Parīkṣit requests enthusiastically that Śukadeva begin his narration. The Lord gives absence of all suffering (amṛtam) or the highest sweetness, or prema at his lotus feet to embodied beings. The word ca indicates he also gives other desirable objects. Please reveal (vadasva) the secret topics of the Lord. This is the meaning of vadasva in the imperative form according to bhāṣanopasambhāsā: vad in the ātmanepada form means “to light up.” (Pāṇini 1.3.47) Or the word may be taken as vada and sva. Sva means “O my friend!” or “O my treasure!” You should speak for our benefit. O most learned one (vidvan)! This indicates Śukadeva’s knowledge of all those pastimes. The first two lines have been explained by Śrīdhara Svāmī as follows. “Please speak the topics for the devotees since you give immortality to those with spiritual insight (antar) who hear your topics through your form as the antaryāmī and you give death to the materialists (bahiḥ) in the form of time.” Or internally and externally you act in the forms of antaryāmī and time. You give bliss by your form of Viṣṇu situated internally through hearing your topics. You give suffering by your forms situated externally such as time or Yama when there is no hearing of your topics. Or you act internally and externally to give sweetness to the devotees and act externally and internally to give death to the materialists. Māyā-manuṣyasya: you appear like a normal human being, but this is only apparent because you are beyond material qualities, though you perform pastimes like a human. Or though appearing as a human (māyā) you are actually not human (amanuṣyasya), since you show powers like riding Garuḍa, defeating Śiva and bewildering Brahmā. Or māyā can mean mercy for Viśva-koṣa says māyā means mercy and pride. You appear in a human form with mercy. Or māyā can mean knowledge according to Trikaṇḍa-śeṣa and Nighantu. You appear as the supreme Brahman in human form with full knowledge. Another meaning: you went beyond the rules in dealing with people possessing bodies. Persons who could die at will, who were hard to kill, such as Bhīṣma and Droṇa, you had killed (mṛtum). Having killed others like Pūtanā and Kaṁsa, you gave them liberation (amṛtam) which is hard to attain though they were enemies. The word ca indicates that he gave them not only liberation but the goal of his highest devotees. Please recite such actions performed by your free will, because you are situated internally and externally as the three puruṣa avatāras and in various forms of time. It is very suitable that you perform these actions at will since you are situated internally and externally. The rest of the verse can be interpreted as above. Because of the power revealed through giving death or immortality in the earthly pastimes and because of the sweetness of the human actions in the earthly pastimes, the nature of Kṛṣṇa becomes easily revealed in his form on earth, more than in his form in Goloka. Therefore speak of these pastimes. Having previously heard of these pastimes, Parīkṣit was now very eager to know, since Kṛṣṇa in one form was most astonishing as both the source of all avatāras (Svayam Bhagavān) and was an avatāra (making his appearance on earth).

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa personally rescues His surrendered devotees — entering Uttarā's womb to save Parīkṣit, ferrying the Pāṇḍavas across Kurukṣetra's ocean.
    Practical Applications
    • When facing an overwhelming situation today, explicitly take shelter of Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet before acting — name the 'ocean' you cannot cross alone.
    • Recall one specific instance where you were protected without your own effort, and offer thanks to Kṛṣṇa as the unseen cakra-pāṇi behind it.
    • Read or hear one pastime of Kṛṣṇa's protection of His devotees (Pāṇḍavas, Prahlāda, Draupadī) and let it replace anxiety about your own vulnerabilities.
    Reflection Questions
    • When I face my own Kurukṣetra — a relationship, illness, or career battle that feels populated by Bhīṣma-sized fish — do I actually take shelter of Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet, or do I only invoke Him decoratively while paddling with my own strength?
    • Where in my life have I already been protected like Parīkṣit in the womb — rescued by a cakra I never saw — and have I let that remembrance soften me into gratitude, or have I quietly credited my own cleverness?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Arjuna was probably your age when Kṛṣṇa first told him 'fight.' Notice that Kṛṣṇa didn't tell him to drop his bow and meditate in a cave — He told him to do his work, harder, but with a different center. What 'bow' are you currently trying to put down because surrender feels easier than competence?
    • The 'great fish' in your ocean right now are not literal warriors — they're the people and standards you grew up revering: a parent's expectations, a teacher's authority, a tradition's weight. Crossing doesn't mean dishonoring them; it means not being eaten by them. There is a difference.
    • Don't outsource your kṣatriya energy to monks. Parīkṣit is recounting this verse from the perspective of someone about to die in seven days and still asking for kathā — not for escape, but because hearing about Kṛṣṇa is what a warrior does when the real battle is unavoidable.
    householder
    • Uttarā's surrender wasn't a one-time event before the missile struck — it was her standing condition. Audit your household: is Kṛṣṇa the standing center, or the emergency contact? The cakra came because she was already living inside the relationship.
    • The verse pairs the macro (Kurukṣetra) with the micro (one womb, one child). Your dharma has both scales every day: the public battles at work and the small protective acts at home. Don't be heroic in one and absent in the other.
    • Notice that Parīkṣit calls Arjuna 'my grandfather' — gratitude across generations is itself a spiritual practice. Speak Kṛṣṇa's name in front of your children specifically about your own elders' surrender, not as abstract theology. That is how the boat passes hands.
    senior
    • You are now in the position Parīkṣit inhabits in this verse — looking back, naming mercies, telling the next generation what actually carried you. Don't underestimate how much your specific testimony matters. Generalities don't transmit; named rescues do.
    • If you have grown bodily weak, remember: Parīkṣit received Kṛṣṇa's protection while still in the womb — before he could chant, serve, or even breathe on his own. The same Lord protects at the other end of life when capacity also thins. Your job now is less doing and more receiving with attention.
    • The verse ends with a request: 'Please describe His glorious activities.' Make this your daily posture — ask younger devotees and family members to tell you what they are hearing, reading, realizing. Do not only transmit; receive from them too.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Romanticizing Kṛṣṇa's protection of the Pāṇḍavas while ignoring that Arjuna still had to draw his bow — using śaraṇāgati as a substitute for sincere effort rather than its foundation.
    • Sliding into the māyāvāda misreading of māyā-manuṣyasya as 'Kṛṣṇa was only apparently personal' — forgetting Prabhupāda's emphasis that He is the Supreme Personality of Godhead playing on His own internal (yogamāyā) energy, not an impersonal force wearing a mask.
    • Wanting Kṛṣṇa as bestower of amṛta (rescue, liberation, sweetness) while resenting Him as bestower of mṛtyu (the very entanglements and reverses that drive us to surrender) — selectively accepting half of the same mercy.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Parīkṣit calls Kṛṣṇa the bestower of BOTH liberation AND material entanglement. If Kṛṣṇa hands out bondage too, is surrender really a free choice, or are we just on the receiving end of whichever side He decides to deal? Defend your position from the verse, not from sentiment.
    • Arjuna had Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer and still had to fight, kill kinsmen, and bleed through eighteen days. The 'boat of His lotus feet' didn't airlift the Pāṇḍavas out of Kurukṣetra — it carried them through it. Does this mean shelter in Kṛṣṇa is fundamentally different from rescue?
    • Uttarā was protected because she surrendered — but countless surrendered devotees throughout history have watched their children die. Is the Parīkṣit episode a promise, a precedent, or simply one līlā we shouldn't generalize from? Argue without softening either side.
    Role Play

    You are counseling a 34-year-old kṣatriya-natured software engineer whose startup is collapsing. He says: 'I've been chanting sixteen rounds for six years. I surrendered this company to Kṛṣṇa at the start. Now I'm watching it sink and my wife is pregnant. If Uttarā got the cakra, where is mine?' Respond personally — engage the verse, the māyā-manuṣya principle, and his specific situation. Do not retreat into platitudes about 'Kṛṣṇa's plan.'

    Objections & Responses
    • The 'ocean of Kurukṣetra' metaphor is poetic exaggeration. Bhīṣma was one man on a chariot, not a sea monster. Devotees overdramatize ordinary historical events to manufacture awe.
      Consider the asymmetry Parīkṣit is naming. Bhīṣma had a boon to choose his time of death and on day three alone felled tens of thousands. For Arjuna — even as a master archer — facing his pitāmaha whom he had touched the feet of since childhood, the obstacle was not merely military but ontological: how do you raise a weapon against the man who taught you dharma? That is the 'great fish' — not Bhīṣma's body count but the moral and emotional engulfment he represented. The metaphor isn't inflation; it's precision about what was actually being crossed.
    • Saying Kṛṣṇa 'plays on His own internal energy' (māyā-manuṣya) sounds like a theological escape hatch — whenever Kṛṣṇa does something embarrassingly human (eats, sleeps, loses, grieves), we just invoke yoga-māyā and the problem disappears.
      Fair pushback. The doctrine would be an escape hatch IF it were applied selectively to clean up inconvenient passages. But Parīkṣit applies it precisely where Kṛṣṇa LOOKS most powerful — entering the womb with cakra in hand. He is not hiding Kṛṣṇa's humanness; he is naming that BOTH the human-appearing Kṛṣṇa and the cakra-wielding Kṛṣṇa are the same Person operating through internal potency rather than external nature. The test of the doctrine is whether it explains the whole pattern, including Kṛṣṇa weeping at Subhadrā's departure or bowing to Sudāmā's feet. It does — that's the claim. Argue with the claim, not the convenience.
    Analogy

    The Pāṇḍavas crossed the Kaurava ocean as if stepping over a calf's hoofprint, because they did not swim — they took the boat of Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet. The same ocean drowned everyone who tried to swim by their own strength. Parīkṣit, addressing his own near-incineration in the womb, is naming the principle by which his entire family survived: the only safe vehicle through saṁsāra is Bhagavān's feet, not one's own arms.

    Stories
    Kuntī's prayer at the parting

    When Kṛṣṇa was about to leave Hastināpura after the war, Kuntī ran out and prayed (SB 1.8): 'Let calamities come again and again, so that we may see You again and again, for in calamity we always remembered You.' She named the very rescue Parīkṣit references here — the brahmāstra, Aśvatthāmā's weapon, Kṛṣṇa entering the womb with the Sudarśana.

    Kuntī's logic is not masochism; it is precision. The fish in the Kurukṣetra ocean (Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa) were not swallowed because the Pāṇḍavas were excellent swimmers. They were not swallowed because they had stopped swimming.

    Gajendra in the lake

    The elephant-king, seized by a crocodile, struggled for a thousand years on his own strength. Only when he gave up the calculation and offered a single lotus, calling out to the Lord who is independent of every conditioning, was he lifted (SB 8.2–3).

    Parīkṣit's grandfathers' ocean was a battlefield; Gajendra's ocean was a lake; both crossings required the same vehicle. The verse's vatsa-padam — the calf's hoofprint — is what saṁsāra becomes from the moment one stops trying to swim.

    Important Words
    • rāmaḥ — Balarāma
      From ram, 'to delight.' Balarāma is rāma in the original sense — He in whom the devotees take pleasure. Distinguish from Daśaratha-Rāma; here Bala-rāma is svayaṁ-prakāśa of Saṅkarṣaṇa, the original servitor-elder-brother of Kṛṣṇa.
    • saṅkarṣaṇaḥ — the first Deity in the quadruple group
      From sam + karṣ, 'to draw together.' Saṅkarṣaṇa is so named because at the end of each kalpa He withdraws (draws back together) the manifested creation. The same Person who is the cosmic withdrawer plays as a child's elder brother in Vraja — acintya-bhedābheda in person.
    • garbha-sambandhaḥ — connected with the womb
      Sambandha = connection. The very word names the first of the three Gauḍīya divisions (sambandha-abhidheya-prayojana). Here it is used at the physical level, but the question (how is connection possible without ordinary mechanics?) is exactly the deep question of Bhagavān's relation to embodied jīvas.
    • deha-antaram — transferring bodies
      Deha + antara, 'another body.' The ordinary law for the jīva — karma-driven transmigration (BG 2.13, tathā dehāntara-prāptiḥ). Parīkṣit's question highlights that Balarāma is not under this law: His 'transfer' is not the jīva's saṁsāra.
    My dear Śukadeva Gosvāmī, you have already explained that Saṅkarṣaṇa, who belongs to the second quadruple, appeared as the son of Rohiṇī named Balarāma. If Balarāma was not transferred from one body to another, how is it possible that He was first in the womb of Devakī and then in the womb of Rohiṇī? Kindly explain this to me.
    Purport

    Here is a question particularly directed at understanding Balarāma, who is Saṅkarṣaṇa Himself. Balarāma is well known as the son of Rohiṇī, yet it is also known that He was the son of Devakī. Parīkṣit Mahārāja wanted to understand the mystery of Balarāma’s being the son of both Devakī and Rohiṇī.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    My dear Śukadeva Gosvāmī, you have already explained that Saṅkarṣaṇa, who belongs to the second quadruple, appeared as the son of Rohiṇī named Balarāma. If Balarāma was not transferred from one body to another, how is it possible that He was first in the womb of Devakī and then in the womb of Rohiṇī? Kindly explain this to me.
    Commentary

    In the next four verses there is inquiry about the particulars of Krsna’s birth. The general description was given in the 9th canto (24. 54) There he is called sankarsana and ahisvara, the seventh child of Devaki and Vasudeva. "Since elsewhere you have refered to Sankarsana as the son of Rohini, how could he come from Devaki’s womb without having to change bodies?" This is the indication.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    In four verses Parīkṣit asks specific questions. You mentioned in SB 9.24.54 that Balarāma or Saṅkarṣaṇa was one among the sons of Devakī. But you also said that he was the son of Rohiṇī (SB 9.24.46). These statements referred to the same person.

    Personal Guidance
    Balarāma is Saṅkarṣaṇa Himself — His womb-to-womb passage is no ordinary transmigration but Kṛṣṇa's personal yoga-māyā arranging the līlā.
    Practical Applications
    • Refuse the impersonalist reflex that flattens Kṛṣṇa's and Balarāma's appearances into 'just another birth' — chant their names today knowing They descend, not transmigrate.
    • When a scriptural detail confuses you, follow Parīkṣit's example: ask your guide directly with vinaya rather than fabricating your own explanation.
    • Offer one act of seva to Balarāma today (a praṇāma, a remembrance before study) acknowledging Him as the source of spiritual strength, not a demigod.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do I quietly assume the body is the self — treating my own changes of body, role, or station as if they were transfers of *me* — and how would I act differently today if I held Balarāma's truth that the soul does not migrate even when the vessel does?
    • In what part of my sādhana am I trying to 'figure out' Kṛṣṇa's and His associates' movements with mundane logic, like Parīkṣit's apparent puzzle, instead of standing in vinaya and asking a guru — and what specific question have I been too proud or too lazy to put before a senior Vaiṣṇava?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When friends or social media flatten Kṛṣṇa into 'one of the Hindu gods' or 'a symbol of love,' practice the small courage of correction — say once today, plainly: 'In my understanding, He is the Supreme Person, not a symbol.' Notice the discomfort; do not smooth it.
    • Before your next exam or interview, consciously distinguish the body that is performing (which will pass through youth, middle age, old age — BG 4.20 territory of acting without attachment) from the soul that is eternal. Write the distinction on the corner of your notes. Act from the second.
    • Pick one peer-pressure situation this week — a party, a group chat, a trend — where you've been quietly going along. Ask: am I serving my friends' souls or just their bodily comfort? Then choose the harder, real-compassion move, even if it costs you cool points.
    householder
    • In your next family decision (school for the kids, a job offer, a property purchase), explicitly name which axis you're deciding on — material welfare or spiritual welfare of the souls involved. Both can matter, but refuse to let the first silently swallow the second.
    • Teach your children — even once this week, at the dinner table — that Kṛṣṇa is not one deity among many and not a metaphor. Use simple language, not jargon. The verse's distinction (Balarāma is not a transmigrating jīva) is exactly the distinction you are quietly transmitting or failing to transmit every day.
    • When stress about money or career rises, deliberately invoke vairāgya by remembering: this body and its career are passing through stages; the relationship with Kṛṣṇa is not. Offer the day's earnings, mentally, before you sleep — sevā reframes the same work without changing the work.
    senior
    • Use the proximity of your own dehāntara — the body's coming change — to deepen, not avoid, hard questions about Kṛṣṇa's nature. Like Parīkṣit, ask your teacher or sādhu-saṅga the question you have been embarrassed to ask. Seven days, seven months, seven years — the posture is the same.
    • Mentor one younger devotee or family member specifically on the personalist line: that Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Person, that Balarāma is Saṅkarṣaṇa Himself, that surrender is to Him, not to an impersonal 'light.' Do not assume they have absorbed this; most have not.
    • Begin actively loosening one attachment this month — a possession, a role, an opinion you have defended for forty years. Offer it consciously as sevā. The verse trains you to distinguish what merely changes bodies from what is eternal; your remaining years are for living on the right side of that line.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Using the 'soul does not change bodies' principle as a shrug — drifting into vairāgya-flavored neglect of one's actual sva-dharma duties (to family, varṇa, āśrama) under the cover of 'I am not this body.'
    • Flattening Balarāma into an impersonal 'energy' or 'principle' to resolve the Devakī-Rohiṇī mystery, instead of honoring Him as Saṅkarṣaṇa, a distinct personal expansion of Kṛṣṇa — and thereby slipping into the impersonalist habit of dissolving persons into concepts.
    • Imitating Parīkṣit Mahārāja's bold inquiry without his qualification — firing speculative 'how can this be?' questions at śāstra in a debating mood, rather than approaching with the humility of a disciple who has already surrendered and is seeking deeper darśana, not ammunition.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Parīkṣit asks how Balarāma could move from Devakī's womb to Rohiṇī's without 'transferring bodies' — share with your partner: when have you confused a transcendental act of Kṛṣṇa with an ordinary material event, and what tipped you off that you were thinking materialistically? Push each other past the safe answers.
    • The question is asked by a king who is seven days from death, to a sage who knows everything. Discuss: why does Parīkṣit still ask 'kindly explain this to me' rather than accept it on faith? Where in your own sādhana have you mistaken silent acceptance for vinaya, when in fact honest questioning would have served Kṛṣṇa more?
    • Balarāma is Saṅkarṣaṇa Himself, not a jīva taking another body (dehāntara). Discuss with your group: which of Kṛṣṇa's or Balarāma's activities have you been quietly explaining to skeptical friends in jīva-terms — 'just a symbol,' 'just a teaching story' — and what would it cost you socially to stop? Disagree honestly about whether that cost is worth paying.
    Role Play

    Two students. Student A is a devotee who has just told a college classmate (Student B, a thoughtful skeptic raised on comparative religion) that Balarāma was simultaneously the son of Devakī and Rohiṇī, and that this was not reincarnation or body-transfer (dehāntara) but the Lord's own inconceivable potency. Student B presses: 'So you're saying the rules don't apply to your god? Isn't that exactly what every tradition says about its own miracles?' Student A must respond as Parīkṣit-like inquirer turned Śuka-like teacher — neither retreating into 'it's just faith' nor pretending it's scientifically demonstrable. After 5 minutes, swap roles. Debrief: where did each of you reach for material compassion (smoothing the discomfort) instead of real compassion (serving the soul of your friend)?

    Objections & Responses
    • This is a contradiction dressed up as mystery. A baby cannot be in two wombs. Calling it 'inconceivable potency' (acintya-śakti) is just a way of refusing to answer the question — it's a thought-stopper, not theology.
      Parīkṣit Mahārāja raises exactly your objection — 'kuto dehāntaraṁ vinā,' how is this possible without transmigration? The verse honors the question; it does not suppress it. The Gauḍīya answer is not 'stop thinking' but 'think more carefully about categories.' The jīva is bound by the laws of dehāntara (BG's framework of bodies changing); Kṛṣṇa and His direct expansions like Saṅkarṣaṇa are not bound by those laws because They are not products of prakṛti. To insist Balarāma must obey jīva-rules is to have already concluded He is a jīva — which is the very point in dispute. Acintya-śakti is not a curtain pulled over ignorance; it names the precise place where our material logic, calibrated for conditioned souls, stops applying. The honest move is to notice the limit, not to pretend the limit is the whole map.
    • Even granting the theology, why does this matter to me? I have exams, a job, a marriage. A debate about whose womb Balarāma was in 5,000 years ago is the definition of irrelevant.
      It matters because the verse is training your discriminative wisdom (viveka) for the choice you make every hour: do I treat Kṛṣṇa as one more item inside the material system, or as the Person who stands outside it? If Balarāma is just another soul shuffling bodies, then bhakti is one more self-improvement project alongside your exams and your marriage — useful, optional, replaceable. If He is Saṅkarṣaṇa Himself, transcendent to dehāntara, then surrender to Him is categorically different from any other investment of your time. Parīkṣit asks this question seven days before his death. He is not doing trivia. He is sorting, at the end of his life, what is material and what is not — and he is showing you that the difference is not abstract. Today, in one decision — what you watch, what you say to your spouse, how you spend the next hour — locate which side of that line you are standing on.
    Analogy

    Asking how Balarāma could be in two wombs without 'changing bodies' is like asking how the same flame can light a second lamp without leaving the first. Saṅkarṣaṇa is not a body to be moved; He is the source-flame from which Rohiṇī's lamp was lit while Devakī's lamp continued to burn. Parīkṣit asks the question precisely so Śukadeva can establish: Bhagavān and His expansions are not subject to the ordinary mechanics of embodiment.

    Important Words
    • mukundaḥ — Kṛṣṇa, who can award liberation
      Mukti + da, 'giver of liberation.' But for the Gauḍīya line, Kṛṣṇa is mukunda primarily because He gives mukti as a side-effect while offering the higher gift — prema. Mukti is a free sample for those who came for the medicine; prema is for those who came for Him.
    • vrajam — to Vrajadhāma
      Accusative. Vraja = the cow-pasturing land, but in Gauḍīya theology Vraja-dhāma is the topmost manifestation of Kṛṣṇa's own abode — the seat of mādhurya-rasa, where the Six Gosvāmīs later recovered the lost līlā-sthalas. To be 'transferred to Vraja' is the line of every aspiring rāgānuga sādhaka.
    • jñātibhiḥ — His relatives
      Instrumental plural of jñāti. In Vraja Kṛṣṇa lives in jñāti-sambandha — with Nanda as father, Yaśodā as mother, Balarāma as brother, the gopas as cousins. The verse foregrounds that Bhagavān's līlā in Vraja is conducted in family relations, not in court or temple.
    • sātvatām patiḥ — the master of all Vaiṣṇava devotees
      Sātvata = the Vaiṣṇava community, devotees in sattva. Patiḥ = lord, husband, master. Kṛṣṇa is not merely a deity to be worshiped; He is patiḥ of the sātvatas — the One who maintains and is maintained by His own devotees in mutual relation.
    Why did Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, leave the house of His father, Vasudeva, and transfer Himself to the house of Nanda in Vṛndāvana? Where did the Lord, the master of the Yadu dynasty, live with His relatives in Vṛndāvana?
    Purport

    These are inquiries about the itinerary of Kṛṣṇa. Just after His birth in the house of Vasudeva in Mathurā, Kṛṣṇa transferred Himself to Gokula, on the other side of the Yamunā, and after some days He moved with His father, mother and other relatives to Nanda-grāma, Vṛndāvana. Mahārāja Parīkṣit was very much eager to hear about Kṛṣṇa’s activities in Vṛndāvana. This entire canto of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is full of activities performed in Vṛndāvana and Dvārakā. The first forty chapters describe Kṛṣṇa’s Vṛndāvana affairs, and the next fifty describe Kṛṣṇa’s activities in Dvārakā. Mahārāja Parīkṣit, to fulfill his desire to hear about Kṛṣṇa, requested Śukadeva Gosvāmī to describe these activities in full detail.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Why did Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, leave the house of His father, Vasudeva, and transfer Himself to the house of Nanda in Vṛndāvana? Where did the Lord, the master of the Yadu dynasty, live with His relatives in Vṛndāvana?
    Commentary

    He went from Vasudeva’s house to Vraja. Here Vraja means Mahavana. After going to Vraja he left the house of Nanda. Where did he go and establish his house along with the cowherd men?

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Mukunda means giver of liberation. Kṛṣṇa should have stayed in Mathurā to give liberation to Kaṁsa instead of going to Vraja. This question will be answered in the eighth and ninth chapters. Or since Mukunda means the happiness of liberation, as derived from mukti with dā (to give) with elision of syllables as in words like pṛṣodara from pṛṣat and udara and since that happiness is useless, the real meaning of Mukunda must be “the giver of the bliss of prema.” Therefore it is suitable that he went to Vraja to give prema, but he still must have produced a pretext for going. Later it will be understood that the Lord made Kaṁsa fear his father and mother by his going to Vraja. Parīkṣit uses the word “father” to indicate Vasudeva because of the apparent birth from Vasudeva, and out of respect because of his relationship with the Yadus. Śukadeva however later identifies Kṛṣṇa’s actual father with the words nandaḥ sva-putram ādāya pretyāgatam udāra-dhīḥ: generous Nanda immediately took his son Kṛṣṇa on his lap as if Kṛṣṇa had returned from death. (SB 10.6.43) Kva means “what particular place.” Jṣātibhiḥ means the cowherds and the Yādavas. Giving up Mahāvana where did he live with the cowherds? Giving up Mathurā, where did he live with the Yādavas? Thus the word has a different meaning in reference to Vṛndāvana and Dvārakā. However Kṛṣṇa considered the cowherds to be his main relatives. yāta yūyaṁ vrajaṁn tāta vayaṁ ca sneha-duḥkhitān jṣātīn vo draṣṭum eṣyāmo vidhāya suhṛdāṁ sukham Now you should all return to Vraja, dear father. We shall come to see you, our dear relatives who suffer in separation from us, as soon as we have given some happiness to your well-wishing friends. SB 10.45.23 It is understood that Śukadeva would explain the significance of leaving Mahāvana and living in Vṛndāvana. Kṛṣṇa is described as the protector of the devotees (sātvatāṁ patiḥ). He lived with his devotees to protect them with suitable pastimes. The answers to this question will be found later in the words of Upananda and the Lord.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa's move from Vasudeva's prison-house to Nanda's Vraja shows that the Lord seeks the soil of pure vātsalya-bhakti — go where Kṛṣṇa actually plays, not where He is merely born.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today which 'Mathurā' (a place of obligation and formality) you remain in out of habit, and identify one 'Vraja' (a setting of warm, personal devotion) you can step toward this week.
    • Sit for ten minutes and hear or read about Kṛṣṇa's Vṛndāvana līlā with the same eagerness as Mahārāja Parīkṣit — ask Śuka-like sources, not your own speculation, for the next detail.
    • Refuse to treat Kṛṣṇa as a distant majestic figure today; address Him by a vātsalya name (Mukunda, Gopāla) in your japa and seva, inviting the intimacy that Vraja embodies.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my own life have I been clinging to the 'house of Vasudeva' — a setting of formal reverence and security — when Kṛṣṇa is actually inviting me into the more intimate, demanding sevā of Vraja?
    • When I hear of Kṛṣṇa moving from Mathurā to Gokula to Nanda-grāma, what does it expose about my own resistance to letting the Lord rearrange my itinerary, relationships, and residence for His pleasure rather than mine?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the 'Mathurā' you were born into — your school's prestige ladder, your friend group's Instagram aesthetic, the career your family assumes you will pursue. Name it specifically this week, in writing.
    • Kṛṣṇa moved to where He could be loved freely, not where He was expected. Identify one 'Vraja' relationship in your life — a sādhu-saṅga, a devotee friend, a temple, a family elder who actually hears you — and visit it on purpose this week, not by accident.
    • Before you post, text, or scroll today, ask: am I performing for Kaṁsa's Mathurā (the algorithm, the peer audience), or am I living for Vraja (the small circle where Kṛṣṇa is actually present)? Cut one performance today.
    householder
    • Parīkṣit asked, 'where did the Lord live with His relatives?' Audit your home this week: is it a place where Kṛṣṇa could plausibly 'live with His relatives,' or only a place where the family's material ambitions live? Make one concrete change — a tulasī, a morning kīrtana, a meal offered before eaten.
    • Distinguish, in one current family decision (school, job, move, money), between material compassion (keeping everyone comfortable) and real compassion (serving the soul). Write both columns. Decide from the second.
    • Kṛṣṇa's move to Vraja was protective — Vasudeva carried Him to safety. As a parent or spouse, what are you carrying your dependents away from this season — what Kaṁsa-influence (a toxic environment, a screen habit, a social pressure) needs the Yamunā crossed today?
    senior
    • At Parīkṣit's stage of life — final chapter, eager to hear Kṛṣṇa's itinerary — what 'Vṛndāvana' do you still need to hear about? Choose one section of the Tenth Canto and commit to hearing it daily, in order, before you go.
    • Kṛṣṇa loosened His grip on Mathurā's royal identity to live as a cowherd boy. Name one prestige-attachment (title, expertise, your role as the family's decision-maker) you can quietly hand over this year, and to whom.
    • Mentor one younger person not by giving them advice, but by telling them about Kṛṣṇa's pastimes in Vraja — the way Śukadeva told Parīkṣit. Legacy in this line is not what you built; it is what kṛṣṇa-kathā you transmitted.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating Kṛṣṇa's transfer to Vṛndāvana as mere biography to be memorized, rather than as the Lord's deliberate choice of an intimate setting — and so missing the personalist invitation entirely.
    • Romanticizing Vraja as a mood or aesthetic ('simple village life,' 'be more present in nature') and quietly substituting that sentiment for actual sevā to Kṛṣṇa and His devotees in one's current āśrama.
    • Imitating Parīkṣit Mahārāja's eagerness to hear about Vṛndāvana while skipping his prerequisite — the disciplined inquiry of a sātvata under a bona fide guru — and thereby drifting into sahajiyā-style familiarity instead of guided śravaṇa.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Parīkṣit Mahārāja asks where Kṛṣṇa lived 'with His relatives' — yet the Lord left His biological father Vasudeva for Nanda Mahārāja. Where in your own life have you confused biological obligation with sva-dharma, and what would it cost you to reorder them the way Kṛṣṇa did?
    • Kṛṣṇa moves from the prison-palace of Mathurā to the cowherd village of Vraja. Discuss with your partner: which 'Mathurā' (prestigious, secure, but constricted) are you still clinging to, and which 'Vraja' (humbler, freer, more intimate with Kṛṣṇa) are you avoiding? Push back if your partner's Vraja sounds like an escape rather than a surrender.
    • Parīkṣit's question is not abstract theology — he is dying in seven days and wants to hear about Kṛṣṇa's itinerary. Is curiosity about Kṛṣṇa's pastimes (līlā) actually bhakti, or can it become a refined form of viṣaya? Disagree concretely: when does hearing kṛṣṇa-kathā nourish the soul, and when does it become spiritual entertainment?
    Role Play

    Two students sit across from each other. Student A is a 28-year-old who has just been offered a high-paying job in their hometown, near aging parents who expect them to stay and 'fulfill their duty.' Student B is the same person's older sibling, who took a similar path twenty years ago and is now quietly bitter. A devotee-friend (a third student, observing) must counsel A — drawing from SB 10.1.9 — on the difference between Vasudeva's house (the place of biological birth and worldly expectation) and Nanda's Vraja (the place where one is actually nourished in bhakti). The friend must NOT tell A what to decide, but must help A distinguish material compassion (keeping parents comfortable) from real compassion (serving the soul — A's own and the parents'). Run it for ten minutes, then swap roles.

    Objections & Responses
    • This whole question is mythological geography — Mathurā, Gokula, Vṛndāvana. Why should a modern person care which village a deity supposedly lived in?
      Parīkṣit Mahārāja did not ask out of tourist interest; he asked because he had seven days to live and wanted to hear Kṛṣṇa's actual movements, in actual places, with actual people. Bhakti in the Gauḍīya line is personalist — Kṛṣṇa is not a symbol or a 'divine spark within,' He is the Supreme Person who took birth, crossed the Yamunā, and lived in Nanda's house. The geography matters precisely because it refuses to dissolve Him into an abstract Absolute. If you let Mathurā and Vṛndāvana become 'just myth,' you are quietly importing impersonalism. Hear them as real places, and Kṛṣṇa stays a real Person you can surrender to today.
    • Kṛṣṇa abandoning Vasudeva's house to live with Nanda sounds like a child being taken from his parents — it seems ethically uncomfortable, even irresponsible, to hold this up as a model.
      Two clarifications. First, this was not abandonment — Vasudeva himself carried the infant Kṛṣṇa across the Yamunā to protect Him from Kaṁsa; the move was Vasudeva's act of love, not Kṛṣṇa's rejection. Second, the verse is not asking you to walk out on your family. It is asking you to notice that Kṛṣṇa's deepest relationships unfold in Vraja, among those who love Him without knowing He is God — pure vātsalya, sakhya, mādhurya. The instruction for the householder is not to flee Vasudeva's house, but to understand that real compassion (serving the soul) sometimes reorders our material expectations of where love is supposed to happen. Sva-dharma is not the same as biological convenience.
    Analogy

    Kṛṣṇa leaving Vasudeva's house for Nanda's home in Vraja is like a king who, owning a palace, chooses to be raised in a cowherd's hut not from poverty but from love. Where He is born establishes His mission; where He is raised reveals His heart. The question 'why Vraja?' is the question of mādhurya itself.

    Important Words
    • vraje — at Vṛndāvana
      Locative of vraja. Where Kṛṣṇa enacts His mādhurya-līlās with the gopas, gopīs, calves, and Yaśodā. The verse pairs vraje with madhupuryām (Mathurā) — the Lord moves between two registers: the intimate (Vraja) and the political (Mathurā).
    • madhupuryām — in Mathurā
      Madhu (sweet, also the name of an ancestor) + purī (city). The aiśvarya-stage of Kṛṣṇa's līlā — where He acts as a prince, kills Kaṁsa, establishes Yadu rule. In Mathurā He is awesome; in Vraja He is sweet. Same Kṛṣṇa, different rasa.
    • keśavaḥ — Kṛṣṇa, the killer of Keśī
      Two readings: 'one whose hair (keśa) is beautiful,' and (per Gauḍīya commentaries) 'the slayer of the demon Keśī.' The verse uses keśavaḥ specifically for the demon-killer Kṛṣṇa, anticipating Kaṁsa's death.
    • a-tat-arhaṇam — which was not at all sanctioned by the śāstras
      A + tat + arhaṇa, 'not worthy of that.' Parīkṣit deliberately raises the dharmic objection. The Bhāgavata's method: state the strongest counter-argument honestly before resolving it. Faith and inquiry are not opposed; Parīkṣit, the perfect devotee, asks the hardest question.
    Lord Kṛṣṇa lived both in Vṛndāvana and in Mathurā. What did He do there? Why did He kill Kaṁsa, His mother’s brother? Such killing is not at all sanctioned in the śāstras.
    Purport

    One’s maternal uncle, the brother of one’s mother, is on the level of one’s father. When a maternal uncle has no son, his nephew legally inherits his property. Therefore, why did Kṛṣṇa directly kill Kaṁsa, the brother of His mother? Mahārāja Parīkṣit was very much inquisitive about the facts in this regard.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Lord Kṛṣṇa lived both in Vṛndāvana and in Mathurā. What did He do there? Why did He kill Kaṁsa, His mother's brother? Such killing is not at all sanctioned in the śāstras.
    Commentary

    Madhu purya referes to mathura and dvaraka—the cities of the descendents of Madhu. Why did he kill his mother’s brother? He should not have done that, since Kamsa was his mother’s brother.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Please tell me Kṛṣṇa’s activities in those places. This is expressed in two verses. Vraja refers to Mahāvāna and Vṛndāvana. Madhupūri means Mathurā and Dvārakā, the cities of the Madhu dynasty. But while living in these places he went elsewhere and performed pastimes as well. Those pastimes should also be narrated. Keśava means “he who subordinates (vayate) Brahmā (ka) and Śiva (īśa) by his powers. Or va can mean “to exist.” The meaning is then “he who has Brahmā and Śiva as his excellent servants.” Therefore, many astonishing activities are possible in Kṛṣṇa. Why did he kill Kaṁsa? Addhā means “in person.”
