    Important Words
    • pañcatvam āpanne — when the body turns into five elements
      Pañca-tva (five-ness, the five elements: earth, water, fire, air, ether) + āpanne (locative absolute, 'when [it] has reached'). The body returns to its components — Sāṅkhya's dissolution-analysis used here in pastoral context.
    • dehī — the proprietor of the body, the living being
      Deha + -in, 'one who has a body.' The same word Kṛṣṇa uses in BG 2.13 (dehino 'smin yathā dehe). The deha is not the dehī. The verse keeps the distinction sharp — body dissolves; dehī continues.
    • karma-anugaḥ — following the reactions of his own fruitive activities
      Karma + anuga, 'following after.' The dehī does not choose his next body; karma chooses for him. Gauḍīya doctrine of karma is strict — the only way out of the karma-anuga chain is bhakti, which is karma-non-conforming.
    • avaśaḥ — spontaneously, automatically, without control
      A + vaśa (control), 'not under own control.' The verse is doctrinally exact: the dehī, at the moment of bodily death, is a-vaśa. There is no neutral observer's moment. Whoever has been preparing the consciousness all life — that conditioning takes over.
    When the present body turns to dust and is again reduced to five elements — earth, water, fire, air and ether — the proprietor of the body, the living being, automatically receives another body of material elements according to his fruitive activities. When the next body is obtained, he gives up the present body.
    Purport

    This is confirmed in Bhagavad-gītā, which presents the beginning of spiritual understanding. dehino ’smin yathā dehe kaumāraṁ yauvanaṁ jarā tathā dehāntara-prāptir dhīras tatra na muhyati “As the embodied soul continually passes, in this body, from boyhood to youth to old age, the soul similarly passes into another body at death. The self-realized soul is not bewildered by such a change.” ( Bg. 2.13 ) A person or an animal is not the material body; rather, the material body is the covering of the living being. Bhagavad-gītā compares the body to a dress and elaborately explains how one changes dresses one after another. The same Vedic knowledge is confirmed here. The living being, the soul, is constantly changing bodies one after another. Even in the present life, the body changes from childhood to boyhood, from boyhood to youth, and from youth to old age; similarly, when the body is too old to continue, the living being gives up this body and, by the laws of nature, automatically gets another body according to his fruitive activities, desires and ambitions. The laws of nature control this sequence, and therefore as long as the living entity is under the control of the external, material energy, the process of bodily change takes place automatically, according to one’s fruitive activities. Vasudeva therefore wanted to impress upon Kaṁsa that if he committed this sinful act of killing a woman, in his next life he would certainly get a material body still more conditioned to the sufferings of material existence. Thus Vasudeva advised Kaṁsa not to commit sinful activities. One who commits sinful activities because of ignorance, tamo-guṇa, obtains a lower body. Kāraṇaṁ guṇa-saṅgo ’sya sad-asad-yoni janmasu ( Bg. 13.22 ). There are hundreds and thousands of different species of life. Why are there higher and lower bodies? One receives these bodies according to the contaminations of material nature. If in this life one is contaminated by the mode of ignorance and sinful activities ( duṣkṛtī ), in the next life, by the laws of nature, one will certainly get a body full of suffering. The laws of nature are not subservient to the whimsical desires of the conditioned soul. Our endeavor, therefore, should be to associate always with sattva-guṇa and not indulge in rajo-guṇa or tamo-guṇa ( rajas-tamo-bhāvāḥ ). Lusty desires and greed keep the living entity perpetually in ignorance and prevent him from being elevated to the platform of sattva-guṇa or śuddha-sattva-guṇa. One is advised to be situated in śuddha-sattva-guṇa, devotional service, for thus one is immune to the reactions of the three modes of material nature.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    When the present body turns to dust and is again reduced to five elements—earth, water, fire, air and ether—the proprietor of the body, the living being, automatically receives another body of material elements according to his fruitive activities. When the next body is obtained, he gives up the present body.
    Commentary

    Birth means accepting a body and death means giving up a body. Both are inevitable. With that intention he speaks this verse. When the body is about to die, one receives another body, and then gives up the old body. But one should not lament for the loss of enjoyment along with loss of the body. Therefore Vasudeva says " karmanuga...avasah" the new body is decided by ones actions of this life. If you have the karma to enjoy in the future, then certainly you will get that enjoyment. Therefore you should give up killing a woman, which will produce suffering in the next body.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “It is true that death will occur but, with no body, enjoyment cannot be accomplished. It is proper to protect the body for gaining enjoyment for a short time.” The body is produced from the five elements and after some time there is cessation. The possessor of the body (dehī) cannot be destroyed, since it is different from the body. The cause of receiving another body is obedience to karma. Because one must receive the karmas there is no endeavor needed to receive the next body. Under the control of karma, by itself, one gets the next body. One repeatedly accepts (anuprāpya) and repeatedly gives up (anutyājate) bodies. Anu should be understood for the verb tyājate. The ātmanepada of the verb is poetic license.

    Personal Guidance
    At death the soul is dragged helplessly into a new body shaped by this life's karma — so live now in śuddha-sattva, in Kṛṣṇa's service.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice each time you indulge a lusty or greedy impulse today, and refuse it as karmic seed for a lower future body.
    • Choose one tamasic habit (intoxication, harming others, careless speech) and drop it today, knowing nature — not your wishes — writes the next body.
    • Anchor today in śuddha-sattva by performing one act of devotional service to Kṛṣṇa — chanting, offering food, or hearing the Bhāgavatam — before sleep.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which fruitive activities am I currently feeding — through habit, ambition, or indulgence — that are quietly shaping the kind of body and circumstances I will inherit next?
    • Where in my daily life am I drifting into rajo-guṇa or tamo-guṇa under the illusion that I am 'free' to choose, when in fact the laws of nature are silently casting my next vapuḥ?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Before posting, sending, or screenshotting something tonight, pause and ask: what kind of next-body habit am I building right now — am I feeding rajas (restless craving for reaction) or tamas (cruelty disguised as a joke)? The 'automatic' mechanism in this verse starts with micro-choices like this one.
    • Pick one friendship or group chat where you have been performing a version of yourself you do not actually respect. Recognize that this performance is a costume — like the body, a covering — and step out of it this week, even at social cost. You are practicing the dhīra-skill of not identifying with the dress.
    • When exam stress or a breakup makes you feel like 'this is the end of me,' name it for what it is: a transition inside one body, not the soul's annihilation. Memorize 'dehino 'smin yathā dehe' as the line you say to yourself before sleep on the worst nights.
    householder
    • In the next big family decision — a job change, a school for the kids, a property purchase — name out loud which guṇa is actually driving you (sattva, rajas, or tamo). Vasudeva's argument to Kaṁsa is that the mode you act from now literally shapes the body you wear next; do not let your spouse and children pay that bill.
    • Set up one daily family act of śuddha-sattva that is non-negotiable — a few minutes of kīrtana, prasāda offered before eating, reading one verse aloud at the table. Prabhupāda says this is what immunizes against the three modes; the household is the laboratory.
    • When you discipline or counsel your child this week, distinguish real compassion (serving their soul's long trajectory across bodies) from material compassion (sparing them today's discomfort). The verse asks you to parent with the next body in view, not just this semester's grades.
    senior
    • Walk through your home and identify three possessions you have been quietly treating as extensions of yourself. Begin giving them away or assigning them now, while you can do it consciously — practicing the giving-up of the present body before the body itself is given up.
    • Identify one younger person — a grandchild, a neighbor's kid, a junior at the temple — and commit to transmitting one specific Vaiṣṇava habit to them this year (a prayer, a verse, the offering of food). Your legacy is not the estate; it is the saṁskāra you plant that travels with them into their next body and yours.
    • Each evening, formally rehearse the moment of bodily departure: lie down, release the day's identifications, and chant the holy name as if this were the transition itself. Vasudeva is reminding Kaṁsa — and us — that the next body is decided by the consciousness in which we act and remember; train that consciousness now while the faculties still cooperate.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating the verse as a comforting abstraction about reincarnation while ignoring its sharp warning: this body's habits are actively engineering the next body's sufferings.
    • Hearing 'automatically receives another body' and lapsing into fatalism — 'whatever happens, happens' — instead of recognizing it as urgent motivation to associate with sattva-guṇa and śuddha-sattva (devotional service) right now.
    • Reducing the teaching to a generic 'soul changes bodies like clothes' platitude and losing the personalist thrust — that surrender to Kṛṣṇa, not mere philosophical detachment from the body, is what makes one immune to the three modes.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Vasudeva uses the certainty of bodily transmigration to dissuade Kaṁsa from a sinful act. In your own decision-making, do you actually let the next-body consequence weigh on you, or do you operate as if this life is the only ledger? Share an honest example where the two framings would have produced different choices.
    • Prabhupāda says the laws of nature are not subservient to the whimsical desires of the conditioned soul. Where in your own life are you still negotiating with those laws — assuming sincerity, intelligence, or good intent will exempt you from a karmic outcome you have already set in motion?
    • The verse says the soul receives the next body 'automatically' (avaśaḥ — helplessly) according to fruitive activity. If that automatic mechanism is real, why does devotional service (śuddha-sattva) free one from it? Try to articulate the difference between karma-shaped transmigration and bhakti-shaped destination — and surface where you disagree with each other.
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A plays a successful but materially-driven cousin who has just been diagnosed with a serious illness in middle age and is panicking — bargaining, denying, raging at the unfairness. Student B plays a Vaiṣṇava family member visiting for the evening. Student B must, without quoting scripture at the cousin or using the word 'karma' as a weapon, actually convey the substance of SB 10.1.39 — that the body is a covering being changed, that fruitive activity shapes what comes next, and that śuddha-sattva through devotional service is the one shelter not subject to the automatic mechanism. After ten minutes, swap roles. Then debrief: where did real compassion (serving the soul) and material compassion (soothing the body's fear) pull in opposite directions, and which one did you default to?

    Objections & Responses
    • There is no empirical evidence for reincarnation. Using fear of a 'next body' to shape this life's ethics is just a control mechanism dressed up as metaphysics.
      Vasudeva is not wielding fear as a control device — he is appealing to Kaṁsa's intelligence with the same logic Kṛṣṇa gives in Bg. 2.13: you have already watched one body change from infancy to youth to whatever you are now, and the same self has carried through. Transmigration is just that observed continuity extended past one death. Prabhupāda points out that the variety of species itself — hundreds of thousands of grades of bodies — is the empirical evidence: if bodies were not allotted according to guṇa and karma, the gradation would be arbitrary, which nothing in nature is. The Gauḍīya teacher does not ask you to believe on threat; he asks you to notice that you already accept bodily change within this life and to follow the logic one step further.
    • Telling people their suffering or low birth is the result of their own past sinful activity is cruel and victim-blaming. It rationalizes injustice.
      The verse is not addressed to the sufferer to shame them; it is addressed to the actor — to Kaṁsa, who is about to commit the violence — to warn him off. That is its whole pastoral force. A Gauḍīya teacher never weaponizes karma against a person already in difficulty; the response there is seva, real compassion, helping them toward śuddha-sattva and devotional service, which Prabhupāda explicitly says makes one immune to the reactions of the three modes. The doctrine is a brake on the perpetrator and a door for the sufferer, never a verdict pronounced over someone else's life.
    Analogy

    When the body returns to the five elements, the soul automatically receives another body according to karma — like a worker who finishes one shift and is immediately assigned the next, with no break in employment. The verse demolishes the popular fantasy of a free interval between bodies. Karma's bookkeeping is continuous; the only exit is bhakti.

    Important Words
    • padā ekena — on one foot
      Padā (instrumental of pada, foot) + ekena (with one). The walking analogy: the foot on the ground holds the body while the other lifts. Karma-grip on the present body holds until the next body has been gripped. The verse forbids the fantasy of a footless moment.
    • tṛṇa-jalaukā — a worm on a vegetable
      Tṛṇa (grass, leaf) + jalaukā (leech, worm; here a leaf-worm or aphid). The image is borrowed from older Upaniṣadic sources (cf. Bṛhad-āraṇyaka 4.4.3). Bhāgavata uses it for one specific purpose: to show that transmigration is leaf-to-leaf, not leaf-to-sky-to-leaf.
    • dehī — the living entity
      Same dehī as in verse 39. The verse continues developing the same subject: it is dehī who walks, dehī who transmigrates, dehī who is the constant through changes. Bhakti is dehī's only available resistance to the chain.
    • karma-gatim — the reactions of fruitive activities
      Karma + gati (motion, destination). Together: 'the karma-trajectory.' The dehī undergoes karma-gati — he is moved by karma. The grammar refuses agency: he goes through karma's motion, not the other way around.
    Just as a person traveling on the road rests one foot on the ground and then lifts the other, or as a worm on a vegetable transfers itself to one leaf and then gives up the previous one, the conditioned soul takes shelter of another body and then gives up the one he had before.
    Purport

    This is the process of the soul’s transmigration from one body to another. At the time of death, according to his mental condition, the living being is carried by the subtle body, consisting of mind, intelligence and ego, to another gross body. When higher authorities have decided what kind of gross body the living entity will have, he is forced to enter such a body, and thus he automatically gives up his previous body. Dull-minded persons who do not have the intelligence to understand this process of transmigration take for granted that when the gross body is finished, one’s life is finished forever. Such persons have no brains with which to understand the process of transmigration. At the present moment there is great opposition to the Hare Kṛṣṇa movement, which is being called a “brainwashing” movement. But actually the so-called scientists, philosophers and other leaders in the Western countries have no brains at all. The Hare Kṛṣṇa movement is trying to elevate such foolish persons by enlightening their intelligence so that they will take advantage of the human body. Unfortunately, because of gross ignorance, they regard the Hare Kṛṣṇa movement as a brainwashing movement. They do not know that without God consciousness one is forced to continue transmigrating from one body to another. Because of their devilish brains, they will next be forced to accept an abominable life and practically never be able to liberate themselves from the conditional life of material existence. How this transmigration of the soul takes place is very clearly explained in this verse.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Just as a person traveling on the road rests one foot on the ground and then lifts the other, or as a worm on a vegetable transfers itself to one leaf and then gives up the previous one, the conditioned soul takes shelter of another body and then gives up the one he had before.
    Commentary

    In this verse Vasudeva gives examples to show how one gives up the present body after attaining the new body ( in subtle form, via karma). A man puts his forward foot on the ground firmly and then withdraws his back leg from the ground and puts it forward, not putting both feet forward at the same time. However in this example the feet are fixing themselves and withdrawing themselves from the same ground. As this may be unsatisfying to the mind, he gives another example. A caterpillar, after taking support of one blade of grass in front of him, gives up the previous blade of grass.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Dehī means the possessor of the body. Instead of jalauka the variation jalūka is sometimes seen.

    Personal Guidance
    Death is just the soul stepping from one body to the next — like a foot lifting or a worm crossing leaves; only Kṛṣṇa-consciousness ends the walk.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice when you flinch at the thought of death today, and remind yourself the body is the leaf, not the soul crossing it.
    • Speak to one person caught in bodily fear — illness, aging, loss — and gently turn the conversation toward the eternal soul and shelter in Kṛṣṇa.
    • Refuse to spend this human birth like the 'brainless' — chant Hare Kṛṣṇa attentively for a fixed number of rounds today, treating sādhana as the one act that ends transmigration.
    Reflection Questions
    • Like the worm that will not release one leaf until its foot is firmly on the next, which body-based identity (role, relationship, possession) am I refusing to release because I have not yet placed my weight on Kṛṣṇa?
    • If 'higher authorities' decide my next body based on my mental condition at death, what is the actual content of my mind in its unguarded moments today — and what trajectory is it quietly setting?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • You have already 'died' as the child in your old school photos — that body and its friendships are gone, and you are still here. Sit with one such photo for two minutes tonight and notice who is doing the noticing; this is the same continuity the verse points to past the final transition.
    • Your phone trains your mental condition every hour. The verse says the mind at the moment of death decides the next body — extrapolate: the mind at the moment of every sleep decides tomorrow's mood, focus, and desires. For one week, put down the phone 30 minutes before sleep and chant or read instead. Watch what shifts.
    • Peer pressure works because you secretly believe this body and this friend group are you. Pick one situation this week — a party, a group chat, a trend — where you have been performing to belong, and skip it deliberately. Notice the fear that comes up; that fear is the worm's grip on the old leaf.
    householder
    • The mortgage, the school admissions, the promotion — these are leaves the worm is currently standing on. Name out loud, with your spouse this week, which leaf you are most terrified to leave. Then together decide one concrete way to loosen that grip — a financial cushion, a will, a frank talk with the kids — so fear is not steering the household.
    • Your children are watching what mental condition you cultivate at the end of each day. If you collapse into news, scrolling, or grievance every night, you are training their saṁskāras as much as your own. Institute one family practice — a tulasī offering, a verse read aloud, ārati — that becomes the last input of the day for everyone in the house.
    • When a parent or in-law is aging or dying, distinguish real compassion from material compassion. Material compassion arranges comfort for the body; real compassion arranges Kṛṣṇa's name in the room. Do both, but do not skip the second because the first is socially easier.
    senior
    • You are now closer to the foot-lift than the foot-plant. Spend 15 minutes this week writing down what mental condition you want to be in at the moment of death — concretely, what name on the lips, what image before the eyes — and then audit your daily routine against that target. Adjust one thing.
    • Legacy understood materially is another leaf — the firm, the house, the reputation. Legacy understood as a Vaiṣṇava is what you transmit of Kṛṣṇa to grandchildren, students, and neighbors. Identify one younger person who has no one giving them this verse, and begin meeting with them monthly. Do not wait for them to ask.
    • Loosen one possession this month — not symbolically, actually. Give away a piece of property, a collection, an heirloom, while you can still witness its right placement. Each release is rehearsal for the final release the verse describes, and each one weakens the worm's reflex to clutch the leaf it is about to leave.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating transmigration as an abstract metaphysical doctrine to debate or defend, rather than as the immediate logic that should reshape today's choices about how the mind is being trained.
    • Using the 'soul is eternal' teaching as emotional anesthesia — bypassing real grief, responsibility, or the urgency of sādhana, instead of letting the verse sharpen vairāgya toward this body and seriousness toward the next.
    • Assuming that intellectual assent to transmigration is the same as being prepared for it — forgetting Prabhupāda's point that the subtle body carries you according to your mental condition, not according to your stated philosophy.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Prabhupāda calls modern scientists and philosophers 'brainless' for denying transmigration. Is that polemic still useful in your circle today, or does it close more doors than it opens? Where in your own life have you been intellectually polite about this verse's claim, and what has that politeness cost you?
    • The verse uses two images: a walker shifting weight foot to foot, and a worm crossing leaf to leaf. One feels dignified, the other slightly humiliating. Which image lands harder for you, and why? Share a moment in the last year when you were clearly the worm.
    • If 'higher authorities' decide the next body based on the mental condition at death, then sādhana is essentially rehearsal for one moment. Do you actually live as if that is true? Where would your daily schedule have to break for that conviction to be visible to someone watching you?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A is a hospice nurse who has just sat with a dying patient — a kind, secular man who told her, 'When the lights go out, they go out. That's it.' Student B is a Gauḍīya devotee friend she calls that night, shaken. Student A must voice the patient's view honestly and her own sympathy with it; Student B must respond using SB 10.1.40 — the foot-and-leaf images, the role of the subtle body, the mental condition at death — without lecturing, without quoting verse numbers, and without offering vague comfort. After 6 minutes, swap roles. Then debrief: where did the devotee slip into platitude? Where did the verse actually land?

    Objections & Responses
    • There is zero empirical evidence for transmigration. Calling scientists 'brainless' for refusing to believe an unfalsifiable claim is not a response — it is a tantrum. Why should I take this verse seriously rather than as pre-modern speculation?
      Fair — the polemical edge in the purport is a feature of Prabhupāda's preaching style, not the argument itself. The argument is this: every one of us has already watched the body of a five-year-old, a fifteen-year-old, and a thirty-year-old 'die' inside this single lifetime, while the one who remembers them remains. The verse simply extends that observed continuity past one more transition. The empirical question — 'is there a witness behind these changing bodies?' — is one you can examine in your own experience right now. Śāstra describes the mechanism (subtle body, mental condition at death); your job is not to accept it on faith but to test the prior claim of a continuous self, on which the rest stands. Surrender to Kṛṣṇa is what gives this examination weight; without Him it stays an interesting hypothesis.
    • If 'higher authorities' decide my next body and I am 'forced' into it, this is just karmic determinism. Where is my agency? It sounds like I am being processed by a cosmic bureaucracy.
      The verse does describe a forced transfer — but the force is the momentum of your own ahaṅkāra and saṁskāras, not an external bureaucracy. The 'higher authorities' administer; they do not author. What they administer is the mental condition you yourself cultivated. That is precisely where agency lives — in this human body, right now, in what you feed the mind. The Gauḍīya answer is sharper still: bhakti to Kṛṣṇa cuts the karmic chain that the administrators would otherwise have to enforce. You are not negotiating with the bureaucracy; you are stepping out of its jurisdiction by taking shelter of Him personally. Sarva-dharmān parityajya is the exit, not a loophole.
    Analogy

    Just as a person walking rests one foot before lifting the other, or as a worm on a leaf transfers itself to the next leaf before relinquishing the first, the conditioned soul accepts another body before giving up the present one. The Bhāgavata's choice of image — the walker, the worm — refuses the romantic interval; transmigration is not a journey through space but the leaf-to-leaf grip of attachment.

    Important Words
    • svapne — in a dream
      Locative of svapna, 'dream.' The Bhāgavata's favored analogy for ordinary consciousness. In Gauḍīya: jāgrat-svapna-suṣupti are all conditioned states; turīya is the bhāva-state of pure devotion. The dream-analogy is doctrinally precise, not poetic.
    • abhiniviṣṭa — is fully absorbed
      Abhi (toward) + ni-viṣṭa (entered). The same word is used in BG 13.18-style descriptions. The verse identifies the operative mechanism: it is abhiniveśa (deep absorption) that authors the next embodiment. Bhakti's task is to make Kṛṣṇa the object of abhiniveśa.
    • dṛṣṭa-śrutābhyām — by what has been seen and heard
      Dṛṣṭa (seen) + śruta (heard). Both feed the mind. The Gauḍīya commitment to controlled hearing (śravaṇa-saṁyama) starts here: what you let in through eye and ear becomes the material from which your next body is built.
    • prapadyate — surrenders to
      Pra + pad, 'falls toward, surrenders to.' Same root as prapatti. The verse uses prapadyate of the conditioned soul surrendering to its dream — bhakti uses the same word for surrendering to Bhagavān (BG 18.66, mām ekaṁ śaraṇaṁ vraja). Same verb; opposite direction.
    • apasmṛtiḥ — experiencing forgetfulness of the present body
      Apa (away) + smṛti (memory). Forgetfulness. Kṛṣṇa says (BG 15.15) mattaḥ smṛtir jñānam apohanaṁ ca — from Him come both memory and forgetfulness. The Bhāgavata reminds: smṛti and apasmṛti are Bhagavān's own administration; the devotee asks for the right one.
    Having experienced a situation by seeing or hearing about it, one contemplates and speculates about that situation, and thus one surrenders to it, not considering his present body. Similarly, by mental adjustments one dreams at night of living under different circumstances, in different bodies, and forgets his actual position. Under this same process, one gives up his present body and accepts another [tathā dehāntara-prāptiḥ].
    Purport

    Transmigration of the soul is very clearly explained in this verse. One sometimes forgets his present body and thinks of his childhood body, a body of the past, and of how one was playing, jumping, talking and so on. When the material body is no longer workable, it becomes dust: “For dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.” But when the body again mixes with the five material elements — earth, water, fire, air and ether — the mind continues to work. The mind is the subtle substance in which the body is created, as we actually experience in our dreams and also when we are awake in contemplation. One must understand that the process of mental speculation develops a new type of body that does not actually exist. If one can understand the nature of the mind ( manorathena ) and its thinking, feeling and willing, one can very easily understand how from the mind different types of bodies develop. The Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, therefore, offers a process of transcendental activities wherein the mind is fully absorbed in affairs pertaining to Kṛṣṇa. The presence of the soul is perceived by consciousness, and one must purify his consciousness from material to spiritual, or, in other words, to Kṛṣṇa consciousness. That which is spiritual is eternal, and that which is material is temporary. Without Kṛṣṇa consciousness, one’s consciousness is always absorbed in temporary things. For everyone, therefore, Kṛṣṇa recommends in Bhagavad-gītā (9.34) , man-manā bhava mad-bhakto mad-yājī māṁ namaskuru. One should always be absorbed in thought of Kṛṣṇa, one should become His devotee, one should always engage in His service and worship Him as the supreme great, and one should always offer Him obeisances. In the material world one is always a servant of a greater person, and in the spiritual world our constitutional position is to serve the Supreme, the greatest, paraṁ brahma. This is the instruction of Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu. Jīvera ‘svarūpa’ haya-kṛṣṇera ‘nitya-dāsa’ (Cc. Madhya 20.108). To act in Kṛṣṇa consciousness is the perfection of life and the highest perfection of yoga. As Lord Kṛṣṇa says in Bhagavad-gītā (6.47) : yoginām api sarveṣāṁ mad-gatenāntarātmanā śraddhāvān bhajate yo māṁ sa me yuktatamo mataḥ “Of all yogīs, he who always abides in Me with great faith, worshiping Me in transcendental loving service, is most intimately united with Me in yoga and is the highest of all.” The condition of the mind, which flickers between saṅkalpa and vikalpa, accepting something and rejecting it, is very important in transferring the soul to another material body at the time of death. yaṁ yaṁ vāpi smaran bhāvaṁ tyajaty ante kalevaram taṁ tam evaiti kaunteya sadā tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ “Whatever state of being one remembers when he quits his body, that state he will attain without fail.” ( Bg. 8.6 ) Therefore one must train the mind in the system of bhakti-yoga, as did Mahārāja Ambarīṣa, who kept himself always in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Sa vai manaḥ kṛṣṇa-padāravindayoḥ . One must fix the mind at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa twenty-four hours a day. If the mind is fixed upon Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, the activities of the other senses will be engaged in Kṛṣṇa’s service. Hṛṣīkeṇa hṛṣīkeśa-sevanaṁ bhaktir ucyate: to serve Hṛṣīkeśa, the master of the senses, with purified senses is called bhakti. Those who constantly engage in devotional service are situated in a transcendental state, above the material modes of nature. As Kṛṣṇa says in Bhagavad-gītā (14.26) : māṁ ca yo ’vyabhicāreṇa bhakti-yogena sevate sa guṇān samatītyaitān brahma-bhūyāya kalpate “One who engages in full devotional service, who does not fall down in any circumstance, at once transcends the modes of material nature and thus comes to the level of Brahman.” One must learn the secret of success from the Vedic literatures, especially when the cream of Vedic knowledge is presented by Bhagavad-gītā as it is. Because the mind is ultimately controlled by the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Kṛṣṇa, the word apasmṛtiḥ is significant. Forgetfulness of one’s own identity is called apasmṛtiḥ. This apasmṛtiḥ can be controlled by the Supreme Lord, for the Lord says, mattaḥ smṛtir jñānam apohanaṁ ca: “From Me come remembrance, knowledge and forgetfulness.” Instead of allowing one to forget one’s real position, Kṛṣṇa can revive one’s original identity at the time of one’s death, even though the mind may be flickering. Although the mind may work imperfectly at the time of death, Kṛṣṇa gives a devotee shelter at His lotus feet. Therefore when a devotee gives up his body, the mind does not take him to another material body ( tyaktvā dehaṁ punar janma naiti mām eti ); rather, Kṛṣṇa takes the devotee to that place where He is engaged in His pastimes ( mām eti ), as we have already discussed in previous verses. One’s consciousness, therefore, must always be absorbed in Kṛṣṇa, and then one’s life will be successful. Otherwise the mind will carry the soul to another material body. The soul will be placed in the semen of a father and discharged into the womb of a mother. The semen and ovum create a particular type of body according to the form of the father and mother, and when the body is mature, the soul emerges in that body and begins a new life. This is the process of transmigration of the soul from one body to another ( tathā dehāntara-prāptiḥ ). Unfortunately, those who are less intelligent think that when the body disappears, everything is finished. The entire world is being misled by such fools and rascals. But as stated in Bhagavad-gītā (2.20) , na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre. The soul does not die when the body is destroyed. Rather, the soul takes on another body.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Having experienced a situation by seeing or hearing about it, one contemplates and speculates about that situation, and thus one surrenders to it, not considering his present body. Similarly, by mental adjustments one dreams at night of living under different circumstances, in different bodies, and forgets his actual position. Under this same process, one gives up his present body and accepts another [tathā dehāntara-prāptiḥ [Bg. 2.13]].
    Commentary

    Vasudeva now shows and example from everyday life. Just as in a dream one sees a body similar to the one in waking state (idrsam), so a person whose consciousness is deeply absorbed in someone through seeing (such as a king) or through hearing (for example, hearing about Indra) one sees oneself as the king or Indra, so that one can enjoy similar to the king or Indra, and one forgets ones original body.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    According to Śrīdhara Svāmī an example is given to understand by personal experience. Hi indicates that one forgets even in the waking state. What is seen or heard applies to both dreaming and waking states. One can thus understand the difference between the ātmā and the body. In dreams and in fantasy by giving up identity with the body and becoming absorbed in different body, one can realize one’s difference from one’s body. Because of the control of karma, on attaining the new body one gives up the old body. This of course confirms that attaining another body is unavoidable

    Personal Guidance
    Just as the mind builds dream-bodies from what it dwells on, at death it carries the soul into a new body shaped by its strongest absorption — so absorb it in Kṛṣṇa now.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice three times today when your mind is dragging you into a fantasy 'body' — a future role, a past glory, a grievance — and re-anchor it at Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet by chanting His name.
    • Before sleep tonight, deliberately offer the day's seeing and hearing to Kṛṣṇa, so the mind rehearses Him rather than viṣaya as you cross into the dream state.
    • Refuse to feed the inputs (scrolling, gossip, idle entertainment) that you would not want to be your last thought at death — cut one such input starting today.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which 'dream-body' am I currently inhabiting in waking life — what mental rehearsal of a future self, role, or circumstance have I surrendered to, forgetting the body and duty actually in front of me?
    • If at this moment I had to give up this body, what bhāva would my mind carry me toward — and does my daily sādhana actually train it toward Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet, or toward something else I haven't admitted?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Audit one week of your scrolling and series-watching. The verse says we 'surrender' to whatever we repeatedly see and hear (dṛṣṭa-śrutābhyāṁ manasānucintayan) — the influencer's body you keep watching, the relationship you keep imagining, the version of yourself you keep rehearsing in your head. Name out loud the one fantasy-body you have been building, and cut the input feeding it for seven days.
    • Before an exam or a hard conversation, notice how much of the night before is spent in manoratha — replaying imagined scenarios, fantasy victories, fantasy disasters. Replace ten minutes of that loop with chanting Hare Kṛṣṇa or reading one verse with translation. You are not killing ambition; you are refusing to let the mind cast you in a body that does not exist yet.
    • When a friend group or a romantic interest starts to define who you are — 'I am the kind of person who...' — recognize this as an ahaṅkāra-body the mind is stitching together. Speak with one elder devotee or mentor this month who can mirror back to you the eternal soul beneath the college-self you are constructing.
    householder
    • Notice the bodies you are mentally rehearsing for your children — the doctor-child, the IIT-child, the obedient-child. The verse warns that what we contemplate, we surrender to. Sit with your spouse this week and ask: which of these projected futures is for the child's soul, and which is a manoratha of our own ahaṅkāra wearing a parental costume?
    • At the end of each workday, before opening the next screen, pause for two minutes and offer the day's actions to Kṛṣṇa (man-manā bhava mad-bhakto). The householder's danger is not laziness — it is that every working hour silently builds the body of a 'successful professional' the mind intends to inhabit forever. Interrupt that construction daily.
    • Examine one major financial or career decision pending right now. Ask honestly: am I choosing this because dharma and family welfare require it, or because I have been contemplating a lifestyle-body (the house, the title, the vacation) and am now surrendering to that imagined form? Bring this to a senior Vaiṣṇava before you decide.
    senior
    • The vivid memories of childhood and middle-age that now visit unbidden are not nostalgia — Prabhupāda explicitly says the mind continues to work even as bodies dissolve, and these are the very mechanism that will shape the next birth. Each time a memory-body rises, audibly say 'Kṛṣṇa' and turn the mind toward His lotus feet. Practice this now, while the mind is still trainable, so it is automatic at the final hour.
    • Identify one attachment — a property, a grudge, a role you held — that you are still mentally inhabiting decades after it ended. This is a phantom body the mind refuses to cremate. Take one concrete act this month to formally release it: write the will, make the call, give the thing away. Loosen the grip before the grip becomes the next womb.
    • Mentor at least one younger devotee or family member specifically on the verse's teaching of dehāntara-prāpti — not as doctrine, but as your own observed experience of bodies passed through. The senior years are the unique window when this teaching can be transmitted with the authority of someone who has actually watched bodies come and go. Do not let that window close in silence.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating transmigration as an abstract metaphysical doctrine to debate, rather than as the urgent reason to fix the mind on Kṛṣṇa today — turning the verse into theory while the mind keeps building its next material body unchecked.
    • Assuming that because Kṛṣṇa can revive a devotee's smṛti at the moment of death, one can postpone serious sādhana now — ignoring that the apasmṛtiḥ-controlling mercy comes to those who have actually trained the mind in bhakti-yoga like Mahārāja Ambarīṣa, not to those who merely intend to.
    • Confusing vivid manorathena fantasy life — planning, replaying, speculating — with genuine contemplation, and so mistaking a mind absorbed in viṣaya for a mind being purified, when in fact each rehearsed scenario is shaping the next body.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Prabhupāda says the mind 'develops a new type of body that does not actually exist' through manorathena. Share with your partner one fantasy-body you currently inhabit in your daydreams (the future-you who has lost the weight, gotten the promotion, won the argument). Then disagree: is rehearsing this future a harmless motivation, or is it the very mechanism of dehāntara-prāpti this verse warns against? Push each other — don't settle for 'it depends.'
    • The verse equates dreaming, contemplating what we've seen-and-heard, and transmigration as one continuous process. In your group, argue both sides: (a) modern media — the films we binge, the feeds we scroll — is a serious soteriological emergency because we are literally building our next body in viṣaya; (b) this is overstated; bhakti-yoga can absorb these inputs without harm. Where does each of you actually stand, not just theoretically?
    • Apasmṛtiḥ — forgetfulness of one's real position — is what Kṛṣṇa Himself can grant or withdraw. Yet Prabhupāda also insists we must train the mind via sādhana like Mahārāja Ambarīṣa. Discuss the apparent tension: if Kṛṣṇa controls smṛti and apohanam, why exert ourselves at all? Where does each of you over-rely on one side — passive 'Kṛṣṇa will handle it' or anxious 'I must fix my mind by sheer effort'?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A is a hospice volunteer sitting with a dying 70-year-old man who whispers, 'I keep seeing my childhood home, my mother calling me in for dinner — am I going crazy?' Student B is the dying man. Student A must respond from this verse — without quoting Sanskrit at the bedside — helping him understand that the mind's vivid return to a past body is not madness but the very mechanism by which the soul will soon transit to a next body, and gently turning his attention toward Kṛṣṇa as the only shelter that breaks the cycle. After 5 minutes, swap. Then debrief: where did you slip into generic 'it's okay, let go' platitudes versus actually transmitting the verse's teaching on dehāntara-prāpti and apasmṛtiḥ?

    Objections & Responses
    • This is just pre-scientific cosmology dressed up as psychology. Dreams are neurological — REM sleep, memory consolidation. Equating them with 'transmigration' is a category error. Why should I take the leap from 'the mind imagines bodies in dreams' to 'therefore the soul transmigrates to a new body at death'?
      The verse is not arguing from dreams to transmigration as a deductive proof — it is offering a direct experiential analogy you can verify in your own consciousness right now. You already know, without a microscope, that something in you persists through last night's dream-body, through your eight-year-old body, through the body you had before this conversation. That continuity is not neurology; neurology is what the continuity observes. Prabhupāda's point is sharper: the same subtle mechanism (manorathena — mental rehearsal of what is seen and heard) that fabricates a dream-body tonight is fabricating, by accumulation, the gross body you will wear next. Dismiss that and you have not refuted the verse; you have only declined to look. The Gauḍīya invitation is not 'believe this'; it is 'observe your own mind for one week and notice whether it is, in fact, building bodies it intends to inhabit.'
    • If Kṛṣṇa controls remembrance and forgetfulness Himself (mattaḥ smṛtir jñānam apohanaṁ ca), and He gives the devotee shelter even when the mind is flickering at death, then the whole urgency around training the mind collapses. I'll just chant a bit, call myself a devotee, and trust Him to bail me out at the end. Why the heavy sādhana?
      This is the exact misreading Prabhupāda anticipates by citing Mahārāja Ambarīṣa in the same purport. Kṛṣṇa's rescue at the moment of death is not a courtesy extended to anyone who claimed the label; it is extended to those whose mind has been actually placed at His lotus feet — sa vai manaḥ kṛṣṇa-padāravindayoḥ — through years of hṛṣīkeṇa hṛṣīkeśa-sevanam. The mind at death does not suddenly turn toward Kṛṣṇa if it spent fifty years turning toward viṣaya; it goes where it has been trained to go (yaṁ yaṁ vāpi smaran bhāvaṁ). Surrender is not a verbal contract that bypasses the mind's grooves — it is the substance that wears those grooves into the shape of bhakti. The 'shelter' you are counting on is real, and it is reserved for the one who has actually taken shelter, daily, in small acts, long before the final breath.
    Analogy

    Vasudeva explains transmigration by the analogy of a dream: in sleep, by mental adjustment, one sees oneself in different bodies and forgets the body lying on the bed. Death is a longer version of the same mechanism — the mind, absorbed by its dominant thought, projects the next body and forgets the present one. The verse teaches that the next body is being authored, right now, by what the mind is rehearsing tonight.

    Stories
    Bharata Mahārāja and the deer

    Emperor Bharata, after renouncing his kingdom, was performing severe austerities by the river when he rescued an orphaned deer. His affection for the fawn grew until, at the moment of death, his mind was fixed on the deer rather than on Bhagavān (SB 5.7–8).

    He was reborn as a deer in his next life — but because of his prior practice, he retained memory of his fall and resolved not to be caught again by saṅga. In his third life as Jaḍa-Bharata he refused to speak or engage, lest any new attachment author another wrong rebirth.

    The verse here teaches the principle Bharata's life demonstrates: at the moment of death, the mind's last absorbing thought becomes the next body. Vasudeva is using this principle to reason with Kaṁsa, but the verse remains as the personal warning to every hearer.

    Important Words
    • daiva-coditam — impelled by accident or deliberation
      Daiva (fate, providence) + codita (impelled). The mind speculates because daiva impels it. The verse refuses the modern fantasy of pure free will at the level of mind; speculation itself is karma-driven. Only bhakti reaches above daiva.
    • vikāra-ātmakam — changing from one type of thinking, feeling and willing to another
      Vikāra (modification) + ātmaka (consisting of). The mind is constituted of changes. In Gauḍīya psychology, the mind's vikāra-nature is precisely what bhakti steadies — not by suppressing the changes but by giving them one fixed object (Kṛṣṇa).
    • māyā-raciteṣu — where the material energy creates a similar body
      Māyā + racita (constructed). The next body is constructed by māyā — the deluding potency. The conditioned soul does not author it himself; he merely supplies the mental template. The body is māyā's product, the mind is the order-form.
    • prapadyamānaḥ — being surrendered
      Present participle of pra-pad. The conditioned soul is constantly prapadyamāna — surrendering — but to the wrong object: to material thinking. Bhakti is not the introduction of surrender; it is the redirection of an already-ongoing surrender.
    At the time of death, according to the thinking, feeling and willing of the mind, which is involved in fruitive activities, one receives a particular body. In other words, the body develops according to the activities of the mind. Changes of body are due to the flickering of the mind, for otherwise the soul could remain in its original, spiritual body.
    Purport

    One can very easily understand that the mind is constantly flickering, changing in the quality of its thinking, feeling and willing. This is explained by Arjuna in Bhagavad-gītā (6.34) : cañcalaṁ hi manaḥ kṛṣṇa pramāthi balavad dṛḍham tasyāhaṁ nigrahaṁ manye vāyor iva suduṣkaram The mind is cañcala, flickering, and it changes very strongly. Therefore Arjuna admitted that controlling the mind is not at all possible; this would be as difficult as controlling the wind. For example, if one were in a boat moving according to the wind on a river or the sea, and the wind were uncontrollable, the tilting boat would be very much disturbed and extremely difficult to control. It might even capsize. Therefore, in the bhava-samudra, the ocean of mental speculation and transmigration to different types of bodies, one must first control the mind. By regulative practice one can control the mind, and this is the purpose of the yoga system ( abhyāsa-yoga-yuktena ). But there is a chance of failure with the yoga system, especially in this Age of Kali, because the yoga system uses artificial means. If the mind is engaged in bhakti-yoga, however, by the grace of Kṛṣṇa one can very easily control it. Therefore Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu has recommended, harer nāma harer nāma harer nāmaiva kevalam. One should chant the holy name of the Lord constantly, for the holy name of the Lord is nondifferent from Hari, the Supreme Person. By chanting the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra constantly, one can fix the mind on the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa ( sa vai manaḥ kṛṣṇa-padāravindayoḥ ) and in this way achieve the perfection of yoga. Otherwise, the flickering mind will hover on the platform of mental speculation for sense enjoyment, and one will have to transmigrate from one type of body to another because the mind is trained only in relation to the material elements, or, in other words, to sense gratification, which is false. Māyā-sukhāya bharam udvahato vimūḍhān ( Bhāg. 7.9.43 ). Rascals ( vimūḍhān ), being controlled by mental speculation, make huge arrangements by which to enjoy life temporarily, but they must give up the body at the time of death, when everything is taken away by Kṛṣṇa’s external energy ( mṛtyuḥ sarva-haraś cāham ). At that time, whatever one has created in this life is lost, and one must automatically accept a new body by the force of material nature. In this life one may have constructed a very tall skyscraper, but in the next life, because of one’s mentality, one may have to accept a body like that of a cat, a dog, a tree or perhaps a demigod. Thus the body is offered by the laws of material nature. Kāraṇaṁ guṇa-saṅgo ’sya sad-asad-yoni janmasu ( Bg. 13.22 ). The spirit soul takes birth in higher and lower species of life only because of his association with the three qualities of material nature. ūrdhvaṁ gacchanti sattva-sthā madhye tiṣṭhanti rājasāḥ jaghanya-guṇa-vṛtti-sthā adho gacchanti tāmasāḥ “Those situated in the mode of goodness gradually go upward to the higher planets; those in the mode of passion live on the earthly planets; and those in the mode of ignorance go down to the hellish worlds.” ( Bg. 14.18 ) In conclusion, the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement offers the topmost welfare activity for human society. The saner section of human society must therefore take this movement very seriously for the benefit of all humanity. To save oneself from the repetition of birth and death, one must purify his consciousness. Sarvopādhi-vinirmuktaṁ tat-paratvena nirmalam . One must be freed from all designations — “I am American,” “I am Indian,” “I am this,” “I am that” — and come to the platform of understanding that Kṛṣṇa is the original master and we are His eternal servants. When the senses are purified and engaged in Kṛṣṇa’s service, one achieves the highest perfection. Hṛṣīkeṇa hṛṣīkeśa-sevanaṁ bhaktir ucyate . The Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement is a movement of bhakti-yoga. Vairāgya-vidyā-nija-bhakti-yoga. By following the principles of this movement, one becomes disassociated from material mental concoctions and is established on the original platform of the eternal relationship between the living entity and the Supreme Personality of Godhead as servant and master. This, in summary, is the purpose of the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    At the time of death, according to the thinking, feeling and willing of the mind, which is involved in fruitive activities, one receives a particular body. In other words, the body develops according to the activities of the mind. Changes of body are due to the flickering of the mind, for otherwise the soul could remain in its original, spiritual body.
    Commentary

    Now a question arises. The mind can only enjoy because of the influence of the devatas over the mind, so that he become absorbed in the image of a king or Indra. But how is it possible for the mind to get enjoyment meant for someone else? This verse answers that question. Whatever objects among the five elements (earth, water, etc) the mind, always subject to so many impressions (vikaratmika), becomes attacted to, those objects it attains. Because of its close association with the mind, the soul (asau dehi) also enjoys those objects (prapadyamana jayate) along with the absorbed mind.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “It is true one will get a body, but it is difficult to get the body of a king.” By the impulse of karma, without endeavor, the ignorant jīva, though different from his body and senses, thinks in this way and is born with another body. By the great force of karma, instructed by the voice from the sky, you should understand that your death by a son of Devakī is inevitable in a future life. Giving up this sinful act which will cause great suffering in the future, since you have an accumulation of old karmas, now and hereafter you should do pious acts to avoid death for some time, like Mārkaṇḍeya, in order to attain a fortunate body. In a previous life for instance, the ṣaḍ-garbhas, sons of Marīci, were born as grandsons of Hiraṇyakaśipu, as related in Hari-vaṁśa.

    Personal Guidance
    The flickering mind, shaped by the guṇas at death, drags the soul into its next body — fix it on Kṛṣṇa now through the holy name.
    Practical Applications
    • Chant a fixed daily round of the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahā-mantra and refuse to negotiate it down, however busy the day becomes.
    • Notice each time the mind darts toward a sense object today, and gently bring it back to Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet rather than indulging the chase.
    • Before sleep tonight, drop one designation — 'I am this body, this nationality, this role' — and rest in 'I am Kṛṣṇa's eternal servant.'
    Reflection Questions
    • At the moment of death, the mind I have trained all my life will choose my next body — what mental habit am I cultivating right now that I would be ashamed to wear as a form in my next birth?
    • Where in my day does the cañcala mind drag me into vikāra — and what would it look like to deliberately fix it on Kṛṣṇa's name in that exact moment instead of at a 'convenient' time later?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Audit the last thing your mind touches before sleep for the next seven nights — Instagram reel, a crush, an exam result, a song. That residue is training your mind for its real final exam. Replace the last five minutes with a few rounds of japa or hearing a verse, and watch what your dreams shift to.
    • Notice how a single insult from a friend group, or a single bad grade, can hijack your whole mental weather for days. That is the cañcala mind Arjuna described. Pick one such trigger this week and, the moment it lands, chant Hare Kṛṣṇa once aloud before you react — small experiment in not letting the mind capsize the boat.
    • Stop curating an identity ('I am a future doctor,' 'I am the funny one,' 'I am the activist'). Prabhupāda calls these upādhis — designations that decide your next body. For one day, introduce yourself internally as 'an eternal servant of Kṛṣṇa who is currently a student' and notice how much social anxiety quietly drops.
    householder
    • The skyscraper-to-cat example is for you. List the three biggest things you are presently building — a house, a portfolio, a child's career. Now ask: if I died mid-project, which of these would my mind clutch at, and is that the mentality I want to carry? Begin offering each project's outcome to Kṛṣṇa at your morning ārati, by name.
    • Your children are watching what your mind defaults to under stress — money pressure, in-laws, work calls. That default is the saṁskāra you are bequeathing them, more than any school you choose. This week, when you feel the mind tilt, audibly chant one mantra in front of them instead of complaining; let them see the boat being righted.
    • Sit with your spouse and identify one shared attachment — a particular standard of living, a status symbol, a fear about the children's future — that is silently steering family decisions. Don't try to renounce it. Just name it, and together resolve to read this verse and one related verse (BG 3.19) aloud before the next big decision involving it.
    senior
    • Death is now closer than the start of your career. Begin building the mental furniture you actually want in the room at the moment of departure: a tulasī plant by the bed, a photo of Kṛṣṇa at eye level from the chair you sit in most, recordings of the holy name playing during meals. You are stage-setting the last scene.
    • Inventory the grudges, the unfinished projects, the property disputes, the resentment toward a child who didn't turn out as you hoped. Each is a hook the mind will reach for at the end. Pick one this month and actively release it — a phone call, a written forgiveness, a will signed — so it does not become the thought that takes you into the next body.
    • Mentor the younger people in your family or saṅga not by giving advice but by letting them watch you chant, hear, and prepare. Your visible loosening from house, bank balance, and reputation is a teaching no lecture can match — and it is itself the abhyāsa that fixes your own mind on Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet before the wind picks up.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating mind-control as a private willpower project — trying to subdue the cañcala mind by force or technique, when the verse and purport point to bhakti-yoga and the holy name as the only sustainable shelter in Kali-yuga.
    • Reducing this verse to a generic 'thoughts create reality' or law-of-attraction lesson, missing that the issue is transmigration into a literal next body shaped by the guṇas — not merely the quality of one's current mood or career.
    • Hearing 'the body develops according to the activities of the mind' and concluding that material self-improvement (better habits, better thinking, better planning) is the solution — when the purport is exposing all such mental arrangements as māyā-sukha that Kṛṣṇa strips away at death.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Prabhupāda says the next body is shaped by the mind's last thinking, feeling and willing. Share with your partner: what is the dominant mood your mind drifts into when it has nothing to do — and if death came in that drift, what kind of body would that mentality earn? Push past the polite answer.
    • The verse implies that even a 'good' person absorbed in family, career or charity — but not in Kṛṣṇa — still gets a body shaped by guṇa-saṅga, not by their self-image. Where in this group do we secretly believe our decency will save us from another birth? Disagree openly if you think the verse is being too harsh.
    • Prabhupāda contrasts artificial yoga (which can fail in Kali-yuga) with bhakti-yoga and the holy name. Has anyone here actually tried to control the mind by force — meditation apps, breathwork, willpower regimes — and what happened? Compare that honestly with what chanting has or hasn't done for your mind.
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A is a hospice volunteer sitting with a 70-year-old man in his last week. The man is lucid, frightened, and keeps replaying scenes from his career, his unfinished house renovation, and a grudge against his brother. He asks Student A, 'What happens to all this when I go?' Student B plays the dying man; Student A must respond as a Gauḍīya practitioner who has internalized SB 10.1.42 — without quoting the verse, without lecturing, and without flinching from the truth that whatever occupies his mind right now will shape what comes next. After 5 minutes, swap. Then debrief: where did you reach for material comfort instead of pointing him toward Kṛṣṇa? Where did the truth feel cruel, and was it actually cruel or only uncomfortable?

    Objections & Responses
    • This is fear-based religion. Telling people their mental state at death determines their next body is just a sophisticated version of 'be good or you'll go to hell' — it weaponizes mortality to control behavior.
      The verse isn't a threat; it's a description of how nature already works, the way gravity is described, not imposed. Kṛṣṇa is not punishing the flickering mind — He is explaining that consciousness has consequences, the same way a doctor explains that smoking has consequences. The Gauḍīya teacher's tone is not 'beware' but 'here is the mechanism, and here is the way out — chant, and the mind that would otherwise drag you into another womb is fixed at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.' Fear without remedy is cruelty. Diagnosis with cure is mercy. SB 10.1.42 is the diagnosis; harer nāma is the cure Prabhupāda hands you in the same purport.
    • Modern neuroscience shows the mind is just brain activity. When the brain dies, the mind dies. There is no 'mental state at death' that carries forward into another body — that's pre-scientific cosmology.
      Notice that neuroscience has not actually located consciousness; it has located correlates of consciousness. The hard problem — why there is any first-person experience at all — remains untouched. The Bhāgavatam isn't competing with neurology about neurons; it's pointing to the dehī, the one who possesses the body, who is categorically different from the brain that lights up on a scan. You don't have to take this on faith. Test it: sit and watch your own mind for ten minutes. Notice that you are watching it. Who is the watcher? That witness is not flickering — only the mind is. The verse is describing what happens to the dehī when the mental envelope it has cultivated finally dissolves. If that watcher is real — and your own experience says it is — then where it goes next is not a small question.
    Analogy

    At the moment of death, the body to come develops according to the mind's habit — the way a river finds its bed by the soil it has long worn. The mind's daily current carves the channel; the body simply follows the channel at exit. The verse's ethic is severe: every thought today is a chisel-stroke on tomorrow's body. The soul could remain in its original spiritual form — if the mind would stop carving.

    Important Words
    • jyotiḥ — the luminaries in the sky
      From jyut, 'to shine.' Same root as jyotis (light). The soul is its own jyotis — self-luminous (BG 13.18, jyotiṣām api taj jyotiḥ). The verse contrasts the soul's true jyotiḥ-nature with the distorted shapes the agitated mind makes of him.
    • sva-māyā-raciteṣu — in the situation created by one's mental concoctions
      Sva (own) + māyā (illusion) + racita (constructed). 'In the constructions made by one's own māyā.' The verse points to a personal māyā — the conditioned soul's own mental construction-set, distinct from the cosmic māyā in verse 42.
    • rāga-anugataḥ — according to his attachment
      Rāga (attachment, coloring) + anugata (following). The shapes the soul takes are determined by his rāga. Gauḍīya: this same rāga, redirected to Kṛṣṇa, becomes rāgānuga-bhakti — the topmost bhakti is rāga turned toward its rightful object.
    • vimuhyati — becomes bewildered by identification
      Vi + muh, 'thoroughly deluded.' From the same root as moha, mohini, mūḍha. The verse names the operative result: vimuhyati — bewilderment of identity. The bewilderment is curable; bhakti is its medicine.
    When the luminaries in the sky, such as the moon, the sun and the stars, are reflected in liquids like oil or water, they appear to be of different shapes — sometimes round, sometimes long, and so on — because of the movements of the wind. Similarly, when the living entity, the soul, is absorbed in materialistic thoughts, he accepts various manifestations as his own identity because of ignorance. In other words, one is bewildered by mental concoctions because of agitation from the material modes of nature.
    Purport

    This verse gives a very good example by which to understand the different positions of the eternal spiritual soul in the material world and how the soul takes on different bodies ( dehāntara-prāptiḥ ). The moon is stationary and is one, but when it is reflected in water or oil, it appears to take different shapes because of the movements of the wind. Similarly, the soul is the eternal servant of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, but when put into the material modes of nature, it takes different bodies, sometimes as a demigod, sometimes a man, a dog, a tree and so on. By the influence of māyā, the illusory potency of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the living entity thinks that he is this person, that person, American, Indian, cat, dog, tree or whatever. This is called māyā. When one is freed from this bewilderment and understands that the soul does not belong to any shape of this material world, one is situated on the spiritual platform ( brahma-bhūta ). This realization is sometimes explained as nirākāra, or formlessness. This formlessness, however, does not mean that the soul has no form. The soul has form, but the external, agitating form he has acquired because of material contamination is false. Similarly, God is also described as nirākāra, which means that God has no material form but is sac-cid-ānanda-vigraha. The living entity is part and parcel of the supreme sac-cid-ānanda-vigraha, but his material forms are temporary, or illusory. Both the living entity and the Supreme Lord have original, spiritual forms ( sac-cid-ānanda-vigraha ), but the Lord, the Supreme, does not change His form. The Lord appears as He is, whereas the living entity appears because material nature forces him to accept different forms. When the living entity receives these different forms, he identifies with them, and not with his original, spiritual form. As soon as the living entity returns to his original, spiritual form and understanding, he immediately surrenders to the supreme form, the Personality of Godhead. This is explained in Bhagavad-gītā (7.19) . Bahūnāṁ janmanām ante jñānavān māṁ prapadyate. When the living entity, after many, many births in different forms, returns to his original form of Kṛṣṇa consciousness, he immediately surrenders unto the lotus feet of the supreme form, Kṛṣṇa. This is liberation. As the Lord says in Bhagavad-gītā (18.54) : brahma-bhūtaḥ prasannātmā na śocati na kāṅkṣati samaḥ sarveṣu bhūteṣu mad-bhaktiṁ labhate parām “One who is thus transcendentally situated at once realizes the Supreme Brahman and becomes fully joyful. He never laments nor desires to have anything; he is equally disposed to every living entity. In that state he attains pure devotional service unto Me.” Surrender unto the supreme form is the result of bhakti. This bhakti, or understanding of one’s own position, is the complete liberation. As long as one is under an impersonal understanding of the Absolute Truth, he is not in pure knowledge, but must still struggle for pure knowledge. Kleśo ’dhikataras teṣām avyaktāsakta-cetasām ( Bg. 12.5 ). Although one may be spiritually advanced, if one is attached to the impersonal feature of the Absolute Truth one must still work very hard, as indicated by the words kleśo ’dhikataraḥ, which mean “greater suffering.” A devotee, however, easily attains his original position as a spiritual form and understands the Supreme Personality of Godhead in His original form. Kṛṣṇa Himself explains the forms of the living entities in the Second Chapter of Bhagavad-gītā, where He clearly says to Arjuna that He, Arjuna and all other living entities, who were previously in their original forms, are separate individual identities. They were individuals in the past, they are now situated in individuality, and in the future they will all continue to maintain their individual forms. The only difference is that the conditioned living entity appears in various material forms, whereas Kṛṣṇa appears in His original, spiritual form. Unfortunately, those who are not advanced in spiritual knowledge think that Kṛṣṇa is like one of them and that His form is like their material forms. Avajānanti māṁ mūḍhā mānuṣīṁ tanum āśritam ( Bg. 9.11 ). Kṛṣṇa is never puffed up by material knowledge and is therefore called acyuta, whereas the living entities fall down and are agitated by material nature. This is the difference between the Supreme Lord and the living entities. In this connection it is to be noted that Vasudeva, who was situated in a transcendental position, advised Kaṁsa not to commit further sinful activities. Kaṁsa, a representative of the demons, was always ready to kill Kṛṣṇa, or God, whereas Vasudeva represents a transcendentally situated person to whom Kṛṣṇa is born (Vāsudeva is the son of Vasudeva). Vasudeva wanted his brother-in-law Kaṁsa to refrain from the sinful act of killing his sister, since the result of being agitated by material nature would be that Kaṁsa would have to accept a body in which to suffer again and again. Elsewhere in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (5.5.4) , Ṛṣabhadeva also says: na sādhu manye yata ātmano ’yam asann api kleśada āsa dehaḥ As long as the living entity is entangled in the fruitive activities of so-called happiness and distress, he will receive a particular type of body in which to endure the three kinds of suffering due to material nature ( tri-tāpa-yantraṇā ). An intelligent person, therefore, must free himself from the influence of the three modes of material nature and revive his original, spiritual body by engaging in the service of the Supreme Person, Kṛṣṇa. As long as one is materially attached, one must accept the process of birth, death, old age and disease. One is therefore advised that an intelligent person, instead of being entangled in so-called good and bad fruitive activities, should engage his life in advancing in Kṛṣṇa consciousness so that instead of accepting another material body ( tyaktvā dehaṁ punar janma naiti ), he will return home, back to Godhead.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    When the luminaries in the sky, such as the moon, the sun and the stars, are reflected in liquids like oil or water, they appear to be of different shapes—sometimes round, sometimes long, and so on—because of the movements of the wind. Similarly, when the living entity, the soul, is absorbed in materialistic thoughts, he accepts various manifestations as his own identity because of ignorance. In other words, one is bewildered by mental concoctions because of agitation from the material modes of nature.
    Commentary

    Now he gives an example to show how the soul, due to association with mind, attains the same destination. Jyotih refers to the light of the sun or moon. Udakesu refers to water, oil or ghee. On the surface of the water the image of the sun is reflected but it changes shape as the wind blows the surface and produces ripples. In the bodies (gunesu) created by the Lord’s maya (svamaya racitesu), or by ones own ignorance, the jiva (puman), following the mind which is filled with desires for enjoyment (raganugata), becomes bewildered and takes up the same desire for enjoyment. By killing Devaki you will obstruct the souls desire for getting enjoyment. Even if you die, you will enjoy in the next body, because you will attain a good body since your good karmas must bear result. And killing her will make you endure suffering. Your death announced in the sky by the future son of Devaki is unavoidable, as it is under the force of karma. Therefore it is better to accept that death. All you can do is have Markandeya perform some ceremonies as preventative measures.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    This absorption in bodies is filled with ignorance. Adaḥ means “situated in the sky without trembling.” Sva-māyā means the Lord’s māyā. The jīva is bewildered by bodies made of the Lord’s māyā.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “Let us not speak of ordinary human bodies. Is not the body of a king very rare?” Though the luminaries are situated in the sky without trembling, they appear to move in their reflections in the water. The jīva similarly becomes bewildered in bodies made by his ignorance (svamāyā) or the Lord’s māyā present in him. The actions of these bodies is illusory. Or the previous verse described the jīva going from body to body. By that, one attains a king’s body. At the time of death by absorption of the mind impelled by karmas about to fructify, with a desire to be a king, one attains a king’s body. Maraṇe yā matiḥ sā gatiḥ: one attains what one thinks of at death. “Let us accept that in another birth one becomes a king. But one must make effort to protect the body in the womb and when the child is small in order that the person may enjoy.” Just as the reflection of the planets in the water follow the movements of the wind on the water and seems to tremble, the jīva, being attached to objects of enjoyment (guṇeṣu), becomes completely bewildered and thinks one object is enjoyable and another is not. If one does not have attachment in childhood or any age, one will not suffer from enjoyment of objects, just as one will be happy by enjoying the objects, by having attachment. How can killing the child solve the problem?
