    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa personally summons His devotees from the higher planets to play in His pastimes — even those who appear to oppose Him are part of His līlā.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today the people around you who feel like 'opponents' and consider that they too may be playing a role in Kṛṣṇa's larger plan for your bhakti.
    • Read aloud one verse from the Tenth Canto and pray for the privilege of witnessing the Lord's pastimes through hearing.
    • Refuse to see your family and friends as accidents — treat each relationship as a stage Kṛṣṇa has set, and serve them as fellow participants in His līlā.
    Reflection Questions
    • This verse reveals that even those who 'externally appeared to be followers of Kaṁsa' were demigods playing a part in Kṛṣṇa's pastimes — where in my own life have I judged someone as an obstacle when they may actually be an instrument in a larger arrangement I cannot see?
    • If Kṛṣṇa personally summons devotees from the heavenly planets to witness His pastimes, what does it mean that I have been given this human birth with access to this very narrative — and what am I doing with that summons today?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • That classmate who beat you out for the internship, the friend who ghosted you, the professor who graded you harshly — pick one this week and write down: what role might they be playing in your formation that you cannot yet see? Do not post it; just sit with it.
    • Your social feed is a gallery of people who look more 'chosen' than you — better grades, better partners, better aesthetics. The verse reframes this: every soul is placed exactly where Kṛṣṇa needs them. Spend one full day this week without checking who else got what. Notice what your mind does in the silence.
    • Find one older devotee on campus or in your sangha — not the most charismatic, just one who is steady — and ask them how they ended up in bhakti. The verse's point is that the right people are placed around you; your job is to recognize them past the externals.
    householder
    • The difficult in-law, the frustrating boss, the child who tests you the most — treat one of them this month as a soul Kṛṣṇa has placed in your household for a reason you may not understand. Do not change your boundaries; change the silent commentary you run about them.
    • When making your next significant family decision (school for the kids, a job change, a move), explicitly include this question in your deliberation: 'Whose spiritual life depends on the answer I give here?' The Yadus and gopas understood their domestic arrangements were part of a larger arrangement; ours are too, even when invisible.
    • Identify one relationship in your extended family that you have written off as 'just toxic.' Before the next gathering, do one small act of service for that person — a phone call, a remembered birthday, a meal sent over — without expectation of change. Practice seeing past the kaṁsa-vesha (the Kaṁsa-costume) to the soul underneath.
    senior
    • Look back over the people who shaped your life — including the ones who hurt you most. Write a short list of those whose role you can now see was, in retrospect, providential. Share it with one younger person this month; this is the kind of testimony only your stage of life can give.
    • Mortality concentrates the question of who and what we have been clinging to. Practice loosening your grip on one possession, one role, or one expectation each month — not by giving it away dramatically, but by mentally offering it to Kṛṣṇa and noticing what relaxes in the body. The Yadus knew they were temporary; so are you.
    • Mentor someone half your age into bhakti this year — not by lecturing, but by inviting them into your sādhana (japa, reading, prasāda). The verse shows that sādhu-saṅga is how Kṛṣṇa moves souls into position. Your last decades are for being one of those positioning hands.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this verse as a charter for spiritual elitism — concluding 'the devotees around Kṛṣṇa were special demigods, so I cannot aspire to that intimacy' — when the purport actually describes yoga-bhraṣṭas (fallen yogīs) being given a second chance, which is an invitation, not a closed door.
    • Using the 'they were all demigods in disguise' framing to romanticize one's own circle, casting family and friends as cosmic players in a personal drama — a subtle ahaṅkāra that puts oneself at the center of a Kṛṣṇa-līlā that isn't happening here.
    • Treating the demigod identity of Kaṁsa's apparent followers as license for moral relativism — 'if even the villains are demigods, then good and evil don't matter' — missing that the Lord still came vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām, and the play of demon-killing was real within the līlā.
    Discussion Prompts
    • The verse says even those who externally appeared to follow Kaṁsa were demigods sent to participate in Kṛṣṇa's pastimes. Share a time when someone you judged as an obstacle later turned out to be playing a necessary role in your spiritual life. Where did your judgment fail you, and where might it still be failing you today?
    • Prabhupāda quotes BG 6.41 — the yoga-bhraṣṭa is born into a pious or wealthy family and may even be promoted to where the Lord's pastimes are happening. Discuss with your partner: does this make our present circumstances feel like a gift, or like a debt? Is there a difference between the two, and which one motivates you more honestly?
    • The Yadus, Vṛṣṇis, and gopas were all 'almost as good as demigods' — yet they appeared as ordinary cowherds, mothers, and townsfolk. Debate: when we look for sādhu-saṅga today, are we looking for the right markers, or are we still drawn to externals (charisma, position, public reputation)? Give a concrete example from your own life.
    Role Play

    Two students sit across from each other. Student A is a serious sādhaka who has just learned that a colleague at work — someone who openly mocks their bhakti practice and has been undermining their projects — was actually instrumental in a promotion they just received. Student B plays a fellow devotee that A is venting to. A must wrestle aloud with whether to keep treating this colleague as an adversary or to recognize, in light of SB 10.1.62-63, that even those who 'externally appeared to be followers of Kaṁsa' may be playing a role in the Lord's larger arrangement. B should not let A off easy with cheap spiritualization — push A to articulate what concretely changes in tomorrow's interaction, without becoming naive or sentimental. After 7 minutes, swap roles.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like elitism dressed in Sanskrit. Saying that Kṛṣṇa's family and friends were 'demigods' from higher planets makes ordinary devotees feel like they could never have that kind of intimacy with the Lord. Isn't this just spiritual aristocracy?
      The verse is not drawing a line that excludes us — it is showing why those particular souls were placed in those particular roles for that particular līlā. The same Lord who summoned demigods to play His parents and cowherd friends also says in the Gītā that He is bhakti-priya — He is conquered by devotion, not by pedigree. Prabhupāda emphasizes the yoga-bhraṣṭa point precisely so we do not despair: pious birth is itself a sign of incomplete devotional service from a previous life being carried forward. The intimacy of Vṛndāvana is not closed; it is the destination of sincere bhakti, not an inherited privilege. The aristocracy reading is the ahaṅkāra reading — it makes the verse about status. The bhakti reading makes it about Kṛṣṇa's careful arrangement of every soul, including yours.
    • If even Kaṁsa's followers were secretly demigods playing a role, doesn't this collapse moral seriousness? Then nobody is really an enemy, nothing is really wrong, everyone is just acting out a script. Why bother with vairāgya or tapas if the whole thing is choreographed?
      The verse does not say that ordinary human evil is choreographed — it says that for this specific descent of the Lord, devotees were summoned to fill every role so that the pastimes could unfold. That is not a metaphysics of moral relativism; it is a statement about the unique circumstances of Kṛṣṇa-līlā. In our own lives, we are not in Vṛndāvana 5,000 years ago — we are in the field of karma, where wrong is wrong and our choices have real reactions. What the verse offers us is not an excuse to drop sādhana but a corrective to our small-mindedness about who Kṛṣṇa is using and how. Tapas and vairāgya remain non-negotiable precisely because we are not yet the kind of soul who can be trusted with a part in the līlā. The verse should sober us, not relax us.
    Analogy

    The verse pulls back to reveal the cast: the Vraja cowherds led by Nanda, the Yadu queens, the friends and well-wishers, even those who appeared to be Kaṁsa's followers — all were demigods. The earthly drama is a divine theater performance where the supporting cast came down for one role. The Bhāgavata teaches that the same scene one watches as ordinary biography is, from the cosmic side, a fully cast līlā with assigned roles.

    Important Words
    • bhagavān — the most powerful representative of the Supreme Personality of Godhead
      Bhagavān used here of Nārada — a fully empowered devotee can carry the title (in a derivative sense). The Bhāgavata extends bhagavān to its highest devotees because they bear Bhagavān's authority. Distinguish: Kṛṣṇa is bhagavān svayam; Nārada is bhagavān by empowerment.
    • nāradaḥ — the great sage Nārada
      From nara (man) + da (giver) — 'giver to men.' Nārada is the cosmic transmitter of bhakti — author of the Nārada-bhakti-sūtra, transmitter to Vyāsa (who composed the Bhāgavatam), to Vālmīki (who composed the Rāmāyaṇa). His arrival is always doctrinally significant.
    • bhūmeḥ bhārāyamāṇānām — of those who were a burden on the earth
      Bhūmi (earth, gen. bhūmeḥ) + bhāra (burden) + māṇa (being). The same diagnosis as verse 17 — Earth burdened by demoniac kings. Nārada confirms the cosmic frame to Kaṁsa: you are one of those whose elimination is being arranged. He tells the asura his place in the chart.
    • vadha-udyamam — the endeavor to kill
      Vadha (killing) + udyama (effort, undertaking). The verse uses the precise word: vadha-udyamam, the endeavor toward killing. Kaṁsa is told there is an ongoing operation. The Bhāgavata records the moment Kaṁsa first realizes he is the target, not the agent.
    Once the great saint Nārada approached Kaṁsa and informed him of how the demoniac persons who were a great burden on the earth were going to be killed. Thus Kaṁsa was placed into great fear and doubt.
    Purport

    It has already been discussed that mother earth implored Lord Brahmā to give her relief from the distress created by the burdensome demons and that Lord Brahmā informed her that Lord Kṛṣṇa Himself was going to appear. Kṛṣṇa says in Bhagavad-gītā (4.8) : paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge Whenever there is a burden created by the demons and whenever the innocent devotees are distressed by demoniac rulers, the Lord appears in due course of time to kill the demons with the assistance of His real representatives, who are technically called demigods. In the Upaniṣads it is stated that the demigods are different parts of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. As it is the duty of the parts of the body to serve the whole, it is the duty of Kṛṣṇa’s devotees to serve Kṛṣṇa as He wants. Kṛṣṇa’s business is to kill the demons, and therefore this should be a devotee’s business also. Because the people of Kali-yuga are fallen, however, Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu, out of kindness for them, did not bring any weapon to kill them. Rather, by spreading Kṛṣṇa consciousness, love of Kṛṣṇa, He wanted to kill their nefarious, demoniac activities. This is the purpose of the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement. Unless the demoniac activities on the surface of the world are diminished or vanquished, no one can be happy. The program for the conditioned soul is fully described in Bhagavad-gītā, and one simply has to follow these instructions to become happy. Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu has therefore prescribed: harer nāma harer nāma harer nāmaiva kevalam kalau nāsty eva nāsty eva nāsty eva gatir anyathā Let people chant the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra constantly. Then their demoniac tendencies will be killed, and they will become first-class devotees, happy in this life and in the next.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Once the great saint Nārada approached Kaṁsa and informed him of how the demoniac persons who were a great burden on the earth were going to be killed. Thus Kaṁsa was placed into great fear and doubt.
    Commentary

    Narada informed Kamsa (samsayam asa) how the devatas were appearing in the various families.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Nārada had all knowledge (bhagavān) and thus knew that Kaṁsa had become peaceful, thinking that the Lord would not appear. Or bhagavān indicates Nārada’s most merciful nature. He was acting for the benefit of the world by hastening the appearance of the Lord through speaking with Kaṁsa. He spoke to Kaṁsa: tripiṣṭapād āpatito mathuropavane sthitaḥ preṣayām āsa kaṁsāya sa dūtaṁ muni-puṅgavaḥ sa dūtaḥ kathanām āsa nāradāgamana nṛpe sa nāradasyāgamanaṁ śrutvā tvarita vikraṁaḥ nirgajāmāsuraḥ kaṁsaḥ svapuryāḥ padmalocanaḥ sa dadarśātithiṁ ślāghaṁ devarśīṁ vītakalmaṣam tejasā jvalam ākāraṁ vapuṣā sūryavarcasam so ‘bhivādyarsahe tasmai pūjāṁ cakre yathāvidhi āsanaṁ cāgnivaṛṇabhaṁ visṭrejyopajahāra saḥ nisasādāsane tasmin sa vai śakru-sakho muniḥ uvāca cograsenasya sutaṁ paramakopanam pūjito ‘haṁ tvayā viṛa vidhi-dṛṣṭena karmaṇā gate tvevaṁ mama vacaḥ śruyatāṁ gṛhyatāṁ ca vai anuśṛtya divo lokān ahaṁ brahma-purogamān gataḥ sūrya-sakham tāta vipulaṁ meru-paravatam so ‘ham kadācid devānāṁ samāje meru-mūrdhani saṁgṛhya vīṇāṁ samṣaktām āgacchaṁ brahmaṇaḥ sabhām tatra mantrayatām evaṁ devatānām māyā śrutaḥ bhavataḥ sānugasyeha vodhopāyaḥ sudāruṇaḥ Coming from Svarga to a grove in Mathurā, Nārada sent a messenger to Kaṁsa. The messenger told him of Nārada’s arrival. Hearing of his arrival, lotus-eyed Kaṁsa quickly came out of his city. He saw Nārada, shining like the sun, with no impurities, blazing with effulgence. He welcomed and worshipped Nārada properly and offered him a pure seat. Nārada sat on the seat and spoke to Ugrasena’s son who was full of anger. “You have worshipped me according to the rules. Please hear and understand my words. On the order of the devatās I went to huge Meru, friend of the sun. With my vīṇā I came to the peak of Meru, where the devatās were assembled. I heard the devatās discussing about a very cruel method of killing you and your associates”. Kaṁsa is described as lotus-eyed because his eyes were wide with surprise.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa descends to relieve the earth of demoniac burden — your share in this mission today is to chant His names and refuse to feed demoniac tendencies in yourself.
    Practical Applications
    • Chant a fixed number of Hare Kṛṣṇa rounds today before any other 'urgent' task, treating it as your personal contribution to lifting the earth's burden.
    • Notice one demoniac tendency rising in you — envy, lust, deceit — and refuse to act on it, offering that restraint as service to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Speak Kṛṣṇa's name or a verse to one person today who is suffering under modern 'demoniac' pressures, sharing the medicine instead of merely commiserating.
    Reflection Questions
    • Nārada's warning placed Kaṁsa in fear because his whole life was built on demoniac premises — where in my own life would a clear word from a sādhu about Kṛṣṇa's coming provoke fear rather than joy, and what does that fear reveal about what I am still protecting?
    • Prabhupāda says Kṛṣṇa's devotees share His business of relieving the earth's burden — what specific 'demoniac activity' in my own conduct or environment am I tolerating today instead of actively working to diminish through chanting and Kṛṣṇa consciousness?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When a friend group is drifting into something clearly destructive — substances, cruelty toward an outsider, academic dishonesty — be the Nārada who walks in and names it, even if it costs you the group. Do not hide behind 'it's not my business.'
    • Audit your social media feed this week as if it were Kaṁsa's court: which accounts are demoniac burdens on your attention? Unfollow them with the same decisiveness this verse models — no negotiation, no 'but they're sometimes funny.'
    • Before exams or interviews, instead of praying for outcomes, take five minutes to chant Hare Kṛṣṇa and ask Kṛṣṇa to kill the demoniac tendencies in your own preparation — laziness, panic, comparison with classmates. That is the udyama this verse is really about.
    householder
    • Identify one 'burden on the earth' inside your own home — a habit, a financial entanglement, a toxic relationship you have tolerated for the children's sake — and name it aloud to your spouse this week, the way Nārada named the coming reckoning to Kaṁsa. Schedule the hard conversation; do not wait for Kṛṣṇa to force it through circumstance.
    • In your career, distinguish work that genuinely serves Kṛṣṇa's order in society from work that merely thickens the demoniac burden. You may not be able to leave your job, but you can refuse one specific assignment this quarter that crosses the line — and absorb the cost as your sādhana.
    • Make your home a place where harināma is louder than the news cycle. Institute one daily family kīrtana, however short, as the household's working response to the demoniac noise your children are absorbing all day from screens and peers.
    senior
    • Use the authority of your age to be the Nārada in your extended family — the one person willing to say to a younger relative that the path they are on will end badly. You have less to lose now than anyone; spend that capital before you cannot.
    • Reflect on which attachments still make you, like Kaṁsa, susceptible to 'great fear and doubt' when you hear of death. Each one is a demon still seated on the throne of your heart; offer it specifically into the chanting of the Holy Name each morning.
    • Mentor at least one younger devotee or seeker by transmitting not your opinions but the verses and the Name. Caitanya Mahāprabhu's method — no weapons, only saṅkīrtana — is the legacy a senior is uniquely positioned to leave.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading 'killing the demons' externally — scanning the world for villains to oppose — while ignoring the demoniac tendencies (lust, anger, greed, envy) that are the actual burden Kṛṣṇa came to lift from one's own heart.
    • Treating the harer nāma prescription as a soft, optional devotional flavor rather than as Caitanya Mahāprabhu's actual weapon for this age — chanting casually or ornamentally instead of constantly and with the seriousness of someone engaged in vadhodyamam against their own anarthas.
    • Sliding into impersonal or vague 'cosmic balance' language ('the universe restores itself,' 'evil is destroyed') and forgetting that it is Kṛṣṇa personally, on a definite schedule (sambhavāmi yuge yuge), who appears and that devotees are His personal instruments — not free agents pursuing a generic good cause.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Nārada deliberately approaches Kaṁsa to inform him that the demons will be killed — provoking, not pacifying him. Where in your own life have you been tempted to soothe a 'Kaṁsa' (a person clearly going against dharma) instead of being the agent who hastens the resolution? Share a specific instance, then disagree with your partner if their 'kindness' looks like cowardice to you.
    • Prabhupāda says it is 'a devotee's business' to assist Kṛṣṇa in killing the demons — but Caitanya Mahāprabhu carried no weapon, only the Holy Name. Debate in your group: in your actual workplace or family, what does 'killing demoniac activities' look like this week — confrontation, withdrawal, or chanting? Push back when someone reaches for the easy answer.
    • The verse shows Kaṁsa thrown into 'great fear and doubt' the moment he hears the truth. Where has hearing śāstra recently produced fear or doubt in you rather than peace — and is that a sign you are closer to Kaṁsa's position than to Nārada's? Be willing to disagree about whether spiritual discomfort is always a good sign.
    Role Play

    Two students play a scene set in a modern office. Student A is a project lead who has discovered that a senior colleague is quietly falsifying client reports — clearly adharmic, but powerful and well-liked. Student B plays a 'Nārada' friend who has come to A's desk specifically to tell A the truth about what is coming: this will collapse, people will be hurt, and A's silence is itself participation. Student B must not soften the message to keep the friendship comfortable; Student A must react honestly — fear, denial, deflection, or resolve. After five minutes, swap roles and run it again with a family scenario (an elder relative enabling an addiction in a younger one). Debrief: when did 'Nārada' lose nerve? When did 'Kaṁsa' get heard instead of confronted? What would real Vaiṣṇava udyama have looked like?

    Objections & Responses
    • Isn't it disturbing that a 'great saint' like Nārada actively goes to a tyrant and informs on people who are about to be killed? This sounds less like compassion and more like instigation — a modern reader can't accept a sage who behaves this way.
      The modern reader is reading Nārada through a sentimental lens of compassion as niceness. Nārada's compassion is for the soul, not the body — including Kaṁsa's soul. By informing Kaṁsa, he accelerates the very fear and doubt that will eventually bring Kaṁsa face to face with Kṛṣṇa, which is the only real liberation available to him. He also accelerates the relief of the earth and of the sādhus burdened by demoniac rule. This is precisely the pivot the Gītā insists on: real compassion is sometimes indistinguishable, on the surface, from provocation. A Gauḍīya teacher would say: do not measure a sage by whether he comforts the body; measure him by whether he serves Kṛṣṇa's plan.
    • The whole framing of 'demons who are a burden on the earth' has been used historically to justify violence against whoever someone decides is demoniac. Why should I take this verse seriously in a pluralistic age?
      The verse is not licensing you to identify demons and remove them — that is Kṛṣṇa's prerogative, executed in due course of time, with His own representatives. Notice what Prabhupāda actually prescribes for us in Kali-yuga: not weapons, but the Holy Name. Caitanya Mahāprabhu, knowing exactly how fallen and confused this age is, refused to give us a sword precisely because we cannot be trusted to wield it. Our 'killing of demons' is the killing of demoniac tendencies — beginning inside ourselves — through harināma. Anyone who reads this verse as a mandate for human violence has stopped reading at line one of the purport.
    Analogy

    Nārada arrives at Kaṁsa's court — not to comfort him but to inform him exactly how the demoniac kings will be destroyed. The verse stages the sage's strange mission: he tells the asura the truth. Kaṁsa, hearing the full plan, falls into greater fear and doubt. The Bhāgavata teaches that truth heard without surrender is more terrifying than ignorance. Nārada has, in mercy, accelerated Kaṁsa's crisis.

    Stories
    Nārada's strange mercy

    Nārada Muni is a perpetual traveler — singing Bhagavān's names with his vīṇā, appearing at courts both divine and demonic. He visits Hiraṇyakaśipu's son Prahlāda and seeds his devotion (SB 7.7); he visits the hunter Mṛgāri and converts him (CC Madhya 24). He even visits Kaṁsa.

    In each case, Nārada delivers the truth that the listener most needs and least wants. For Prahlāda, the truth seeded devotion; for Kaṁsa, it precipitated terror and a doubling-down of cruelty. The same sun melts butter and hardens clay. Nārada is the sun; the listener determines the result.

    The verse here is Nārada at his sharpest mercy — telling Kaṁsa the precise outline of his death. Kaṁsa's response (next verse) will be to imprison his sister. The mercy was real; the response is not Nārada's responsibility.

    Important Words
    • matvā surān — thinking of [them] as demigods
      Matvā (gerund of man, 'having thought') + surān (acc. pl. of sura, 'demigods'). Kaṁsa thinks correctly — they are demigods. The Bhāgavata's diagnosis: asuras can think correctly and still act demoniacally. Cognition is not character.
    • garbha-sambhūtam viṣṇum — the children born from the womb, [thinking of them] as Viṣṇu
      Garbha (womb) + sambhūta (originating) + viṣṇu (acc.). Kaṁsa fears Viṣṇu specifically — the form whose hand killed his previous birth as Kālanemi. The Bhāgavata names what the asura cannot escape: the past birth's killer is the next birth's threat.
    • sva-vadham prati — fearing his own death from Viṣṇu
      Sva (own) + vadha (death) + prati (toward). 'With reference to his own death.' Asuras are oriented toward their own vadha — they live in continuous reverse-engineering of their end. Devotees, by contrast, live toward Bhagavān; the end takes care of itself.
    • nigaḍaiḥ — by iron shackles
      Plural of nigaḍa, 'iron chain.' Vasudeva and Devakī are physically chained — preparing the stage for Kṛṣṇa's appearance in chains in chapter 3 (10.3.46–47 — the chains fell at His arrival). The Bhāgavata's narrative chains are also doctrinal: the body in bondage will be visited by Bhagavān.
    • jātam jātam ahan — each one born, he killed
      Jāta (born), repeated for emphasis. Ahan = aorist of han, 'killed.' The verse's syntactic violence: jātam-jātam-ahan, born-born-killed. Six syllables that document six killings. Bhāgavata's narrative grammar carries the trauma.
    After the departure of the great saint Nārada, Kaṁsa thought that all the members of the Yadu dynasty were demigods and that any of the children born from the womb of Devakī might be Viṣṇu. Fearing his death, Kaṁsa arrested Vasudeva and Devakī and chained them with iron shackles. Suspecting each of the children to be Viṣṇu, Kaṁsa killed them one after another because of the prophecy that Viṣṇu would kill him.
    Purport

    Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī, in his notes on this verse, has mentioned how Nārada Muni gave Kaṁsa this information. This incident is described in the Hari-vaṁśa. Nārada Muni went to see Kaṁsa by providence, and Kaṁsa received him very well. Nārada, therefore, informed him that any one of the sons of Devakī might be Viṣṇu. Because Viṣṇu was to kill him, Kaṁsa should not spare any of Devakī’s children, Nārada Muni advised. Nārada’s intention was that Kaṁsa, by killing the children, would increase his sinful activities so that Kṛṣṇa would soon appear to kill him. Upon receiving the instructions of Nārada Muni, Kaṁsa killed all the children of Devakī one after another. The word ajana-śaṅkayā indicates that Lord Viṣṇu never takes birth ( ajana ) and that He therefore appeared as Kṛṣṇa, taking birth just like a human being ( mānuṣīṁ tanum āśritam ). Kaṁsa attempted to kill all the babies born of Devakī and Vasudeva, although he knew that if Viṣṇu were born, He would not be killed. Actually it came to pass that when Viṣṇu appeared as Kṛṣṇa, Kaṁsa could not kill Him; rather, as foretold, it was He who killed Kaṁsa. One should know in truth how Kṛṣṇa, who takes His birth transcendentally, acts to kill the demons but is never killed. When one perfectly understands Kṛṣṇa in this way, through the medium of śāstra, one becomes immortal. As the Lord says in Bhagavad-gītā (4.9) : janma karma ca me divyam evaṁ yo vetti tattvataḥ tyaktvā dehaṁ punar janma naiti mām eti so ’rjuna “One who knows the transcendental nature of My appearance and activities does not, upon leaving the body, take his birth again in this material world, but attains My eternal abode, O Arjuna.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    After the departure of the great saint Nārada, Kaṁsa thought that all the members of the Yadu dynasty were demigods and that any of the children born from the womb of Devakī might be Viṣṇu. Fearing his death, Kaṁsa arrested Vasudeva and Devakī and chained them with iron shackles. Suspecting each of the children to be Viṣṇu, Kaṁsa killed them one after another because of the prophecy that Viṣṇu would kill him.
    Commentary

    Kamsa heard that Visnu who had been his enemy in a previous life, would now be born in the womb of Devaki and would kill him. Hearing from the mouth of Narada, Kamsa believed this. Out of fear of Visnu (ajana, one who has no birth) he killed the children as soon as they were born.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Nārada went particularly far away (vinirgame) because of shame at having directly put Vasudeva in prison, and because Kaṁsa feared he may return to prevent his actions. Kaṁsa understood that the Yadus were the Lord’s associates and that Viṣṇu born with all powers (saṁbhūtam) from Devakī to kill him. Past tense is used for the future event because the time was close or because the event was certain. Or Kaṁsa thought that Viṣṇu who possesses all powers (sambhūtam) was in Devakī’s womb. Another version has sambhūtim. Kaṁsa understood from Nārada that the eighth child of Devakī would kill him and that the relatives were making preparations to kill him. ttatraiṣa devakī yā te mathurāyāṁ pitṛṣvasā yo ‘syā garbho ‘ṣṭamaḥ kaṁsa sa te mṛtyur bhaviṣyati devānāṁ caiva sarvasvaṁ tridivasya gatiś ca saḥ paraṁ rahasyaṁ vedānāṁ sa te mṛtyur bhaviṣyati parato ‘pi paras teṣam svayaṁbhūś ca divaukasām tatas tv etan mahadbhūtaṁ divyam te kathayāmy aham ślāghaśca sa hi te mṛtyur bhūta-pūrvaś ca taṁ smara O Kaṁsa! You will be killed by the eighth child of Devakī, your sister, in Mathurā. He who is the goal of the devatās and the secret of the Vedas will kill you. He is superior to the devatās and without birth. I am telling you this astonishing, divine news. He killed you in the past. Remember that. Piṭrṣvasā means sister related through the father. Some say that Āhuka, Devaka’s father raised Devakī, his granddaughter as his own child. Nigṛhya means imprisoned in Kaṁsa’s house. Ajana means a person who is without birth. Kaṁsa thought he would be born like a normal child. This word thus indicates Kaṁsa’s foolishness. Or it indicates fear of something which was perhaps non-existent.

    Personal Guidance
    Kaṁsa's fearful slaughter only hastened Kṛṣṇa's appearance — the demon's defenses cannot stop the Lord, who takes birth (ajana) only to protect and to slay.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice where fear of losing your position drives you to harm others, and refuse one such pre-emptive 'killing' today — a cutting word, a guarded silence, a withheld opportunity.
    • Read or recite BG 4.9 (janma karma ca me divyam) once today and consciously meditate that Kṛṣṇa's birth and acts are transcendental, not ordinary.
    • Identify one 'iron shackle' you have placed on a devotee or family member out of suspicion, and deliberately loosen it through a concrete act of trust.
    Reflection Questions
    • Kaṁsa believed that by killing each newborn he could outwit a prophecy from the Lord — where in my own life am I expending enormous effort to control an outcome that is not actually mine to determine?
    • The verse hinges on ajana — Viṣṇu, the unborn, who appears nonetheless as a child of Devakī; what assumption am I still carrying that Kṛṣṇa must conform to my categories of how the divine should or should not act?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Identify your own 'Kaṁsa-list' — the people or possibilities you treat as threats to the future you have planned (the rival classmate, the friend who is doing better than you on Instagram, the parent's expectation, the GPA that 'must' stay above a number). Write the list. Notice that fear of losing your imagined future is the engine.
    • This week, when peer pressure tells you to 'shackle' someone with gossip, exclusion, or a cutting comment to protect your own social position, name it silently as the Kaṁsa-impulse and refuse it once. Just once. Tell a sādhu-saṅga friend afterwards.
    • Pick one decision you are currently making out of fear of an outcome (choosing a major, ghosting someone, hiding a struggle from your parents) and ask: what would I do if I trusted that Kṛṣṇa, not my prediction, governs the result? Then do that thing today — not after graduation, today.
    householder
    • Audit one 'iron shackle' you have placed in your home this month — the controlling rule with your teenager, the financial leash on your spouse, the silent treatment after a disagreement. Remove it deliberately, and notice what fear surfaces in you when you do. That fear is your work.
    • In a major family decision this week (school for a child, a job change, money for an aging parent), explicitly distinguish material compassion (their comfort, their career, their bodily ease) from real compassion (their soul's progress toward Kṛṣṇa). Choose the action that serves the second even when it costs the first. Do this once, with full awareness, before you generalize it.
    • Each evening for one week, sit with your spouse for five minutes and offer the day's actions and their results to Kṛṣṇa together. Not as ritual — as the practical refusal of the Kaṁsa-illusion that you are the controller of your family's fate.
    senior
    • Name the prophecies you have been living under — 'I will be forgotten,' 'my children will not call,' 'my body will fail and I will be a burden.' These are your private versions of Kaṁsa's prophecy. Write them down and read them aloud once. The naming itself loosens their grip.
    • Choose one attachment you have been quietly chaining — a property, a role in the family, a grudge you have nursed for decades, a skill you refuse to hand on because then 'they won't need me.' Begin the act of release this week: transfer one document, train one successor, speak one forgiveness. Tyāga is practiced in concrete handovers, not in feelings.
    • Mentor one younger person not toward worldly success but toward Kṛṣṇa — share one verse, one purport, one story from your own sādhana. Do this without expecting they will become 'devotional' on your timeline. The offering is the point; the fruit belongs to Him.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading Kaṁsa as merely 'the bad guy' and missing the mirror — the same fearful, calculating ahaṅkāra that chains Devakī and Vasudeva operates in us whenever we try to eliminate every threat to our position rather than surrender to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Treating Nārada's role as cruel or duplicitous; the student concludes 'so deception is fine if the end is good' instead of recognizing that only a pure devotee, acting under Kṛṣṇa's direct arrangement, can play such a role — it is not a template for our conduct.
    • Taking ajana-śaṅkayā as license for impersonalism — 'see, Viṣṇu has no real birth, so His form is symbolic' — when the verse and purport teach the opposite: He genuinely appears in a transcendental form (mānuṣīṁ tanum āśritam), and knowing this in tattva is what liberates.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Nārada deliberately fed Kaṁsa information that he knew would lead Kaṁsa to commit more sin and hasten Kṛṣṇa's appearance. Share with your partner: was this compassion or cruelty? Where in your own life have you confused 'being nice' (material compassion for the body) with actually serving someone's soul? Push each other — don't settle for an easy reconciliation.
    • Kaṁsa heard the prophecy and responded with iron shackles and infanticide. We rarely chain anyone, but we do react to perceived threats with control — micromanaging a spouse, surveilling a child's phone, hoarding money against an imagined future. Name one specific 'iron shackle' you have placed on someone you love because of fear of your own loss. Did your partner help you see one you hadn't named?
    • The verse insists that Viṣṇu is aja — never born — yet appears to take birth. Some in your group will find this a beautiful mystery; others will call it a contradiction or a face-saving theological move. Argue both sides honestly for ten minutes. What is actually at stake for a sādhaka if Kṛṣṇa's birth is 'just like ours' versus divyam (transcendental)?
    Role Play

    Two students. Student A is a parent whose adult child has just announced they are leaving a stable career to pursue full-time bhakti service in a temple far from home. Student A has spent twenty years building security for this child and feels the prophecy of their own old-age abandonment coming true. Student B is a senior devotee Student A has come to for counsel. Student A must voice the Kaṁsa-impulse honestly — the urge to 'shackle,' to threaten withdrawal of inheritance, to predict ruin, to manufacture obstacles 'for the child's own good.' Student B must distinguish, in real time, between material compassion (protecting the child's body and career) and real compassion (serving the child's soul), without becoming preachy. Run for eight minutes, then swap roles. Debrief: where did the Kaṁsa-logic sound most reasonable? Where did it expose itself as fear of personal loss dressed up as love?

    Objections & Responses
    • Nārada Muni knowingly provoked Kaṁsa into killing six infants. By any modern ethical standard — and frankly by the Gītā's own emphasis on ahiṁsā — that makes Nārada complicit in mass murder. How can a Gauḍīya teacher defend this without sounding like an apologist for cruelty?
      Stay with the discomfort — don't rush past it. The Gauḍīya answer is not 'the ends justify the means.' It is that Nārada sees what we do not: those infants are not annihilated, they are liberated souls returning to Kṛṣṇa's eternal abode (the Bhāgavatam later identifies them as Marīci's sons completing a curse). Kaṁsa's body-vision sees murder; Nārada's tattva-vision sees the soul's passage, exactly the dhīra-dṛṣṭi the Gītā cultivates. The objection assumes the body is the person — the very assumption the verse is dismantling. A Gauḍīya teacher does not deny the horror of Kaṁsa's act; he points out that calling Nārada complicit requires us to first agree with Kaṁsa about what a person is. We don't.
    • This whole framing — 'Viṣṇu is never born but appears to be born' — sounds like theological cope. Either Kṛṣṇa was born like a human or He wasn't. Saying both feels like a way to keep the comforting story while protecting the doctrine.
      It feels that way only if we assume birth means one thing. The verse teaches the opposite: divyam janma — a category of birth that is not the soul's forced entry into a body driven by past karma, but a free, conscious descent of the Lord in His own eternal form. Mānuṣīṁ tanum āśritam — He takes a humanlike form, He does not become bound by it. The test is not philosophical neatness; it is the verse Prabhupāda quotes: janma karma ca me divyam evaṁ yo vetti tattvataḥ — one who knows this in tattva is not born again. That is a falsifiable claim about your own life, not a doctrinal hedge. A Gauḍīya teacher would ask: are you willing to let the verse work on you long enough to test it, or are you settling the question before you have lived with it?
    Analogy

    After Nārada's departure, Kaṁsa concludes that all the Yadus are demigods and any child of Devakī may be Viṣṇu. He arrests Vasudeva and Devakī in iron shackles and, suspecting each newborn to be Viṣṇu, kills them one by one. The verse describes the asura's reasoning under existential threat — accurate at every step, and lethal at every step. The Bhāgavata teaches: correct information without surrender produces only more efficient cruelty.

    Important Words
    • ghnanti — they kill
      Third plural present of han, 'kill.' The verse uses the present tense: this is the ongoing condition, not a one-time event. Greed-driven kings kill, generation after generation. The Bhāgavata's social diagnosis is timeless.
    • asu-tṛpaḥ — those who envy the lives of others for their personal sense gratification
      Asu (life-breath) + tṛp (satisfy). 'Those who satisfy themselves by [taking] others' lives.' Bhāgavata names a specific psychological type: the asu-tṛp, whose sense-gratification is bound up with others' loss. Bhakti's offer: have tṛpti from Bhagavān, not from others' bodies.
    • lubdhāḥ — greedy
      From lubh, 'to covet.' The asu-tṛp is named precisely as lubdha — greedy. Bhāgavata's mode-analysis: lobha is one of the six enemies (kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, mātsarya). When lobha rules a king, the kingdom becomes a hunting ground.
    • rājānaḥ — such kings
      Plural of rājan. The verse generalizes: rājānaḥ. Not 'a king' — kings, plural. The Bhāgavata refuses individual exceptionalism; the pattern is structural. Kaṁsa is one instance of a recurring social phenomenon, and the warning extends to every age.
    Kings greedy for sense gratification on this earth almost always kill their enemies indiscriminately. To satisfy their own whims, they may kill anyone, even their mothers, fathers, brothers or friends.
    Purport

    We have seen in the history of India that Aurangzeb killed his brother and nephews and imprisoned his father to fulfill political ambitions. There have been many similar instances, and Kaṁsa was the same type of king. Kaṁsa did not hesitate to kill his nephews and imprison his sister and his father. For demons to do such things is not astonishing. Nonetheless, although Kaṁsa was a demon, he was aware that Lord Viṣṇu cannot be killed, and thus he attained salvation. Even partial understanding of the activities of Lord Viṣṇu makes one eligible for salvation. Kaṁsa knew a little about Kṛṣṇa — that He could not be killed — and therefore he attained salvation although he thought of Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, as an enemy. What then is to be said of one who knows Kṛṣṇa perfectly from the descriptions of śāstras like Bhagavad-gītā ? It is therefore the duty of everyone to read Bhagavad-gītā and understand Kṛṣṇa perfectly. This will make one’s life successful.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Kings greedy for sense gratification on this earth almost always kill their enemies indiscriminately. To satisfy their own whims, they may kill anyone, even their mothers, fathers, brothers or friends.
    Commentary

    This was not a surprising action for evil men like Kamsa. That is the intention of this verse. What to speak of killing father, brothers, and friends, they will kill even their own mothers. The order of seriousness is from first (mother) to last (friend).

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “Was Kaṁsa not ashamed of killing a baby?” This verse answers. The list begins with the person invoking the most affection, the mother. Greedy kings, to satisfy their own life airs (asutṛpaḥ), greedy for kingdoms, kill even their mother, what to speak of their father and others. Prāyaśaḥ means that not all kings act in this manner. Thus it shows Kaṁsa’s extreme debasement.

    Personal Guidance
    Unchecked greed for sense gratification will make a king strike down even his own kin — guard your heart from the lubdha-rāja sleeping inside you.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today the one relationship you are quietly willing to bruise to protect a personal ambition, and name that ambition out loud as lobha.
    • Refuse to wield any small 'kingship' you hold — over a sibling, employee, or child — to extract sense gratification, and instead use that authority to serve them.
    • Before each meal or purchase today, pause and ask whether this is santoṣa or asu-tṛp (insatiable craving), and offer the act to Kṛṣṇa to break the demoniac pattern.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my own life have I quietly justified harming someone close to me — in word, withheld attention, or broken trust — because some 'whim' of mine (status, comfort, ambition) demanded it?
    • If even Kaṁsa attained salvation through partial awareness of Kṛṣṇa as an enemy, what excuse can I offer for not studying Bhagavad-gītā seriously, given the access I have been given?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the next time you 'unfollow,' freeze out, or talk down a friend who became inconvenient to your image, your group, or your goals — that is the small-scale Kaṁsa instinct (asutṛpa, lubdhā) operating through your phone.
    • During exam season or a competitive internship hunt, write down one thing you would not do to win — a classmate you would not undermine, a parent you would not lie to, a value you would not trade. Tape it where you study. The verse exists because in heat, people forget.
    • Pick one Sanskrit term from the related values — santoṣa or brahmacharya — and apply it for one week to a single appetite (scrolling, snacking, gossip, hookups). Notice what happens to your study, sleep, and relationships when one viṣaya is restrained.
    householder
    • Audit one major family decision from the last year — a move, a school, a career jump, a property matter — and ask honestly: whose interests did I subordinate, and did I tell myself a story to make it sound noble? This is how lubdhā hides inside 'providing for the family.'
    • When money or inheritance discussions come up with parents or siblings, name the Kaṁsa-temptation out loud (at least to yourself) before the meeting: 'I will be tempted to maximize my share and call it fairness.' Naming it weakens it; pretending it isn't there strengthens it.
    • Each evening, in front of the family altar, offer the day's earnings and decisions to Kṛṣṇa explicitly — not as ritual, but as a check on whether the day's work would embarrass you to lay before Him. If it would, that is the verse's warning landing on your own household.
    senior
    • Look at your will, your estate plan, your unfinished conversations with adult children — where are you still holding power as leverage (over inheritance, approval, time)? The verse warns that even at the end, the king-instinct grasps. Loosen one grip this month: a conversation forgiven, a clause simplified, a possession given early.
    • Where you once might have crushed a rival in business, family, or community to get your way, now mentor someone you would once have seen as competition. This reverses the asutṛpa current — you become the opposite of the king in the verse: one whose remaining strength feeds others rather than consumes them.
    • Meditate daily on the fact that Kaṁsa, for all his crimes, attained salvation through constant remembrance of Viṣṇu (even fearful) — and resolve that your remembrance, with the time you have left, will be loving and unbroken. Memorize one verse from the related list (BG 12.6 or 2.62) and let it run under your day.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this verse as being about 'other people' — corrupt politicians, historical tyrants like Aurangzeb or Kaṁsa — and missing that asutṛpa lubdhā (greed for sense gratification) names the same impulse that runs my own day.
    • Concluding from Kaṁsa's salvation that thinking of Kṛṣṇa as an enemy is a viable path; the verse is meant to shame us into proper sādhana, not license casual or adversarial God-consciousness.
    • Treating 'read Bhagavad-gītā' as an intellectual checkbox — collecting verses and translations — instead of letting daily study actually restrain the lubdhā tendencies the verse exposes.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Kaṁsa imprisoned his father and killed his nephews to secure his throne. Where in your own life have you (or someone you respect) sacrificed a relationship — even subtly — for ambition, comfort, or reputation? Was the cost visible at the time, or only later?
    • The verse claims that 'kings greedy for sense gratification' will 'almost always' kill even kin. Do you actually believe ordinary people are this corruptible when power and viṣaya are on the table, or is this Vyāsa exaggerating? Argue both sides honestly in your pair.
    • Prabhupāda says even Kaṁsa attained salvation because he knew Viṣṇu could not be killed — while many 'devotees' who think of Kṛṣṇa as friend may not. What does this do to your idea of what qualifies someone for liberation? Does it make you more confident or more uneasy about your own sādhana?
    Role Play

    Two students play siblings inheriting a family business after their father's death. One sibling (the 'Kaṁsa figure') wants to push the elderly mother into a care facility she doesn't want, buy out the other sibling at below-market value, and pivot the business in a direction the father explicitly opposed — all justified as 'necessary for growth.' The other sibling must respond not with modern legal/ethical arguments alone but from the standpoint of this verse: name what is actually happening (lubdhā, asutṛpa — greed for sense gratification dressed as pragmatism), and try to help the brother see it without moralizing. The class then debates: at what exact line did practical ambition cross into the territory the verse warns about?

    Objections & Responses
    • This verse is just ancient political cynicism — 'all kings are murderous tyrants.' It has nothing to say to me; I'm not running a kingdom and I'm not killing anyone.
      Read 'king' as anyone with power over others — a manager, a parent, the head of a household, even the manager of your own senses. The verse isn't a sociology of monarchy; it's a diagnosis of what unrestrained viṣaya-tṛṣṇā does to a person who has the means to act on it. You may not literally kill, but ask honestly: whose flourishing have you quietly traded away — a parent's wishes ignored, a sibling's share quietly reduced, a friend dropped because they became inconvenient — to feed something you wanted? The verse names that pattern. Without brahmacharya and santoṣa, the same logic that produced Kaṁsa produces the smaller Kaṁsas we each carry.
    • If even Kaṁsa — a child-murderer — got salvation just by thinking of Viṣṇu (even as enemy), then the whole moral apparatus of the tradition collapses. Why bother with sādhana, sva-dharma, restraint?
      This is the classic misreading, and Prabhupāda anticipates it. Kaṁsa's 'salvation' came at a terrible price — a life consumed by fear, paranoia, the murder of his own kin, and finally death at Kṛṣṇa's hand. He attained mukti despite that life, not because of it, and only because his constant, fearful meditation on Viṣṇu happened to be uninterrupted. You and I do not have that kind of obsessive concentration on Kṛṣṇa even in devotion, let alone in enmity. The purport's actual punchline is the opposite of permissive: if even partial, hostile knowledge of Kṛṣṇa liberates, then how foolish to neglect the Bhagavad-gītā, which offers full, loving knowledge. The point is not 'sin is fine' but 'do not waste the rare gift of being able to know Him favorably.'
    Analogy

    Greedy kings, the verse observes, will kill anyone — mother, father, brother, friend — to satisfy their sense gratification. Kaṁsa is being placed in a general category, not singled out. The Bhāgavata is doing political theology: power without surrender produces the same fruit in every age. The verse's sober tone is a warning to every devotee tempted to think kingship is itself a problem solver.

    Important Words
    • kālanemim — by the name Kālanemi
      Kāla (time) + nemi (rim of a wheel). 'The rim of the wheel of time.' The asura whose name embeds time's wheel is himself caught on it. Etymology as theology: Kālanemi's very name announces his bondage.
    • viṣṇunā hatam — was killed by Lord Viṣṇu
      Viṣṇunā (instrumental of Viṣṇu) + hata (past participle, 'killed'). Bhagavān as the agent of the prior killing. Kaṁsa learns that the same person killed him before. The verse's grammatical irony: knowing your killer's identity does not, by itself, save you.
    • yadubhiḥ — with the members of the Yadu dynasty
      Instrumental plural of Yadu. The Yadus, who house the future Kṛṣṇa, become Kaṁsa's blanket enemy. Bhāgavata: the asuric reflex is to enlarge the target — from the prophesied eighth child to the entire dynasty. Mātsarya grows by enlargement.
    • vyarudhyata — acted inimically
      Vi + rudh, 'opposed.' Imperfect. Kaṁsa actively opposed the Yadus. The verse closes with the verb of his ongoing posture — vyarudhyata, he-was-opposing. The asuric life is grammatically active, perpetually pushed against.
    In his previous birth, Kaṁsa had been a great demon named Kālanemi and been killed by Viṣṇu. Upon learning this information from Nārada, Kaṁsa became envious of everyone connected with the Yadu dynasty.
    Purport

    Persons who are demons, enemies of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, are called asuras. As stated in Bhagavad-gītā, the asuras, because of their enmity toward the Supreme Personality of Godhead, take birth after birth in asura families and therefore glide down to the darkest hellish regions.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    In his previous birth, Kaṁsa had been a great demon named Kālanemi and been killed by Viṣṇu. Upon learning this information from Nārada, Kaṁsa became envious of everyone connected with the Yadu dynasty.
    Commentary

    Knowing from Narada that he had previously as Kalanemi been killed by Visnu and had now been born as Kamsa in Mathura, he made the Yadus his enemies. Surasena indicates Mathura, which is within Surasena. Thus the statement "He enjoyed Surasena:" means "He enjoyed Mathura and the surrounding lands."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He was previously killed by Viṣṇu, the Lord who spreads himself throughout the universe by his powers. This indicates Viṣṇu’ṣ ability to kill him. Kaṁsa was able to remember his previous birth because of Nārada’s statement bhūtapūṛvaṁ ca tam smara: remember that previous birth.

    Personal Guidance
    Envy of Kṛṣṇa and His devotees is not a passing mood — it is a karmic posture that follows the asura from birth to birth.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice the first flicker of envy when a devotee is praised today, and immediately offer a silent praṇāma to Kṛṣṇa instead of feeding the thought.
    • Refuse to align yourself — in speech, humor, or sympathy — with anyone mocking the Yadu-paramparā of devotees Kṛṣṇa claims as His own.
    • Before sleep, name one resentment you carried today and consciously hand it to Kṛṣṇa, so it does not harden into the asura-saṁskāra Kaṁsa carried across lives.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I, like Kaṁsa, nursing an old grievance — treating someone connected to a past wound as an enemy today, rather than seeing them as a soul before me?
    • When I learn something about my own past (a failure, a karmic debt, a previous defeat), do I respond with vairāgya and surrender to Kṛṣṇa, or do I respond like an asura — by sharpening my enmity and plotting against the very people Kṛṣṇa has placed near me?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the next time you feel a flash of envy when a classmate or someone in your feed gets recognition — name it as matsaratva, not 'I just don't like them.' Naming it honestly is the first cut against the Kaṁsa-pattern.
    • Audit one group you have written off wholesale — a clique at school, a 'type' of person on social media, students from a rival college. Choose one individual from that group this week and have a real conversation; refuse the dynasty-level grudge.
    • When you learn something unflattering about yourself (from a teacher, a parent, a hard piece of feedback), do not weaponize it the way Kaṁsa weaponized Nārada's news. Take it to your japa or to a senior devotee within twenty-four hours, before the ahaṅkāra builds a story around it.
    householder
    • Watch for blanket resentments at work — 'that whole department,' 'those vendors,' 'people from that background.' These are the householder's version of resenting the Yadus. Each week, identify one and replace it with a specific, named, person-by-person assessment.
    • In family life, do not pass dynasty-grudges to your children. If there is a cousin's family, an in-law's circle, or a community you carry old enmity toward, decide deliberately what you will and will not say in front of the kids — they inherit the matsaratva otherwise.
    • When a peer is promoted, praised, or prospering — especially someone you quietly compete with — perform one concrete act of honor toward them within the week (a sincere message, a referral, an introduction). Use vairāgya from the fruit of your own work (BG 2.47) as the fuel.
    senior
    • Old enmities calcify with age. Make a list of people and groups you have carried lifelong resentment toward; before this body is given up, take one off the list each month through a letter, a call, or sincere internal forgiveness offered before the Deity.
    • Kaṁsa's tragedy was that knowledge of his past did not soften him — it sharpened his enmity. As you reflect on your own life-review, watch for the same temptation: do not let memoir become a ledger of grievances. Let it become an offering.
    • Mentor the young in your family or community away from dynasty-grudges — the 'we don't deal with those people' inheritances. Your final teaching is what you refuse to pass on, as much as what you pass on.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this verse as ancient mythology about one demon king, rather than recognizing the same asuric pattern — birth-after-birth enmity toward Kṛṣṇa and His devotees — as a tendency latent in one's own ahaṅkāra.
    • Mistaking Kaṁsa's daksya and tejas (his sharpness, his vigour, his strategic intelligence) as virtues in themselves; these qualities, divorced from devotion to Kṛṣṇa, only deepen the descent into darker regions, not elevate the practitioner.
    • Using the doctrine of asuric birth-after-birth to write off difficult people in one's life as 'demons,' thereby justifying one's own envy and hostility toward them — the very mood of Kaṁsa — instead of examining where that asuric mood lives in oneself.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Kaṁsa learned of his past life as Kālanemi and used that knowledge to deepen his enmity. Share with your partner: when you have learned something true about yourself (a tendency, a past pattern), did it move you toward Kṛṣṇa or did it harden a familiar identity? Disagree if you must — is self-knowledge automatically purifying?
    • Prabhupāda says asuras take birth after birth in asura families and 'glide down to the darkest hellish regions.' Discuss: does this mean a person born into a demonic environment has no agency? Where does the line fall between saṁskāra and choice? Push back on each other.
    • The verse shows envy (matsaratva) directed at an entire dynasty — not one person but everyone connected to the Yadus. In your own life, name a group (a profession, a community, a family) toward whom you carry blanket resentment. Is that envy a 'small' character flaw or, as the Bhāgavatam suggests, the seed of asura-bhāva?
    Role Play

    Two students. Student A is a longtime devotee who has just been passed over for a service role they wanted; the role went to a newer devotee from a well-connected family. Student B is their friend. A vents: 'It's always those people — the whole circle protects each other.' B must respond not with therapy-speak ('your feelings are valid') and not with spiritual bypass ('just chant more'), but as a Gauḍīya friend who has read SB 10.1.68 — naming the Kaṁsa-pattern of resenting an entire group, while still honoring the real hurt. Run the scene for five minutes; then swap and run it again with B as the venter.

    Objections & Responses
    • Past-life karma is unfalsifiable. Saying Kaṁsa was Kālanemi in a previous birth, and that this 'explains' his envy, is just a story to make demons seem cosmically demonic. It removes responsibility from upbringing, trauma, social conditions — the things we can actually study and address.
      The Bhāgavatam is not offering a sociological explanation in competition with psychology; it is showing the depth of the disease. Upbringing and trauma are real — Kṛṣṇa Himself accepts that the guṇas act on the embodied soul (BG 13.1, 3.21). What past-life continuity adds is sobering, not exculpating: the ahaṅkāra you nurse today is not new, and it will not end with this body unless you take shelter. Far from removing responsibility, it raises the stakes of this human birth. The point is not 'Kaṁsa couldn't help it' — the point is that envy of the Lord and His devotees, left unchecked across lifetimes, hardens into asura-svabhāva. Look honestly at your own recurring resentments before dismissing the diagnosis.
    • Calling people 'asuras' and consigning them to 'the darkest hellish regions' is exactly the kind of in-group / out-group thinking that makes religion dangerous. It dehumanizes opponents.
      Notice what the verse actually condemns: not a race, not a caste, not a rival sect — it condemns enmity toward the Supreme Personality of Godhead and His devotees. Asura is a diagnosis of a disposition, not a label slapped on people we dislike. Prabhupāda himself, in the line of Caitanya Mahāprabhu, taught that even the lowest can be elevated by the holy name; the Yadus did not exterminate Kaṁsa's family, Kṛṣṇa took that act on Himself for a precise purpose. The Gauḍīya teacher's job is to recognize asura-bhāva first within one's own heart — the matsaratva that flares when a 'rival' is praised — and to treat it with sādhana, not to go hunting outward for asuras to denounce. Used that way, the category protects against in-group cruelty rather than authorizing it.
    Analogy

    Nārada informs Kaṁsa that in his previous birth he was the great demon Kālanemi, killed by Viṣṇu. With this memory installed, Kaṁsa becomes envious of everyone connected to the Yadus. The verse stages the cost of knowing one's previous lives without surrender: the asura now has, in his current body, the resentment of his previous body's death added on. Past-life knowledge without bhakti is a curse, not a gift.

    Stories
    Kālanemi in the Rāmāyaṇa

    Kālanemi appears in the Rāmāyaṇa (Yuddha-kāṇḍa) as the demon Rāvaṇa sends to obstruct Hanumān as Hanumān is rushing back from the Himalayas with the saṁjīvanī herb to save Lakṣmaṇa.

    Kālanemi disguises himself as a sage and attempts to delay Hanumān; Hanumān, after initially being deceived, sees through it and kills him. The asura who tried to obstruct the rescue of the Lord's brother is reborn here as Kaṁsa — the asura who will obstruct the appearance of the Lord Himself.

    The verse is a tight piece of cross-canonical narrative: Bhāgavata records Rāmāyaṇa's villain, reborn for a second round. The Lord's killing of an asura is not the asura's end; without surrender, the body changes but the enmity persists. Bhakti is the only termination of the saṁsāric series.
